title: Buffalo Bills superfans: Rise of the Skarekrow
summary: The armor has been coming along great. There have been some delays (some valid, some me just getting caught up in other things). The delays have not been without their benefits though. Delays mean I’m thinking and if I’m thinking, I’m planning. That’s led to refinements for the things I originally intended to build, and […]
full_text: The armor has been coming along great. There have been some delays (some valid, some me just getting caught up in other things). The delays have not been without their benefits though. Delays mean I’m thinking and if I’m thinking, I’m planning. That’s led to refinements for the things I originally intended to build, and also some side quests as I’ve thought of other things to build. For some reason it started bothering me that I didn’t have a melee weapon designed for this kit. Like… really bothering me. An idea started formulating and at some point the dam burst and I started building. You reap what you Krow For full disclosure, my first thought for a melee weapon was to make a functional vibro-blade prop. Does everyone know the lore on the vibro-blades? Just in case you don’t, in Star Wars, one of the precursors to the lightsaber were vibro-weapons. The premise is that the blade vibrates at such an intense frequency that it becomes sharp enough to cut through nearly anything. Wonder why Din Djarin was able to drop the mudhorn with his knife? Oscillations! I had a good plan for it too. Buy a cheap razor handle that has a vibrating head and affix a plastic blade to it. Then I learned that a company in Seattle has literally made a vibro-knife. I’m not kidding. Here it is . As an aside, if any Good Samaritan wants to buy me one for Wingin’ It, I’m happy to share my Venmo. Back on track, I can’t compete with that. I needed another angle. Something Krow-riffic. I’ll be candid again. When the idea dam burst I was thinking I was making a prototype. It started off way chonkier than what you see above. I grabbed some extra plastic and cut it into five strips. One for the blade and four for the handle. It was a flawed sheet, with a warp in the middle. I used it anyway because I wanted to test if I could make a folding blade on this that locked. Turns out, the answer was “yes.” Once I had the chonky version I noticed something. Those warps created a natural swell in the handle that made it very comfortable and helped balance it by placing a little extra weight in the middle. So I started shaping the handle like what you just saw. Then I started refining the shape. And it was clear that those warps were here to stay. My test build turned into the final build surprisingly easily. All that was left was paint. It’s not perfect. I could have sanded some things better. I could have buffed out the scrape I added in accidentally. That said, the imperfections match the rest of the armor’s “found” look. Now fans of the show might immediately consider me a blasphemer. Din Djarin acquires a beskar spear and when The Armorer sees it (spoiler alert), she insists it be melted down. Why? A beskar weapon is a threat to beskar armor and it could “fall into the wrong hands” and be used against a Mandalorian. Well I say “screw that” for two reasons. The Armorer makes whistling birds for Din Djarin which require beskar. Has anyone read the lore on those? They’re armor piercing micro-missiles that target carotid arteries and detonate. That’s right, they’re horrifying. Tiny assassin missiles that could wipe out a squad of Mandalorians with the push of a button but Din Djarin can’t have a spear? Riiiiiiiiiight You know what else works well against a Mandalorian set of armor? Explosions. You see it in the first season of the show. Din Djarin nearly dies due to head injury inflicted through his helmet thanks to explosions around him. You know who has access to explosions? Literally everyone. So guess what, I’m making a beskar sickle. Mandalorian x Bills mashup – Sickle pic.twitter.com/Z5bNEHsBf6 — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 20, 2026 There’s a good look at the full build, locking mechanism, middle swell, imperfections, and all. You might have noticed that the blade has some copper in it. A fun fact I dug up while researching Mandalorian customs is that most armor is actually beskar alloy which got my brain thinking. The spear Din Djarin used was fairly rigid, as is the armor. I wonder if it’s not a flexible steel. That doesn’t work well for this type of blade so mine is an alloy. There’s a higher “copper” concentration on the spine of the “blade” which should increase overall flexibility while the full beskar edge retains cutting ability. You see what I warned you about at the beginning? I tend to overthink things. One thing I didn’t need to overthink was which “not a knife” small weapon to use. You might say this was a natural fit. Bills x Mandalorian mashup – Hand fit pic.twitter.com/hIbWK1BQku — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 20, 2026 And if you happened to wonder what the chonky version looked like, here it is in all its glory; co-starring the cat that necessitated the litter that supplied the buckets. Bills x Mandalorian mashup – Chonky pic.twitter.com/QjhBrlSbX0 — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) July 20, 2026

title: Bills’ legend Steve Tasker’s Hall of Fame chances just shrank even further
summary: The Pro Football Hall of Fame announced sweeping changes to their voting process on Friday, and it’s going to make the eventual induction of former Buffalo Bills special teams ace Steve Tasker even more difficult. There will no longer be a separate pool of senior nominees who missed selection during their 15-year eligibility window. All […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - JANUARY 6: Punt returner Steve Tasker #89 of the Buffalo Bills is pursued by linebacker Jerry Olsavsky #55 of the Pittsburgh Steelers as he runs with the football during a playoff game at Three Rivers Stadium on January 6, 1996 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. The Steelers defeated the Bills 40-21.(Photo by George Gojkovich/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pro Football Hall of Fame announced sweeping changes to their voting process on Friday, and it’s going to make the eventual induction of former Buffalo Bills special teams ace Steve Tasker even more difficult. There will no longer be a separate pool of senior nominees who missed selection during their 15-year eligibility window. All players who haven’t played in the past five years will be considered together for induction into the Hall of Fame. Previously, as a senior candidate, the selection committee narrowed it from 25 candidates to 9 semifinalists. Then two were put forward to a vote of the full committee. All former players will now fight for 13 semifinalist spots (down from 15 PLUS the 9 senior nominees) and then that finalist list will be limited to a max of five. Finalists will still need 80% of the vote to make it into the Hall of Fame. Tasker was a Senior’s Committee semifinalist this past year, so it stands to reason he would have been among the seven most deserving candidates for that position this year. Instead of going head to head with seven guys, he will need to beat out every eligible player in NFL history for one of 13 semifinalist spots. In 2027, the competition is going to be fierce. First-time eligible players include Rob Gronkowski, Adrian Peterson, Ben Roethlisberger, Alex Mack, Richard Sherman, and Eric Weddle. Returning finalists from a year ago are Willie Anderson, Jahri Evans, Frank Gore, Torry Holt, Eli Manning, Terrell Suggs, Reggie Wayne, Kevin Williams, Jason Witten, Darren Woodson, and Marshal Yanda. Those names alone are more than 17 players for 13 finalist spots. The Hall of Fame (which is not an entity of the NFL) also shrank the number of voters from 50 to 25 plus three alternates. There will no longer be a Hall of Fame voter from all 32 NFL cities. There will still be one coach finalist and one contributor finalist every year. Those will now be an up/down vote with 80% needed to pass. Last year, Bill Belichick was left off the final list in favor of adding another player. Now, off-the-field finalists won’t compete for spots with on-field finalists. full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 10: DeWayne Carter #90 of the Buffalo Bills gestures to the crowd following a preseason game against the Chicago Bears at Highmark Stadium on August 10, 2024 in Orchard Park, New York. The Bears won 33-6. (Photo by Rich Barnes/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the Buffalo Bills announced their initial 53-man roster earlier this week, one of the popular topics focused on third year defensive tackle DeWayne Carter. Fans will recall that Carter was placed on injured reserve prior to the start of the 2025 season, missing the entire year with a torn Achilles. There is always plenty of conversation around who will make the 53-man roster, and Carter was understandably at the center of the defensive tackle discussion. In addition to coming back from an injury, there is a new defensive coaching staff in place that is being led by Jim Leonhard this season. It is understandable that there would be plenty to discuss, especially as Carter had a bit of an uneven rookie season while appearing in 11 games for the Bills. Carter has now added 20 pounds in order to play nose tackle for the Bills, and can be seen as an option to back-up Deone Walker in the middle of the defensive line. When I take all of these factors into consideration, I am OK with being a bit patient with Carrter this season. When coming off a season ending injury, while playing for a new coach, and transforming your body to play a new position – I can give you a bit of grace for this season. With that said, Carter will need to show incremental improvement as he transitions to more of a nose tackle position this season. Getting a jersey on gameday may be a bit of a challenge early this season with the recent signing of Greg Gaines, and it remains to be seen which of the two will serve as Walker’s primary backup. But as I mentioned earlier, the Bills can take some time to develop Carter as he continues his recovery and transformation. I know that some of our readers may feel differently on this subject, so feel free to weigh in below in the comments section.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 8 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - DECEMBER 01: Jordan Gross #69 of the Carolina Panthers during their game at Bank of America Stadium on December 1, 2013 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Streeter Lecka/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #8. Jordan Gross A lot of people who know football will tell you that outside of quarterback, a franchise left tackle is the most important and hardest position to lock in on an offense. The Panthers had that all through the 200s and into the 2010s with Jordan Gross. Gross’s early sports playing days are very typical of good offensive linemen. He’s from a rural state (Idaho), was a three sport athlete in high school, and was elite at all three sports. He was best at football, which earned him a scholarship to Utah, where he developed into an All American by his senior season. He built up enough of a resume to be selected with the eighth overall pick in the 2003 NFL Draft; he was the first offensive linemen off the board. Gross immediately provided return on that investment by starting at right tackle out of the gate. He played every offensive snap in his rookie season and established himself as an above average tackle right away. He would alternate between right tackle and left tackle each season for the first six years of his career, and it wasn’t until his sixth year that he would miss a start. In that season, he starred an offensive line that helped the Panthers to a top 10 offense despite being almost entirely built around the run game. He earned Pro Bowl and All Pro honors for his work that season. He would go on to earn two more Pro Bowl nominations while starting nearly every game for the Panthers over the next five seasons. He was as steady as could be throughout those years, even earning one of those Pro Bowl nominations in his final professional season in 2013. In all, Gross played in 167 games across his 11 year career in Carolina, starting every one of them. He was above average at his worst and elite at his best. Having that at left tackle for over a decade is something every team dreams of. In some ways, the Panthers have been continually trying to replace Gross since his retirement over 12 years ago. After his playing career came to a close, Gross stayed close to the organization, working as a sideline reporter for preseason games and hosting a Panthers-centric TV show with former teammate Travelle Wharton. He’s since returned home to coach football at his old high school and is now the offensive line coach at his alma mater. Gross’s 167 starts are the most in franchise history, and he has earned himself a spot in the Panthers Hall of Honor. His longevity, ability, and closeness to the franchise also earn him a spot at number eight on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

summary: Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! GooseCreek: When and if Ja’Tavion Sanders gets traded, who do you bring […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - JULY 23: Monroe Freeling #57 of the Carolina Panthers enters the field during the Carolina Panthers Training Camp at Carolina Panthers Practice Fields on July 23, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! I got flooded with questions following the fallout of final roster cutdowns, and now we’re on a collision course with the regular season. Let’s dive right in! GooseCreek: When and if Ja’Tavion Sanders gets traded, who do you bring into the Panthers 53 man roster? I’d like to see them bring in Ja’seem Reed to protect him from being poached from the practice squad. I actually do think the Panthers intend to carry 5 TEs for the moment on the active roster. But if they do end up trading Sanders away, I think they’ll bring up LB Tyrell Dodson, offensive line depth, or S Isaiah Simmons. I don’t think they are worried about Ja’seem Reed being poached otherwise they wouldn’t have waived him in the first place for the practice squad. storybook: Who’s winnin the superbowl? The Carolina Panthers, of course. But if not, I’d say possibly the Bills or Broncos. The Rams are everybody’s pick and that almost never works out for a “dream team”. Unless Tom Brady was involved of course. e4*: Will HRH Haynes (it is inevitable I will be) King assume his sovereignty by week 11? No. bolshy: I think both our offense and our defense will be better this year. Which one do you think makes the biggest improvement and why? I think the defense will take the biggest step forward. Added two high impact players on the front seven and built up the depth around it this off-season. DBelt: How many starts will Nick Scott have this season for the Panthers and will he finally receive the All Pro recognition he deserves? I expect him to start every game (just like he did last season) but unless he gets a bunch of picks I don’t expect him to make the All Pro team. That has just never been his game. PurrDurham: How much more improved is our defense with the two new linebackers and other post-cut day signings? My biggest concern for this defense was if they could weather an injury to one of their significant contributors. They appear to have the depth to do so now. That in itself is a huge improvement over last season. Panthers75: Using the app. You can now post photos in these threads. Very nice. Maybe thats old news, idk. I’ve been enjoying the real world since January. Which NFCS team improved the most over this past off-season? I’m glad you’re enjoying the app! I am very much enjoying it too! I would say the Saints were most improved unfortunately, but every team made some material upgrades. It will likely be another close race this season. @WTMealey: Bryce has 17 games to show he can be relatively good enough CONSISTENTLY Let’s say red is definitely moving on Yellow is the decision is difficult Green he’s getting a contract the only question is the details Paint a picture of each of these scenarios not with season long stats but more with x amount of games he does this and y amount of games he does that and….. I’m going to once again remind others (this does not apply to this question but others I have been receiving) that if you are not seeing your question answered about Bryce Young, a lot of times its because there was a derogatory tone to it. I’m perfectly fine with being critical of NFL players, but there’s enough discourse in the comments that turns very negative over a subject that likely isn’t going to change this season regardless of how you feel. Anyway, onto Mealey’s question. Red: We see Bryce Young take a step back to early 2024 form, very little consistency and the same up and down performance. Yellow: We see about the same version of Bryce Young from this past season, where some weeks he’s playing out of his mind and others he’s struggling against teams he shouldn’t be struggling against. Possibly another slow start but quickly gets back to the form we saw at times last season. We see a little more of the great version but still somewhat inconsistent. Green: We see Bryce Young take a big step forward, and we see playoffs Bryce more often than he struggles. I still expect there to be bad games, because its very rare not to have those, but more often than not he’s consistent and we see the ball getting chucked around. I’m not sure what version to expect but I am hopeful year 3 in the Canales/Idzik coaching tree will see more progress as one would expect. schrodingersblackcat: What are the odds our offense gets off to another rocky start next week, just as we have for the past three seasons? (Preseason hasn’t inspired much confidence that things will be different.) If we do struggle for the first few games, do you expect to see Idzik respond differently from the way Dave has in the past? I still do not take anything we see from the preseason’s limited reps with much more than a grain of salt. Week 1 is ugly for most teams so I can see that happening, but I’m not worried about it for the long term. I think Idzik/Canales should have a firmer grasp on what they feel works for their QB and this offense than they did in the previous two seasons, so if there’s lag in the offense getting into a groove I would expect them to add some plays to help get the offense into a rhythm. In theory, they should continue leaning on the run game like they have and that should help with things. Chef: Hey, Brian. So, with the roster looking pretty much finished, what’s the position group that we probably feel better about than we should and what group that doesn’t look so great on paper that is going to outperform expectations? I agree with Shifty Fish that EDGE has been promising but an injury to Jaelan Phillips or even the other two of the top three makes that position very dicey once again. Losing Nic Scourton really hurt things. As far as the position that people might be concerned about that I’m not, I would say running back. There was a bit of concern with Chuba Hubbard basically sitting out the off-season with a hamstring, and then Jonathon Brooks now dealing with soreness plus Trevor Etienne being put on IR. I think Hubbard and Brooks will be fine and they now have a true power back in AJ Dillon. I think running back is going to outperform people’s expectations and I think both Hubbard and Brooks will be productive and involved in the offense. Their skill-sets are different enough that they should compliment each other much better than Hubbard and Rico Dowdle did. DIESEL009: How good are our current starting OTs? Are we going to miss Moton and Ickey, or will they hold it down? I actually think Rasheed Walker at left tackle and Monroe Freelin at right tackle have been relatively solid, all things considered. Freeling is going to have growing pains, we saw that in the preseason, but here’s a pretty good breakdown on some of the film we got to see in the preseason. I think they’ll do just fine. I’m more concerned about an injury for now, but hopefully Taylor Moton will be back sooner than later. Ikem Ekwonu, we still don’t really know when he will be back but the team seems to think he will be. DeacCat: Who will our leading rusher he this year? Pepsi or Coke? I think Chuba Hubbard will end up being the leading rusher but I could see Jonathon Brooks having the most yards from scrimmage. He brings the receiving element that Chuba just doesn’t have, so I could see him getting quite a few passing and manufactured touches. I’m definitely a Coke guy. Vanilla Coke to be precise. Mozzie11: For roster building, do you stick with Pickett who has experience but will probably not be able to advance the team anywhere if he has to play any extended time. Or do you look to the future and replace him with Levis or Milton knowing having to use either this year is more of a crap shoot? I don’t see any reason you move on from the guy who spent…

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 9 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - NOVEMBER 29: Jake Delhomme #17 of the Carolina Panthers passes against the New York Jets at Giants Stadium on November 29, 2009 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Nick Laham/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #9. Jake Delhomme We’re inside the top 10 now, which means we’ve got fan favorites all over the place. Today, we look at one of the most widely liked fan favorites of all time, the Ragin’ Cajun himself, Jake Delhomme. Delhomme had one of the more unlikely rises to starting NFL quarterback that you’ll ever see, though in hindsight, there were some early signs of future success. He played college football at what was then known as Southwestern Louisiana (now known as University of Louisiana at Lafeyette). There, starting in his freshman year, he was a standout passer at the mid-major level. Despite a decorated career and some elite counting stats, Delhomme went undrafted and signed up the road with the New Orleans Saints. He spent a couple of years on the Saints practice squad and in NFL Europe, where he backed up Kurt Warner one year and won a championship the next as part of a two quarterback system. He ended up spending six seasons in New Orleans but rarely saw the field, though he did show some promise in some fill-in duty and in the preseason. He finally escaped New Orleans in search of a starting gig and found his way to Carolina, who had just gone 7-9 with 36 year old journeyman Rodney Peete as their starter. He started the opener on the bench, but it didn’t take long for his number to get called. After a first half that saw the Panthers pick up one first down while gaining a total of 16 yards (after losing a total of 18 yards over their last three drives), John Fox went with Delhomme. The Panthers wouldn’t look back. Delhomme would lead four scoring drives (while also throwing two interceptions), the last of which ended with the game winning touchdown to Ricky Proehl with 16 seconds left. That half a game would prove to be the perfect encapsulation of the Jake Delhomme experience. He ended up leading the Cardiac Cats to a surprise appearance in the Super Bowl with five fourth quarter comebacks and seven game winning drives in the fourth quarter during the regular season and one more game winning drive in the playoffs. He went toe to toe with Tom Brady in the Super Bowl and threw what still stands as the longest pass in Super Bowl history, but he and the Panthers came up short in the game. He was never the most efficient passer, and he was prone to turning the ball over with his gunslinging ways, but he gave his guys a chance and he wasn’t afraid to force the issue. And he always saved his best play for when the stakes were the highest. He earned a Pro Bowl nomination in 2005 and led the Panthers to an 11-5 record. His performance took a slight dip in 2006, and that would prove to be early signs of the approaching fall off. He started the 2007 season very strong but suffered an elbow injury in Week 3 that would ultimately require Tommy John surgery. He would return to throw a game winning touchdown on the final play of Week 1 of the 2008 season. He would recapture his Cardiac Cat magic with another four fourth quarter comebacks and five game winning drive, but he finished the season with just 15 touchdowns against 12 interceptions. The season ended with one of if not the most depressing performances Panthers fans have seen. He threw five interceptions and lost a fumble in a 33-14 beatdown at the hands of the Cardinals, and he would never be the same. Fresh off a new contract extension, he turned the ball over five times in the season opener of the next season. Through six games, he had thrown just four touchdowns while getting picked off 13 times and losing a pair of fumbles. He would finish that season with eight touchdowns and 21 turnovers. That would be the end of his career in Carolina. He went on to spend a mess of a season in Cleveland in 2010. Then, in 2011, he was brought in by the Texans as an emergency backup with a couple of their quarterbacks on the shelf. He came off the bench in the last game of the season and almost ended his career just the way it started, with a game winning drive with just 14 seconds on the clock. Unfortunately, a botched snap ruined the potential game winning 2-point conversion, and that would be the last snap of Delhomme’s career. Delhomme is about as pure a Carolina Panther as there is. He remained a very vocal fan of the team after his retirement and rejoined the organization as a color commentator on the radio broadcast, where he still refers to the Panthers with “we” and “our” pronouns when calling the game. Few players are as synonymous with the Panthers as Delhomme, and for that, he lands at number nine in the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.
author: Jonathan DeLong

title: Chicago Bears Question of the Day: Who goes over 1,000 receiving yards this year?
summary: Ben Johnson has said he wants the Chicago Bears offense to be the highest-scoring of all-time. That’s obviously a bold goal, and if we are being honest, probably not one the Bears will hit this year. Don’t get me wrong, I expect the Bears offense to be excellent. I expect it to be a top […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 28: Luther Burden III #10 of the Chicago Bears catches a pass for a touchdown against the San Francisco 49ers during the first quarter of the game at Levi's Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ben Johnson has said he wants the Chicago Bears offense to be the highest-scoring of all-time. That’s obviously a bold goal, and if we are being honest, probably not one the Bears will hit this year. Don’t get me wrong, I expect the Bears offense to be excellent. I expect it to be a top 5 offense in the league. But being the greatest of all-time is something that will, more likely than not, not happen. But that’s okay; it’s going to be a really fun season watching this offense and seeing what Caleb Williams can do in the passing game. But that makes you think, if this Bears offense is as explosive as Ben Johnson thinks it can be, that would certainly mean that the passing yardage is going to be higher than we’ve ever seen in Chicago. This certainly feels like the season a healthy Caleb Williams would become the first Bears QB to surpass 4,000 yards passing, and if he does, we know that means 4,000+ receiving yards on the other side of the ball. That leads us to today’s question. What players will have over 1,000 yards receiving this year? This makes for a fun debate. We all love Jahdae Walker, but I think even the biggest Walker fans understand that he’s not going north of 1,000 yards. Neither is Kalif Raymond. Neither is Cole Kmet. The Bears have three players capable of going over 1,000 yards: Luther Burden, Rome Odunze, and Colston Loveland. Which ones go over? Is it all three? Answer: As long as the receiving core is relatively healthy, I think you can definitely make an argument that any of the three can do it. I will start with Rome Odunze. I think Rome falls short of the 1,000-yard line. I think he’s a key part of the offense, but I think he falls more into a secondary role this year amongst this trio and probably ends up around 800 yards or so. Last year, Loveland had 713 yards receiving. Most of those came over the last 12 games of the season, and if you average his numbers over those 12 games and project them to 17, that number actually jumps to 930. So does that mean Loveland goes over 1,000 yards? If he plays 17 games, I think he absolutely does. But I do have a hunch that Loveland misses just a couple of games. If that’s the case and he plays like 15 games, I think he ends up coming up just short and has about 950 yards or so on the season. That leaves Luther Burden, and that’s where things change. I think Burden does, in fact, become the explosive playmaker this team has needed, and he is the guy that goes over 1,000 yards on the season. I think it won’t be like 1500 yards, but I do think he gets somewhere around 1100 yards. So while three players are capable of going over 1000 yards, I think Burden is the only one. That isn’t being pessimistic; that’s being optimistic about the rest of the weapons. If my yardage guesses are correct, those three tally about 2850 total receiving yards. Let’s say Raymond and Kmet each get about 400 yards. If Walker gets around 300 yards, Swift gets around 250 yards. Sam Roush and Savion Thomas each just get 200 yards; that’s 4700 passing yards! This isn’t the Cincinnati Bengals with Chase and Higgins and not much else. The Bears have a lot of talented skill players on offense, and because of it, Burden is the only guy who will go north of 1,000 yards. What do you say, Bears fans? Do you agree? How many players get 1000 yards this season? Sound off in the comments below!
author: Bill Zimmerman

title: Bears GM Ryan Poles in attendance at Miami-Stanford game
summary: Bears general manager Ryan Poles was in attendance for Stanford’s game against No. 7 Miami (FL) on Friday, Bonta Hill of NBC Sports Bay Area reported. College football is officially in full swing, and with it comes the in-person visits from NFL scouts, coaches, and executives. Poles is hitting the trails early, and as of […]
full_text: Bears general manager Ryan Poles was in attendance for Stanford’s game against No. 7 Miami (FL) on Friday, Bonta Hill of NBC Sports Bay Area reported . College football is officially in full swing, and with it comes the in-person visits from NFL scouts, coaches, and executives. Poles is hitting the trails early, and as of this writing, he’s watching Miami blow out Stanford. This is thanks largely in part to the performance of sophomore wide receiver Malachi Toney, who is not eligible for the 2027 NFL Draft. Upon seeing this news, I took to Twitter/X to share some notable 2027 draft prospects from the game, which was predictably dominated by Miami’s roster: #Bears GM Ryan Poles is at the Miami-Stanford game, per @BontaHill . Miami’s 2027 draft prospects of note: • Ahmad Moten, DT • Justin Scott, DT • Damon Wilson, EDGE • Darian Mensah, QB • OJ Frederique, CB • Mark Fletcher, RB • Cooper Barkate, WR • Mohamed Toure, LB — Jacob Infante (@jacobinfante24) September 5, 2026 Here are some quick notes on each player I have listed, along with two guys I couldn’t fit in the tweet: Ahmad Moten Sr., DT : Pro-ready defensive tackle who’s best over the guard as a 2-tech or 3-tech. Explosive off the snap, diverse in the move he uses to stack and shed blocks. Powerful lower body, has good spatial awareness as a run defender. Ranked No. 11 in the FBS last year in PFN DT Impact Scoring . Has missed 21.1% of his career tackling attempts, heading into 2026. A little too upright at times. Round 1 player. Justin Scott, DT : Best as a 3-technique but can kick inside as a 1-tech or a nose, too. Very good short-area quickness than better agility than most interior defenders. Has a low center of gravity and lands his strikes accurately in the run game. Impressive combination of speed and power. Only two career sacks going into 2026. Spatial awareness against the run and counters as a pass rusher both need work. Round 1 tools but Day 2 tape; I tend to think he’s more of a Round 1 guy. Damon Wilson II, EDGE : Really broke out at Missouri last year. Impressive speed rusher with a dynamic first step and flexibility turning the corner. Diversity as a pass rusher took a big leap in 2025. Doesn’t have typical Dennis Allen size or strength, but he’s very good at getting to the quarterback. Probably an early Day 2 guy as things stand. Darian Mensah, QB : Has excelled everywhere he’s gone and has looked good in Miami’s game against Stanford. Ranked No. 11 in PFN QB Impact Scoring last year. Throws with impressive touch and anticipation. Elastic arm with good timing at all levels of the field. Good athlete. A little skinny and could use an extra 10-15 pounds on his frame. Pocket poise and maneuvering ability under pressure needs some work. Not a Round 1 quarterback but certainly one who could become a starter someday. OJ Frederique Jr., CB : Impressive technician along the perimeter. Has some really intriguing snaps from 2025 blanketing the likes of Jeremiah Smith, Carnell Tate, Charlie Becker, and Elijah Sarratt. Fluid hips with good agility in coverage and impressive assignment awareness in vertical zone shells. Very good deep speed with an aggressive mindset in coverage. Misses too many tackles and a little too skinny. Round 2-3 guy with potential to go Round 1 if he gets stronger. Mark Fletcher Jr., RB : Big-bodied running back. Physical, tough runner who keeps his legs churning through contact and doesn’t shy away from defenders. Has underrated agility with good tempo variance in between the tackles. Doesn’t seem to have elite breakaway speed, which could limit his perceived upside a little bit. Could be a late Day 2 pick based on minimal evaluations. Cooper Barkate, WR : Standout performer at Duke who transferred to Miami along with Mensah. One of the more refined route runners in the class. Quick coming out of his breaks with good leverage obtainment through his stems and good tempo variance against different coverage looks. Questionable exactly how well he’ll test. Could go early Day 3 or late Day 2, but my evaluation of him is in the very early stages. Mohamed Toure, LB : Eighth-year linebacker who will enter the NFL much older than the average prospect. Has two season-ending injuries to his name. Physical, hard-hitting linebacker with solid closing speed and good stack-and-shed abilities in the run game. Comfortable in the box. Upside is limited because of his age. Likely a Day 3 guy. Samson Okunlola, OG/OT : Plays left tackle for Miami but projects best as a guard in the NFL. Rotational player in 2025. Has stellar size at 6’6” and 330 pounds with better flexibility than most his size. Physical with underrated short-area quickness. Strike placement and timing both need a lot of work. Upright in his pads when he gets out in space. Day 3 guy currently with starting upside down the line. Matt Rose, Stanford LB : Good athlete with underrated agility out in pursuit. Capable open-field tackler who plays with a noticeable edge when chasing down ball-carriers. Could be a Day 3 type.

title: NFL Draft College Prospects to Watch: Friday Night Defenders
summary: If you don’t want to read about the 2027 Draft, just skip this one. Enjoy any of the other content on WCG, and check out the app! However, a number of talented college prospects are going to be on display over Labor Day weekend, and a few who seem especially well-suited to Chicago’s lingering needs […]
full_text: If you don’t want to read about the 2027 Draft, just skip this one. Enjoy any of the other content on WCG, and check out the app ! However, a number of talented college prospects are going to be on display over Labor Day weekend, and a few who seem especially well-suited to Chicago’s lingering needs will be playing Friday night. Oklahoma – 7:00 pm Taylor Wein, ED (6’4”, 275lbs) – I need to be clear that Wein would be drafted based on tools and talent, not technique. Is he able to engage his hands? Not really. Does he finish tackles cleanly? Not that I have seen. He is, however, a human freight train who can explode off the edge with a deceptively quick trio of first steps. He disrupts , playing the pass and the run with equal ferocity. I’ll be looking for him to dominate against UTEP, and unless something changes dramatically this season will help determine if he’s a Day 2 or Day 3 player. It’s worth noting—for those who aren’t tired of hearing about it—that Wein is at least the type of player who Dennis Allen seems to want, but he also projects to be able to play in a modern, open-ended NFL defense as well. David Stone, DL (6’3”, 310lbs) – Perhaps the only true “math changer” on this list in the run game, Stone plays with leverage, power, and burst. He shows adequate awareness of play development, and against the run he is truly the kind of player who can alter offensive plans with a very elegant sort of violence. Unfortunately, he has not yet shown the toolkit needed to disrupt the passing game reliably, and his timing is sometimes more reactive than proactive. USC – 8:00 pm Kameryn Crawford, ED (6’5”, 265lbs) – I’m not sure what to make of Crawford, and not just because half of his tape is credited to his prior name of Kameryn Fountain. He lacks the high-end traits that define draftable college players. His athleticism is best described as adequate . His technique is sufficient against the pass and the run. He has average instincts. However, there aren’t really flaws in his game, either. I will be watching to see if he has the chops to progress from being a good college player to a draftable pro. If he continues at the linear progression he has been on and keeps the same general intensity level, he could find himself drafted in the earlier part of Day 3. Miami – 8:00 pm Justin Scott, DL (6’4”, 300lbs) – Scott is a converted basketball player who has surprising interior speed, with the ability to potentially ruin a guard’s day on any snap. He gets under blocks and makes sure that even if he isn’t getting to the quarterback, someone else has the opportunity. He is probably one level shy of being relentless, because he does fatigue as games go on, but he is at worst a disruptive snap eater in the pros, and if he gets his conditioning and hand technique up to the same level as his athletic traits, he could be a true 3T. I’ll be looking to see if he has improved leverage or a better array of moves, even if I don’t know if he will need anything special against the interior of Stanford’s offensive line. He’s on track to be a first-round selection, perhaps in the range where Chicago could grab him. Ahmad Moten, DL (6’3”, 325lbs) – More of Nose than Chicago is likely to consider, Moten is a mediocre tackler whose pads are usually high and whose instincts against the run lag. Against true pass sets, he’s a different player. What he does to crush the pocket in the pass game is worth drafting by itself, and he will doggedly pursue making a play with intensity that can shock a quarterback’s system. You can watch passers visibly flinch as games continue with how he forces them to adjust throwing lanes. If he looks like he has even taken incremental steps toward being a more well-rounded player in 2026, he should be a first-round selection. If his game is still limited, he might fall to the second round, but there are just only so many people with his size and with his initial surge to the ball. Damon Wilson II, ED (6’4”, 250lbs) – So yes, I am basically watching the entire defensive line of Miami. Wilson had nine sacks in 2025, and he got two of those (with five total pressures) against Alabama. His weakness against the run means he might have to start as a designated pass rusher, but in that role it’s hard to complain about what he does. He has a good initial burst around the corner, he stays low with adequate bend, and his ability to target the quarterback through traffic is better than average. I doubt he will be able to increase his draft stock this year to the point where he is considered a first-round prospect (though in the age of NIL with players staying in college longer, it’s harder than ever to predict classes). What does seem likely is that if he either refines his ability to stunt inside as well or if he stiffens against the run even a little, he’s going to be a Day 2 prospect. If he does both? Watch out.

title: Chicago Bears Restructure Multiple Contracts, Gain $17M in Cap Space
summary: With less than two weeks left before the start of the regular season, the Chicago Bears have gained some much-needed breathing room salary cap-wise. In this particular instance, three different players volunteered to make this happen for a team that’s snug against said salary cap. A sum of money that should allow for basic business […]
full_text: With less than two weeks left before the start of the regular season, the Chicago Bears have gained some much-needed breathing room salary cap-wise. In this particular instance, three different players volunteered to make this happen for a team that’s snug against said salary cap. A sum of money that should allow for basic business to be done throughout the rest of the year. Per Field Yates of ESPN the Bears have restructured the contracts of Joe Thuney, Dayo Odeyingbo, and TJ Edwards. In total, these moves open approximately $17M in cap space effective immediately upon the signing of each respective deal. The Bears have restructured the contracts of G Joe Thuney, DE Dayo Odeyingbo and LB TJ Edwards, creating ~$17M in 2026 salary cap space. — Field Yates (@FieldYates) September 4, 2026 I know what you’re thinking – this has to lead into something BIG… right? Well, not necessarily, but this financial shuffle is still noteworthy given the fact that the Bears are finally in compliance with the salary cap. Prior to these moves Spotrac.com had Chicago at $12M over the cap — aka in the red — which is an unideal situation to be in. Barring any additional updates, this should put the Bears at around $5M in space as of the writing of this article. It’s also interesting to note that Dayo Odeyingbo was one of the players who agreed to rework their previously existing contract. Even though he still has an out built into his deal for 2027, this would make any potential cut harder to handle as his salary cap hit increases. For what it’s worth, the Bears are seen as relatively healthy cap-wise heading into next year. As of this very moment, the mass opening of cap space doesn’t indicate that a major trade addition is imminent. If the Bears do wind up swinging for such a move, they do have other options available in terms of extensions and/or more restructures. Notable extension candidates of which could include D’Andre Swift and Montez Sweat.

title: 2026 NFL Season Award Predictions: MVP
summary: Some of the Windy City Gridiron staff made their picks for several 2026 individual season awards, and we capped the predictions off by picking Super Bowl LXI. We’ll run through all our picks in the coming days, and first up is Most Valuable Player. Bryan Orenchuk: For MVP this season, I’m going with Caleb Williams. […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears and Matthew Stafford #9 of the Los Angeles Rams embrace following the NFC Divisional Playoffs game at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images Some of the Windy City Gridiron staff made their picks for several 2026 individual season awards, and we capped the predictions off by picking Super Bowl LXI. We’ll run through all our picks in the coming days, and first up is Most Valuable Player. Bryan Orenchuk: For MVP this season, I’m going with Caleb Williams. Homerism aside, Chicago is going to have to put up loads of points with the state of their defense. In year 2 with Ben Johnson, I’m expecting Iceman to earn the first of many MVPs in a deep playoff run. Josh Sunderbruch: MVP is going to come down to a handful of anointed players, and I think if Joe Burrow stays healthy and his defense just carries the smallest amount of load, the Bengals are going to have the results that let him get the award. Sam Householder: This might be the second or third year in a row I say Joe Burrow. I feel like he’s due, though. It feels kind of now or never for Cincinnati, and if it goes badly, he could want out. Donald Gooch: The only thing keeping Allen from being the best QB in the NFL has been the absence of a quality go-to receiver – and now he has DJ Moore. He will challenge NFL records in touchdown passes, QB rushing yards, and total yards as he walks to an MVP in 2026. TJ Starman: Drake Maye would be my choice for MVP. Based on his production last season and the improvements the Patriots made around him, I feel like he’s set up well to have another fantastic season as long as he remains healthy. Mongo Peanut: Patrick Mahomes. I know he’s had some down years. I know he’s coming off of an injury. I know all of that. Still, he’s one of the best QBs in history, and I think we are all overlooking him. I sense that he and Reid are going to approach this season with something to prove. And voters will gobble up the storyline. Gary Baugher Jr.: The latent homer in me wants to see a Chicago Bears QB named MVP, but the football fan in me tells me he’s still a considerable leap from that (which isn’t out of the question!) All that said, I’ll go with a fully healthy Lamar Jackson to win his 3rd. Erik Duerrwaechter: Caleb Williams. He’s already taken that humongous leap during his second season as a pro, with plenty of room for improvement as well. This year we will see Caleb Williams put everything together and prove why Ryan Poles picked him number one overall in 2024. Lester A. Wiltfong Jr.: I’m picking the Bears to repeat in the NFC North, and if that happens, the hype around Caleb will be sky high. There’s already buzz around him that carried over from Iceman and the Cardiac Bears of 2025, and the Madden cover gave him another national boost. The oddsmakers have him with top-10 MVP odds, and he’s top three as far as the money coming in on him to win. But I think he falls short. I have the Los Angeles Rams winning the NFC West this year, and Mathew Stafford going back-to-back as the League MVP. Jeff Berckes: I hate how a few of my colleagues are picking Caleb Williams because I don’t want the entire site to look like a bunch of homers… but I’m extremely bullish on Williams this season. MVP is often a narrative award loosely backed by some numbers. Everyone hating on the Bears’ defense should put some money on Caleb for MVP, as that will only help pad stats. I think his biggest threat to the award is a healthy Joe Burrow. Superfans: Just as it was spoken by Connor MacLeod in the cinematic masterpiece, Highlander , that came out a few weeks after the most glorious football game ever played, Super Bowl XX, “There can be only one.” And the only one here is Caleb Williams, who shall become just the second Bear to win the NFL MVP Award after Seeetness himself, Walter Jerry Payton, in 1977. If there was any doubt about Caleb’s MVP chances, it just got a massive boost with the unveiling of his new mustachioed look that would make Da Coach himself, Michael Keller Ditka, proud. are they really your friends if they don't ride for you like this? pic.twitter.com/wEHBxNIEho — Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) September 4, 2026 Who is your pick for 2026 NFL MVP?

title: The NFL is Ruining Football with Streaming and International Games
summary: Hello, Chicago Bears fans!  I knew I had officially become an old man when the AARP started sending me letters. As such, it is now my right, duty, and privilege to yell at clouds. The cloud today is the NFL’s headlong bent to move the game to the international stage and engage with as many […]
full_text: LONDON, ENGLAND - OCTOBER 13: Tyson Bagent of Chicago Bears enters the pitch prior to the NFL match between Jacksonville Jaguars and Chicago Bears at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on October 13, 2024 in London, England. (Photo by Harry Murphy/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello, Chicago Bears fans! I knew I had officially become an old man when the AARP started sending me letters. As such, it is now my right, duty, and privilege to yell at clouds. The cloud today is the NFL’s headlong bent to move the game to the international stage and engage with as many networks and streaming services as you can shake a stick at. Thus, I’m going to take a break from talking specifically about the Bears and address an issue that has been with us for a while, but the league seems quite intent on making it worse and worse. And that is its continual departure from the traditional seven-day schedule for NFL football games in season. On Thursday night of Week 1, the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams will open their 2026 season not in California, but at the Melbourne Cricket Ground — a Friday-morning kickoff in Australia packaged for American prime time and streamed on Netflix. It is a 16-hour haul from the West Coast, a 17-hour time difference from the East, and a Wednesday-into-Thursday disruption of the only major American sport that was built around a weekly recovery cycle rather than a daily one. That game is just the latest in what started as a one-off spectacle that a couple of teams in the league had to deal with, to now a regular feature of league play and one that has a substantial impact on every team in the NFL. It is the logical next step in a league business model that has spent a decade slicing its calendar into streaming windows, short weeks, and overseas “home” games. The NFL still sells scarcity better than any other sport. It is also busy spending that scarcity down – to the detriment of its teams, its players, and its dedicated fanbase. Football is Uniquely Unsuited for International Play There is a reason Major League Baseball plays 162 games and the NBA plays 82, while an NFL team plays 17. Football is a collision sport whose preparation and recovery are measured in days and weeks, not hours and overnights. A baseball team can fly overnight, take batting practice, and play again. An NBA team can play on consecutive nights and still field a recognizable product. Even hockey, another physical, high-impact sport, does not require the kind of downtime football has always required. An NFL team that plays on Sunday is not simply “tired.” It is mid-rehabilitation, mid-install, and mid-film study. The next opponent’s scheme has to be learned. Soft-tissue damage has to be managed. The offensive line has to get its timing back. That is why the old NFL week worked. For decades the league was almost entirely a Sunday product, with a single Monday night game as the exception. A one-day difference between Sunday and Monday did not wreck the calendar. Teams knew the rhythm: play, recover, install, practice, travel, play. The product was scarce because the bodies that produced it needed time to heal, and the teams needed time to prepare for next week’s opponent. And the cost of playing the game – the physical and mental toil – was distributed fairly among all the teams. The modern schedule has no such regularity. Thursday Night Football is a standing short week. Streaming partners have pushed for standalone windows, given they are being parceled out just a few games in the schedule. The NFL is clearly eyeing international markets and salivating over the prospect of expanding their fan base by millions of viewers, which is why we see regular-season games played on the international stage. The result is a league that now treats a 17-game season as if it were infinitely flexible, that it simply doesn’t matter how long between one game and the next, and what travel time is necessary to get there. The calendar has been parsed for platforms, not players Thursday Night Football exists because Amazon paid for a night that used to belong to recovery. Netflix has Christmas and now Australia. YouTube has taken exclusive regular-season windows. Peacock and Paramount+ have gotten in the game, literally, as well. The business logic is obvious: more windows, more rights fees, younger audiences. Prime Video’s Thursday package has grown into a 15-million-viewer product and a younger demographic than the broadcast networks. The impact on the football game itself, however, is getting lost in the NFL’s avarice. A Thursday game after a Sunday game is not a slightly shorter week. It is a collapsed one. Meetings still happen. Treatment still happens. A real practice week does not. Coaches have less time to install. Players who might have recovered sufficiently from a minor injury in a normal week either have to play hurt or sit the game out. Former coach Jon Gruden’s recent verdict was blunt: no preparation, no recovery, dump the games. Players have said versions of the same thing for years — Richard Sherman after an Achilles tear blamed the shortened schedule, Doug Baldwin called the turnaround “illegal,” and Christian McCaffrey tied a hamstring strain, one that lingered for most of the season, to the short week. "No preparation, no time to recover, no chance. Get rid of these Thursday night games! Dump them! It’s not fair to the players, it’s not fair to the coaches." – Jon Gruden pic.twitter.com/6gvPxiz5A2 — Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) November 10, 2025 The box-score defense of Thursday night the NFL tends to cite when these kinds of objections are raised is thinner than the league pretends. While it is true that scoring is not reliably lower (several multi-year samples put Thursday totals within a point of Sundays) and penalty rates, in large play-by-play studies, are relatively similar , that is not the same thing as saying the games are as good. Since both teams suffer from the schedule disruption, penalties tend to cancel. Poor play is met with poor play. And we should keep in mind that teams are not evenly selected for these “feature” games. The more streaming services and networks that get a game, the more they demand that their game feature a marquee matchup. Thus there is a selection effect that puts more marketable offenses – better teams – in those games. And there is, in fact, data that shows the rest gaps matter. A team on a short week against a rested opponent is not playing the same game the schedule implies, and late-season home teams on Thursday have historically held a real edge over visitors who just flew in on fumes. Sometimes the sloppy and uneven play that these disruptions cause is not subtle. In November 2025, Denver and Las Vegas produced a Thursday night game in which both teams finished with more penalties than first downs — the second such game in 75 years. That wasn’t an accident, and it wasn’t a coincidence. We get measurably worse football from the NFL when it violates the traditional week of recovery and preparation in the scheduling of its games. Injury studies of the effect of Thursday night games have been inconclusive. An NIH study found no significant spike in Thursday injury counts versus Sunday. On the other hand, we have the players who actually play and travel to the games and their testaments that players arrive less prepared, less healthy, and less able to practice the game they are about to play when they are forced to deal with short weeks. It creates competitive disadvantages for some teams over others. And, further, given the headlong pursuit the NFL is engaged in of the international markets – it is becoming a regular factor for the whole of the season, rather than just one or two weeks. In other words, the NFL is moving into uncharted waters by introducing exponentially more short-week games and at the same time introducing more and more international games that require substantial travel time and adjustment to radically…

title: Chicago Bears Question of the Day: What defines a successful 2026?
summary: Ask this question in any of the last 6+ years, and you would get something to the tune of: “A successful Bears season looks like QB development, improvement by (rattles off a handful of key players) and threaten for a playoff spot” But 2025 changed that. The Bears won their division, won a playoff game, […]
full_text: Dec 20, 2025; Chicago, Illinois, USA; Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) runs onto the field during player introductions before the game against the Green Bay Packers at Soldier Field. Mandatory Credit: David Banks-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Ask this question in any of the last 6+ years, and you would get something to the tune of: “A successful Bears season looks like QB development, improvement by (rattles off a handful of key players) and threaten for a playoff spot” But 2025 changed that. The Bears won their division, won a playoff game, and unearthed a QB+Coach combo that we have been clamoring for for years. So with the 2026 season a week away, expectations have changed. We can no longer just ask for development and to threaten for a playoff spot. What defines a successful 2026 Bears campaign? I won’t be satisfied unless they make the NFC Championship Game. They need to make real progress in the playoffs after last season. This is no easy task, though. Every team in the league is looking to take the “next step”, and unfortunately there aren’t enough spots in the dance to accommodate them all. In fact, the Bears haven’t made consecutive playoff appearances since the 2005 and 2006 seasons, where they showed true incremental progress in improving on a Divisional Round appearance to a Super Bowl appearance. Before that, the Bears haven’t shown sustained playoff success since the stretch of 1984 to 1991, where they made the playoffs in 7 of 8 seasons, winning a Super Bowl and making the Conference Championship in two other seasons. So linear improvement is not guaranteed. Beyond a NFCCG appearance, I think a few other things would help me define this as a successful season. Caleb Williams cements himself as an elite QB by introducing consistency to his moments of genius. Ben Johnson proves he is one of the few HCs that can churn out perennial winning football teams. The Bears pass-catchers all take steps forward, with one of Odunze/Burden/Loveland emerging as a top-tier player at their position. One young defensive player catapults themself into a “feature role”. This could be Jordan van den Berg, Austin Booker, Dillon Thieneman, or a number of other guys. Dennis Allen shows he is the right complement to Ben Johnson by developing and scheming the talent into more consistent performances. It’s unlikely that all of the above hit, but I also don’t think it is far-fetched to think that they can. Bears fans this offseason have been excited, but as we approach the season and some realities creep in (injuries, trades, etc) you can feel expectations tempering. Part of this is the conditioning we have gone through as Bears fans — to never expect too much of our team. But I think it’s time to change that narrative. Expect a lot out of this group. This team is different. Now it’s your turn! What defines a successful 2026 Bears season to you? Sound off in the comments!

title: Major Hall of Fame changes could have major impact on Bengals legends Ken Anderson, Willie Anderson
summary: The Pro Football Hall of Fame has decided to shake up the way it determines who gets a gold jacket, and the changes could have significant implications for several former Cincinnati Bengals. Most notably, the Hall is eliminating the separate Seniors category beginning with the Class of 2027. That is a major development for Ken […]
full_text: Former Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Ken Anderson, left, and offensive tackle Willie Anderson answer questions of a question and answer session during the Super Bowl LVI Opening Night Fan Rally, Monday, Feb. 7, 2022, at Paul Brown Stadium in Cincinnati. The Cincinnati Bengals are set to face off against the Los Angeles Rams in Super Bowl LVI, Sunday, Feb. 13, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif. Cincinnati Bengals Super Bowl Lvi Opening Night Fan Rally Feb 7 The Pro Football Hall of Fame has decided to shake up the way it determines who gets a gold jacket, and the changes could have significant implications for several former Cincinnati Bengals. Most notably, the Hall is eliminating the separate Seniors category beginning with the Class of 2027. That is a major development for Ken Anderson, who was one of three Senior finalists for the Class of 2026, and Willie Anderson, who has spent the past several years knocking on the door of Canton as a Modern-Era finalist. Under the new system, there will no longer be separate pools for Modern-Era players and Seniors. Instead, every eligible former player will compete in the same Players pool beginning five years after retirement. And while that sounds like a move toward simplicity and fairness, it could make the road considerably more difficult for some of the Bengals’ longtime Hall of Fame hopefuls. The Senior category is officially gone The Hall’s previous system essentially gave older players a second avenue toward Canton. Once a player’s Modern-Era eligibility expired after 25 years, he could eventually be considered in the Seniors category. A separate Seniors Blue-Ribbon Committee narrowed the field and ultimately selected three Senior finalists for consideration. That’s how Anderson got his opportunity for the Class of 2026. The Bengals legend was among the nine Seniors semifinalists before ultimately becoming one of three Senior finalists alongside Roger Craig and L.C. Greenwood. Craig was ultimately elected. Anderson wasn’t. Now, there won’t be another Seniors category for him to return to. The Hall announced Friday that all eligible players will instead remain in one pool regardless of how long they have been retired. The annual selection meeting will ultimately consider 13 players, along with one coach and one contributor. Between three and seven total people can be elected, with candidates requiring at least 80% approval. That creates an interesting—and potentially frustrating—situation for Anderson. He has already demonstrated that he can make it through the old Senior process. Now he’ll have to do it against everyone else. Ken Anderson may have lost his clearest path to Canton There is no question Anderson has a Hall of Fame résumé. The longtime Bengals quarterback played from 1971 through 1986, earning four Pro Bowl selections and winning the league MVP award in 1981. He finished his career with 32,838 passing yards and 197 touchdown passes. He also led Cincinnati to its first Super Bowl appearance following the 1981 season. Anderson’s candidacy has long been one of the more fascinating Hall of Fame debates because his career statistics don’t necessarily jump off the page by today’s standards. But the context of his era is important. He was one of the NFL’s most accomplished quarterbacks of the 1970s and 1980s, helped revolutionize the Bengals’ offense under head coach Paul Brown and offensive coordinator Bill Walsh, and was at the center of one of the best teams in franchise history. The Hall’s previous system finally gave him a specific avenue to make that case. In fact, Anderson survived a field of 162 Senior nominees to become one of just three Senior finalists for 2026. Unfortunately for Bengals fans, that system is now gone. And that’s where things get complicated. Under the old system, Anderson only had to compete with the other Senior finalists for one of the available spots in that secondary pool. Within the new system, he’s competing against the entire group of eligible players. That includes modern stars who have recently become eligible, older players who have been waiting for decades and, potentially, other candidates whose résumés previously would have been separated into different categories. The Hall says the changes are designed to eliminate potential “unintended biases” in the old system. For Anderson, however, it means the route that finally got him within one vote of Canton no longer exists. Willie Anderson’s situation is different Then there’s Willie Anderson. The Bengals’ legendary offensive tackle has arguably been even closer to Canton in recent years. Anderson was a Hall of Fame finalist for the fifth time in 2026 and advanced all the way to the final seven before falling short of the required 80% threshold. That was particularly painful because the Hall’s old bylaws gave players who reached the final seven an automatic return to the finalist stage the following year. Anderson was therefore automatically advancing to the 2027 finalist stage. Except that rule is gone, too. The Hall specifically eliminated the provision that allowed candidates who reached the final seven to automatically return as finalists the following year. So Anderson will not simply pick up where he left off. He’ll have to go through the new process. That’s a significant change. But Willie Anderson has something Ken Anderson doesn’t There’s also a reason for Bengals fans to remain optimistic about Willie Anderson. The fact that he reached the final seven in 2026 is meaningful. The Hall’s voters had already narrowed the field from 15 Modern-Era finalists to seven, and Anderson was one of the seven players still under consideration for induction. Ultimately, he did not receive the required 80% support. That isn’t the same thing as being pushed aside early in the process. Anderson was right there. The Hall’s decision to eliminate the automatic carryover rule means he’ll have to earn his way back into the finalist group, but he isn’t starting from scratch in terms of his reputation among the voters. And his résumé remains extremely compelling. Anderson was a six-time first-team All-Pro and seven-time Pro Bowler during his Bengals career. He started 116 consecutive games to begin his career and was one of the defining offensive tackles of his era. If the Hall’s new system truly is designed to identify the most deserving players regardless of how long they’ve been retired, Willie Anderson should remain one of the names at or near the top of the discussion. The numbers game could be the biggest change Perhaps the most important part of the new system isn’t simply the elimination of the Seniors category. It’s the reduction in the number of players who will be considered at the annual meeting. Under the previous system, the Selection Committee considered 15 Modern-Era players plus three Seniors, along with a coach and contributor. Now, it will consider 13 players, one coach and one contributor. That means fewer player candidates will make it to the final stage. And that’s important because the Hall is entering an era in which some enormous names are joining the eligibility pool. The Class of 2027, for example, is expected to include first-time eligible stars such as Rob Gronkowski, Adrian Peterson, Ben Roethlisberger and Cam Newton. Suddenly, longtime candidates like Anderson and Anderson aren’t merely competing against other overlooked players from their generation. They’re competing for attention against some of the most recognizable stars of the modern NFL. Could this ultimately help the Bengals? That’s the great unknown. The Hall says the changes were the result of a 2½-year review designed to improve the integrity of the selection process. The Selection Committee is being reduced from 50 members to 28, with 25 voting members and three alternates. Selectors will also no longer be assigned to individual NFL teams. The final meeting will return to an in-person format, something the Hall believes will…

title: Five as one: Bengals’ offensive line believes continuity can unlock full potential
summary: For most of the Joe Burrow era, the Cincinnati Bengals‘ offensive line has been something to worry about. Maybe it’s finally becoming something to believe in. And, if you listen to Amarius Mims and Dalton Risner, the reason goes well beyond blocking schemes, technique, or individual talent. It’s about five guys becoming one. Risner and […]
full_text: For most of the Joe Burrow era, the Cincinnati Bengals ‘ offensive line has been something to worry about. Maybe it’s finally becoming something to believe in. And, if you listen to Amarius Mims and Dalton Risner, the reason goes well beyond blocking schemes, technique, or individual talent. It’s about five guys becoming one. Risner and Mims sat down together recently for an exclusive interview with Bengals radio voice Dan Hoard , and what emerged was a picture of an offensive line that endured its share of struggles last season but came through them closer and better than when it started. “You see him growing, you see him want to be great,” Risner said of Mims. “He wants to be coached, he wants to see how he can get better. I love playing next to this guy. For years, Cincinnati has tried different combinations in front of Burrow, adding veterans through free agency and young players through the draft. This year, instead of rebuilding the offensive line yet again, the Bengals are bringing back all five starters: Orlando Brown Jr., Dylan Fairchild, Ted Karras, Risner and Mims. And there are signs that continuity will pay off. The line struggled early last season but improved dramatically as the year progressed. Over the last seven games of the season, Pro Football Focus graded Cincinnati’s offensive line among the top five in the NFL. And PFF identified both Risner and Mims among the NFL’s most improved players at their respective positions over the second half of the season. Risner’s PFF grade improved from 56.8 over Weeks 1 through 9 to 79.6 from Weeks 10 through 18. Mims made an almost identical jump, going from 55.1 to 78.2. The improvement in Mims’ pass protection was particularly significant. After allowing 21 pressures and four sacks over the first nine weeks, the former first-round pick surrendered only 14 pressures and no sacks over the final eight. “The last seven or eight games is when it really started to gel,” Mims said. “We weren’t winning as much, but it was obvious we were getting better.” According to Mims, that improvement didn’t come because everything suddenly became easy. It came because the players learned how to deal with things going wrong. “It’s how you overcome those bad games,” Mims said. “I learned from guys like him [Risner] and Orlando: do not let one bad play affect the whole game. We’re in this together. O-line is hard. Five as one. It’s not going to be perfect. It’s just, how can we make this better?” That last phrase may be the key. Five as one. Offensive-line play depends on communication and trust more than any other position group on the field. One player can execute his assignment perfectly, and the play can still fail because of a missed protection or blown assignment somewhere else. Mims believes Cincinnati’s line learned to accept that reality and learned to trust one another. “We may not get the national credit,” Mims said. “As long as we know we have each other’s back, that’s all that matters.” Risner saw the same transformation. “We kept our heads on straight the whole year, kept working, kept working for each other,” he said. “We started to build this continuity. With time, we just aged well, started to get better throughout the year.” Risner’s relationship with Mims is particularly interesting because the two players are at dramatically different points in their careers. Mims is just 23 years old and entering his third NFL season. Risner, 31, is entering his eighth. “He is like a little brother to me. More than a little brother, he is a friend, and I want to see him succeed. I don’t want to let Mims down, I don’t want to let Ted down, I don’t want to let Joe down.” Risner says Mims isn’t simply a talented young tackle. He’s a student of the game. “During the season, we all ask Mims for the scouting report, for the injury report,” Risner said. “He knows all of this. He’s a football guy.” And Risner has been impressed by Mims’ willingness to recognize his own mistakes. “I think Mims is such a pro,” Risner said. “For me, it’s always seeing Mims for the positive things he does. Let’s go out there and take it one play at a time. During the game, it gets hectic. The way he is able to see his wrongs, I gained so much respect for him.” Mims believes that willingness to admit mistakes is essential to becoming the player he wants to be. “Once you’re vulnerable enough to understand where you need to grow, that’s when you become a good player,” Mims said. “Coach listed what we need to get better at, and we just had to go to work.” The admiration clearly goes both ways. “He’s one of the most selfless guys I’ve ever played with,” Mims said of Risner. “It’s always, ‘What can I do, how can I help you?’ That’s what I really like.” That relationship helped bring Risner back to Cincinnati. After joining the Bengals shortly before the beginning of last season, Risner eventually started 11 games. Cincinnati didn’t allow him to reach the open market this spring, re-signing him to a one-year contract before the start of free agency. According to Risner, Mims and Karras were among those pushing for his return. “For him to care enough to say something that kind and to want me back, I’ve never had teammates like Ted and Mims that really campaigned for me to come back,” Risner said. “And that’s why I wanted to come back. “I could have probably made more in free agency somewhere else, but this is where I wanted to be. You don’t have Mims, Ted Karras, OB [Orlando Brown] at other places.” The Bengals have rarely lacked offensive firepower during the Burrow era. The lingering question has been whether the five players up front could provide enough protection and a running game for that talent to reach its potential. For once, Cincinnati enters a season without having to introduce a collection of new offensive linemen to each other. They already know each other. They have struggled together. They have improved together. And, perhaps most importantly, they actually care about one another. “We went through not knowing each other, going through the worst times, then going through the best,” Mims said. “The sky’s the limit for us. “I’m very excited.” So is Cincinnati.
