title: Raiders’ offensive line is an X-factor for the 2026 season
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders are about to head into the regular season with a matchup against the Miami Dolphins. It will be their first test of real football, and they are hoping to start the season off on a good note. One area fans will be interested in is the offensive line’s improvement. The Raiders […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - AUGUST 27: Tyler Linderbaum #65 of the Las Vegas Raiders blocks Keion White #56 of the San Francisco 49ers in the first quarter of their preseason game at Allegiant Stadium on August 27, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. The 49ers defeated the Raiders 18-12. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders are about to head into the regular season with a matchup against the Miami Dolphins. It will be their first test of real football, and they are hoping to start the season off on a good note. One area fans will be interested in is the offensive line’s improvement. The Raiders added Tyler Linderbaum during the offseason and signed Spencer Burford to elevate the group. Early preseason returns suggest the starting offensive line is light years ahead of 2025. With the first-team offensive lineman playing in the preseason, Kirk Cousins was under pressure 5.9% of his snaps. The running game helped Mike Washington Jr average 6.1 yards per carry against the San Francisco 49ers. In his one preseason performance, Ashton Jeanty averaged 5.0 yards per carry. The group’s improvement is clear throughout the film as well. In the play below, the Raiders are running a trap concept, and fans can already see the difference in execution. It says a lot about coach Rick Dennision and the job he is doing as an offensive line coach. Kubiak’s run game is going to be fun to watch. The trap call is set up nicely with a great block from Burford. Glaze and Rogers both climb to the second level opening up the hole for Washington. pic.twitter.com/UlsE6836u4 — Marcus Johnson (@TheMarcJohnNFL) August 28, 2026 If the offensive line brings this type of play into the regular season, it will be an X factor for their win total. It will make Kirk Cousins or Fernando Mendoza comfortable and allow them to make plays. With the running game being vital to Klint Kubiak’s philosophy as a play caller, the group could help create a smash-mouth mentality.

title: Raiders News: Evan Neal, Azeez Ojulari, Ronnie Bell sign to practice squad
summary: Despite the NFL’s cutdown day and claiming cornerback Darrell Luter Jr. on waivers earlier this week, the Las Vegas Raiders are still looking to improve their roster. According to The Athletic’s Sam Warren, the Raiders hosted 16 free agents (listed alphabetically below) for a workout on Thursday, including offensive linemen Evan Neal, edge defender Azeez […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 24: Evan Neal #73 of the New York Giants looks on against the New York Jets in a preseason game at MetLife Stadium on August 24, 2024 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images Despite the NFL’s cutdown day and claiming cornerback Darrell Luter Jr. on waivers earlier this week, the Las Vegas Raiders are still looking to improve their roster. According to The Athletic’s Sam Warren , the Raiders hosted 16 free agents (listed alphabetically below) for a workout on Thursday, including offensive linemen Evan Neal, edge defender Azeez Ojulari and wide receiver Ronnie Bell. G Evan Beerntsen, Northwestern WR Ronnie Bell, Michigan DT David Blay, Miami DB Stephen Hall, Missouri DB Tre Hawkins, Old Dominion C Trey Hill, Georgia OT Christian Jones, San Diego State TE Josh Kattus, Kentucky LB Dasan McCullough, Nebraska DB Latrell McCutchin, Houston G Evan Neal, Alabama DE David Ojabo, Michigan LB Azeez Ojulari, Georgia LB B.J. Ojulari, LSU T Colby Sorsdal, Williams & Mary WR Marquez Valdes-Scantling, South Florida For those keeping score at home, that’s five offensive linemen, four edge defenders, three defensive backs, two wide receivers, one defensive tackle and one tight end. The Ojulari brothers and McCullough are listed as linebackers but are stand-up outside linebackers who play on the line of scrimmage to fall into the “edge” category with Ojabo, who is listed at defensive end. After the workout, the Raiders announced they signed Bell, Neal and Azeez Ojulari to the practice squad, releasing defensive end Jahfari Harvey, offensive tackle Kamar Missouri and tight end Albert Okwuegbunam in corresponding moves. Neal was the seventh overall pick in the 2022 NFL draft but fell out of favor with the New York Giants, getting switched from tackle to guard before being cut at the end of this year’s training camp. Meanwhile, Ojulari is also a former Giant (2021 second-round pick) and spent last season with the Philadelphia Eagles. He has 22 career sacks in five seasons. Bell is the lowest-profile addition, as the 2023 seventh-rounder has accumulated just 10 catches for 113 yards and four touchdowns with the San Francisco 49ers (2023-2024) and New Orleans Saints (2025). However, Bell worked with Klint Kubiak when Kubiak was the 49ers’ passing game coordinator in 2023. Join the conversation! title: NFC North Season Forecast: Green Bay Packers
summary: I continue my series on forecasting the record of each NFC North team this season by focusing this time on the Green Bay Packers. You can find my forecast for the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears by following the links. Green Bay Packers 2025 Season and Offseason Changes The Green Bay Packers had a disappointing […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 10: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers shares a moment with head coach Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers prior to an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lambeau Field on November 10, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images I continue my series on forecasting the record of each NFC North team this season by focusing this time on the Green Bay Packers. You can find my forecast for the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears by following the links. Green Bay Packers 2025 Season and Offseason Changes The Green Bay Packers had a disappointing 2025 season, finishing 9-7-1, a half-game ahead of the Lions and Vikings, and once again gained the 7th seed in the playoffs and were one-and-done. They also finished 4-2 in the division, sweeping the Lions and splitting with the Bears and Vikings, although their loss to the Vikings came in a meaningless week 18 game in which they played their backups. The Packers season began with high expectations after the Packers took a swing for the fences in trading two first-round draft picks and defensive tackle Kenny Clark to the Cowboys for Micah Parsons, who they subsequently signed to a 4-year, $186 million extension ($46.5 million AAV, $136 million guaranteed) making him the highest paid edge rusher and non-quarterback at the time of the deal. Unfortunately for the Packers, Parsons later suffered a torn ACL in week 15 and was lost for the season. The Packers lost every game last season without Parsons. He’ll also miss at least four games this season as he rehabs from the injury. The Packers finished with an offense that ranked 16th in points but 6th in DVOA . Their defense, by contrast, ranked 11th in points allowed but 19th in DVOA. The explanation is that the Packers offense was good at limiting turnovers (they ranked 3rd), but the defense didn’t produce many (they ranked 26th). Overall, the Packers finished 11th in Total DVOA and were that just enough above average team that sneaks into the playoffs but doesn’t do much. Looking at the offseason changes for the Packers, let’s start with a key coordinator change. Packers defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley became the head coach of the Dolphins this offseason and was replaced by the recently fired head coach of the Arizona Cardinals Jonathan Gannon. I don’t think Gannon provides much added value as a coordinator beyond what his defensive roster has to offer. He had one top defense in Philadelphia in 2022 with a pretty solid roster that landed him the head coaching job in Arizona, where his defenses have ranged from mediocre to poor. The Packers have a better defensive roster than the Cardinals, but without Micah Parsons it will be up to Gannon, who historically hasn’t blitzed much, to manufacture a pass rush. And even with Parsons, there are weaknesses Gannon will need to manage. There are also scheme differences the defensive personnel will need to master as the Packers will be going from a 4-3 front under Jeff Hafley to a 3-4 front under Gannon, and primarily a Cover-3 zone coverage scheme to a disguised two-high safety-based zone scheme (including quarters and Tampa-2 variations) under Gannon. The Packers return head coach Matt LaFleur (who was extended) who is the de facto offensive coordinator and play caller, and Adam Stenavich who maintains the offensive coordinator title. In terms of roster changes, the Packers added defensive tackle and former Viking Javon Hargrave to bolster their interior pass rush, but moved on from edge rusher Rashan Gary, hoping Lukas Van Ness can pick up the slack. Hargrave has been a good defensive tackle, but at age 33 he isn’t the force he once was as a pass rusher and can be a liability in run defense at times. They also moved on from linebacker Quay Walker and replaced him with 30-year-old Zaire Franklin who struggled last season. At cornerback the Packers look to start rookie 2nd-round pick Brandon Cisse opposite of Keisan Nixon as outside corners- Cisse replaces Carrington Valentine- with Javon Bullard as slot corner. Overall, not much to move the needle here for the Packers, and the net roster changes may actually a bit of a regression. We’ll see. Offensively, the Packers moved on from some of their receivers like Romeo Doubs as they hope to have kept the best of the bunch- Christian Watson and Matthew Golden as outside receivers and Jayden Reed in the slot. Combined with Tucker Kraft who is returning from an ACL suffered last November, and quarterback Jordan Love, this is easily the strength of the Packers team. Golden still has question marks and Reed is returning from injury- and Watson is oft-injured as well- but if Golden can step up and the rest return to top form and stay healthy, this is a top passing offensive skill group. The issue for the Packers offense is they are still trying to figure out their offensive line and I don’t think they’ve made much progress this offseason. Zach Bako-Bewele (formerly Tom) is a good right tackle, but beyond that things get shakier. 2024 first-round pick Jordan Morgan will start at left tackle, replacing Rasheed Walker last season, while Aaron Banks and Sean Rhyan return at left guard and center respectively. Both were mediocre last season. And at right guard it looks like 2024 5th-round pick Jacob Monk will become the new starter, replacing Morgan who moves to left tackle. This may be the weakest position group on the team, which isn’t good considering how much the rest of the team depends on the offensive line. Lastly, starting running back Josh Jacobs is on the commissioner’s exempt list for an indefinite period at the moment following a domestic incident for which he is making a court appearance next week. It is unclear when Jacobs will return to the Packers lineup, but there is some speculation that it may not be real soon. That leaves a group of mediocre running backs led by Marshawn Lloyd, who has a total of six rushing attempts since being drafted by the Packers in 2024, to fill in his absence. Overall offensively for the Packers, the net roster changes also don’t move the needle but have the potential to regress at least as much as improve. Injuries Last season the Packers finished 15th in adjusted games lost (AGLs) which is pretty close to average. The methodology attempts to account for starters missing due to injury or not playing at 100%. They ranked 21st in offensive AGLs and 6th in defensive AGLs. What we are looking for here are outliers in terms of extraordinarily good or back luck with injuries in the previous season that may revert to the mean or average the following season and therefore result in an adjustment to the team’s projected win total. Certainly losing guys like Micah Parsons for the last part of the season and tight end Tucker Kraft for the last half of the season hurt them on both sides of the ball, but overall they were not outliers when it came to injury luck last season at 15th overall, so like with roster/coaching adjustments, there is no adjustment needed here for regression to the mean in injury luck this season. Luck Factors As I’ve mentioned previously, I’ve had to slightly modify the sources for luck factors this year as one of the sources from last year stopped publishing their data. To determine luck factors, I am going again with the Luck Ratings from Team Rankings , and using the differential between actual and estimated wins from the DVOA stats at FTN . I average the two numbers to get a game adjustment amount. Last season the Packers had estimated wins of 9.6 compared to an actual win total of 9, so a bit of bad luck there. Team Rankings also gave them a -0.6 luck rating, which is the same as the estimated wins. So, with rounding, this results in a one win adjustment to their season projection. However, given the Packers had a tie last season, it seems more appropriate to make this a half-win adjustment instead, which is more accurate and eliminates…

title: Pro Football Hall of Fame Makes Big Changes to Induction Procedures
summary: The Pro Football Hall of Fame announced several significant changes to its induction procedures on Friday, and they look to be pretty bad news for some former, prominent members of the Minnesota Vikings who may have gotten the call to Canton in the future. Among the changes that have been made are the following: It’s […]
full_text: PASADENA, CA- JANUARY 9: Jim Marshall #70 of the Minnesota Vikings looks on from the bench against the Oakland Raiders during Super Bowl XI on January 9, 1977 at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, California. The Raiders won the Super Bowl 32 -14. (Photo by Focus on Sport/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pro Football Hall of Fame announced several significant changes to its induction procedures on Friday, and they look to be pretty bad news for some former, prominent members of the Minnesota Vikings who may have gotten the call to Canton in the future. Among the changes that have been made are the following: The selection committee has been reduced from 50 voting members to 28. There is no longer a separate “Seniors” category. All eligible players will be considered in one pool following the mandatory five-year retirement period. The annual finalist pool will go from 15 modern-era players, 3 Seniors players, 1 coach, and 1 contributor to 13 total players, 1 coach, and 1 contributor. Candidates who reach the final seven will no longer carry over as finalists the next year. Contributor eligibility will now consider a candidate’s entire football résumé, including playing, coaching and other contributions. It’s the second point on the list that I want to draw everyone’s attention to. The “Seniors” category was for players who had been retired for more than 25 years. In recent years, some of the players who had made it into the Hall of Fame from the Seniors category were Roger Craig, Sterling Sharpe, and the late Steve “Mongo” McMichael. It gave an opportunity for players who may have been overlooked during their initial stints of eligibility a second chance at potentially being enshrined. Jim Marshall, who many Vikings fans have been pushing to get into the Hall of Fame for years, was a Seniors finalist in 2004, but did not make it into the Hall that season. He has been on the list of Seniors up for consideration multiple times since then, but has not been one of the three finalists considered since that 2004 season. Now, with the elimination of the Seniors category, it would appear that whatever slim chance there may have been to get the league’s original Iron Man into Canton may have, officially, gone by the wayside. Big changes for the Pro Football Hall of Fame. . .and, if you’re a fan of the Minnesota Vikings, it doesn’t look like they’re necessarily good ones.

title: Kyler Murray’s TruMedia Data Reveals His Potential in Kevin O’Connell’s Offense
summary: On The Real Forno Show, Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano skipped the J.J. McCarthy loop and put the actual starter under the lights. Murray starts Week 1 against Green Bay at U.S. Bank Stadium. The episode — a Vikings 1st & SKOL production — is the same exercise they ran on Sam Darnold in […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 22: Kyler Murray #1 of the Minnesota Vikings looks on after the preseason game against the Baltimore Ravens at U.S. Bank Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images On The Real Forno Show , Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano skipped the J.J. McCarthy loop and put the actual starter under the lights. Murray starts Week 1 against Green Bay at U.S. Bank Stadium. The episode — a Vikings 1st & SKOL production — is the same exercise they ran on Sam Darnold in 2024: take the uncomfortable projection seriously. “Kyler Murray is the most athletic quarterback the Minnesota Vikings have had under center,” Forness said. He is not selling a Lamar Jackson clone. Murray wants to beat you from the pocket and can “kick your ass the second they leave it.” Dave stayed in Missouri mode: “How confident? I’m hopeful. … KOC’s gotta prove it to me once again.” That is the show. Hope plus receipts. Forness used TruMedia splits (1,000-plus attempts since 2019, then full-season 2024). Career EPA/play sits 22nd of 45. Explosive pass rate is 42nd. Air yards per attempt are T-43rd at 6.8 — Kingsbury air raid plus “Murray, who would much rather take the eight yards instead of shoot for 30.” Success rate and sack rate land 15th. Outside the pocket, explosives jump to 19 percent (T-12th) and air yards to 8.3. Scrambles: 210 (5th), 1,736 yards (6th), seven rushing touchdowns. Forced missed tackles look modest because Murray often runs out of bounds. “I’d rather you get out of bounds and not take a hit than lower your shoulder,” Forness said, with McCarthy’s 2025 injuries in the rearview. 2024 is the hope tape. Pocket success rate hits 52.7 percent (7th of 46). Turnover-worthy throws drop to 1.6 percent (4th). Explosives stay low at 10 percent. Off-platform, EPA doubles to 0.16 (10th) and air yards hit 10.4 (5th), while TW throws spike. “Are we sure that maybe Kyler’s not perfectly suited for what Kevin O’Connell wants to do?” Forness asked after noting a 0.4 percent pocket scramble rate. The bet is O’Connell lifts in-pocket explosives with Jefferson, Addison, T.J. Hockenson, Jauan Jennings, Christian Darrisaw, and Brian O’Neill, and uses boots, floods, and scramble-drill rules the Cardinals never had. Key points from the episode: Week 1 starter is Murray, not a camp debate Unique athlete in a McVay/O’Connell tree that has rarely had this profile Height is real; Forness pointed to Drew Brees / Sean Payton passing-lane work Jefferson–Addison scramble chemistry is the untested multiplier Career: average EPA, low explosives, clean TW%, better off-platform 2024: safer pocket, bigger off-platform boom, still not a gunslinger in rhythm Ceiling: non-zero Super Bowl after last year’s Seahawks–Patriots path; sloppy first weeks Red zone: Jennings as the bully; Hockenson still “about 90 percent” of the old version Contract: no tag; Forness doubts $60 million unless Murray is an MVP-level lever; Darnold’s 3/100.5 is the comp Six QBs have won a Super Bowl on a rookie deal since 2000 — Brady, Roethlisberger, Eli Manning, Flacco, Wilson, Mahomes Listen: Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: “If the Vikings are in a position where they have to pay Murray at the end of the year because he was that good, it’s a champagne problem,” Forness said. title: 3-Point Stance: How the Patriots’ offseason approach left the defensive edge vulnerable
summary: Entering the 2026 season, the New England Patriots have a glaring weakness on the defensive edge. After New England’s preseason victory over the Philadelphia Eagles on Aug. 22, head coach Mike Vrabel said he doesn’t think the Patriots have a deep roster. He later explained on WEEI’s The Greg Hill Show that his comments came while […]
full_text: Feb 8, 2026; Santa Clara, CA, USA; New England Patriots linebacker Harold Landry III (2) warms up before the game against the Seattle Seahawks in Super Bowl LX at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Darren Yamashita-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Entering the 2026 season, the New England Patriots have a glaring weakness on the defensive edge. After New England’s preseason victory over the Philadelphia Eagles on Aug. 22, head coach Mike Vrabel said he doesn’t think the Patriots have a deep roster . He later explained on WEEI’s The Greg Hill Show that his comments came while emphasizing the development of the team’s young players. Simply put, the team’s depth remains unsettled. But for the defensive edge room, those question marks range from the top of the depth chart to the bottom. Why is that? For starters, veteran Harold Landry III, who’s supposed to be an every-down starter, is beginning the season on the PUP list after undergoing knee surgery earlier in the offseason. He’s now slated to miss at least the first four games. In free agency, New England added another veteran, Dre’Mont Jones, opting not to re-sign core 2025 defender K’Lavon Chaisson. The Patriots also let capable edge-setter and 2020 third-round pick Anfernee Jennings walk in free agency, who played well in meaningful playoff snaps without Landry available. On paper, an approach emphasizing player development left the position thin and, consequently, with little room for error. Then, factoring in second-round pick Gabe Jacas’ contract situation, the rookie’s delayed start to offseason workouts added a layer of uncertainty to the team’s early-season outlook — regardless of whether New England knew about his knee injury before the draft. Harold Landry’s injury exposes a major concern Landry’s aforementioned knee injury in 2025 persisted up until the Super Bowl in February, where the 30-year-old logged just 14 defensive snaps and spent most of his time in uniform watching from the sideline. He also missed the previous two playoff contests because of the setback. After suffering the initial injury during a Week Six matchup against the New Orleans Saints, Landry aggravated his knee in Week 12 in another game against the Cincinnati Bengals. By late December, the former Tennessee Titan missed a number of practices and was ruled out for the final two weeks of the regular season. Because of Landry’s long recovery, New England will open the season with Jones and 2025 undrafted free agent Elijah Ponder as the starters on the edge. Ponder secured four sacks last year but has yet to establish himself as an every-down presence. Outside of the Jones and Chaisson swap, Jacas was the Patriots’ most substantial addition. Still, even though he’s slated to be the top rotational piece on the depth chart, his preseason performance showcased a raw rookie who needs plenty of learning experience at the NFL level. When speaking with the media on Tuesday, Vrabel was asked about Landry’s and special teams ace Brenden Schooler’s status: “I wasn’t anticipating them being out there … I think the plan was that this is not unexpected.” If Landry’s absence wasn’t unexpected, the Jacas selection may have provided a level of comfort to the coaching staff until the veteran is fully healthy. However, Jacas’ late start has left the defensive edge depth chart thinner than expected while Landry works his way back. The Patriots never added insurance Nonetheless, Vrabel and Co. decided to carry just four outside linebackers on the initial 53-man roster (Jones, Ponder, Jacas, Quintayvious Hutchins) without making any further additions. Hutchins, a seventh-round draft choice, strictly projects as a special teams contributor entering his rookie season. After outside linebackers coach Mike Smith expressed “very high expectations” for Ponder during mandatory minicamp, Vrabel also noted his enthusiasm to see Bradyn Swinson progress, highlighting the coaching staff’s belief in the development of their second-year players. “I think he improved over the course of last season, and certainly has taken to that early on in the spring and what we have been able to do,” Vrabel said at minicamp . “I’m excited about what he’ll be able to do and excited to see him in training camp.” Yet, that optimism ultimately didn’t translate into a roster spot. New England later waived Swinson during roster cutdowns. And subsequently, because of that progression-focused approach, no depth moves were made in free agency or training camp. In March, Chaisson signed just a one-year, $11 million contract with the Washington Commanders. Although he’s not an uber-talented run defender as a three-down player, he could have been a spot starter who complemented Jones by cleaning up plays behind the line of scrimmage. The Patriots also could have signed a cheaper rotational piece with plenty of options on the market. Former Atlanta Falcons outside linebacker Arnold Ebiketie was one of those potential fits. His total contract value with the Philadelphia Eagles sits at only $4.3 million. Additionally, during roster cutdowns, New England chose not to add, even with veterans like Kyle Van Noy available. The team made trades and placed waiver claims in other areas, but not on the defensive edge, which places more responsibility on other units. Heavy responsibility on the interior Whether or not it was the desired outcome, the defensive tackles face another season of heightened responsibility. In 2025, arguably the defense’s biggest weakness was a failure to frequently finish plays behind the line of scrimmage despite the interior producing significant pressure on opposing quarterbacks. According to Pro Football Focus, New England ranked first in the league in pass-rush win rate (21.1%) and pressure rate (15.7%) from players lined up between the offensive tackles. That said, with 35 total sacks on the season, tied with four other franchises, the Patriots ranked 22nd in sacks. Given the current makeup of New England’s defensive edge room, that defensive line dynamic is set to remain. Defensive tackles face a crowded and more compact area of the offensive line to get to the quarterback. If the interior pass rush can’t consistently win its matchups during a game, the Patriots have few proven options on the edge capable of compensating and generating pressure from the outside. Still, that doesn’t mean the defensive edge unit can’t piece everything together towards the end of the regular season. By that time, and given that Landry wasn’t placed on season-ending injured reserve, the veteran should return to the lineup. Furthermore, Jacas and Ponder will have gained more experience to adjust to larger roles. The primary concern is the stretch of contests the team faces without Landry and a raw Jacas, which could account for a decent portion of the regular season. Nevertheless, the defensive line’s production ceiling in 2026 hinges on the development of the edge.

title: Pro Football Hall of Fame makes sweeping changes after Bill Belichick fiasco
summary: After arguably the most puzzling decision in the institution’s history, the Pro Football Hall of Fame has overhauled its election process. To recap: eight-time Super Bowl champion Bill Belichick, who together with quarterback Tom Brady led the New England Patriots to the greatest two-decade run in league history, was denied entry in his first year […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - FEBRUARY 6: Former NFL head coach Bill Belichick walks the red carpet before the NFL Honors award show ahead of the Super Bowl LIX football game at Saenger Theatre on February 6, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images After arguably the most puzzling decision in the institution’s history, the Pro Football Hall of Fame has overhauled its election process. To recap: eight-time Super Bowl champion Bill Belichick, who together with quarterback Tom Brady led the New England Patriots to the greatest two-decade run in league history, was denied entry in his first year of eligibility . The decision was heavily criticized at the time and raised questions about the integrity of the vote and those making the decisions. Seven months later, the Hall of Fame has announced a sweeping re-do . And while Belichick apparently did not prompt the changes — they rather were the result of a two-and-a-half-year review process, according to president and CEO Jim Porter — his snub nonetheless feels like the straw that broke the proverbial camel’s back. So, what are the changes? According to the HOF’s own announcement, they look like this: Committee size: Reduces panel from 50 Selectors to 28. Their voting status (25 voting, 3 nonvoting participants) will be determined on an annual basis. Committee structure: Changes from a geographically based model with one selector per NFL club, 17 at-large selectors and one Pro Football Writers of America representative to 27 at-large selectors and one PFWA representative. Player eligibility: Changes from separate Modern-Era Players and Seniors categories — with players moving to the Seniors category after 25 years of retirement — to a single pool for all eligible players following the mandatory five-year retirement period. Contributor eligibility: Expands from individuals who “contributed to the game outside of playing or coaching” to consideration of a candidate’s full football résumé that may include playing, coaching and other contributions to the sport. Candidates considered at annual meeting: Changes from 15 Modern-Era Players, three Seniors, one Coach and one Contributor to 13 Players plus one Coach and one Contributor with the Coach and Contributor determined by the respective subcommittees. Seniors on final ballot: Eliminates the previous maximum of three Seniors, with all eligible Players now considered together in a single pool regardless of how long they have been retired. Carryover candidates: Eliminates provision allowing candidates who reached the final seven to return automatically as Finalists the following year. “The Hall continually reviews its bylaws to ensure the selection process reflects the highest standards of integrity and the magnitude of election to the Pro Football Hall of Fame,” Porter said in a statement. “There is no more important task at the Hall of Fame than the election of each new class.” The 2027 Hall of Fame process is already underway, with the first group of nominees typically announced in late September or early October. Through several rounds of voting, the group will then be reduced until the final class is announced before the Super Bowl in February. In 2026, Belichick was not part of that group. Ordinarily, one would say that it would be a surprise if he wasn’t included in 2027. Then again, the Hall of Fame showed that it was more than capable of surprises such as this. Whether or not the voting modifications announced on Friday will change this remains to be seen, but the hope is that they will be a step in a positive direction to ensure the same fiasco does not happen again.

title: Patriots mailbag: What comes next with Christian Gonzalez?
summary: Football is less than a week away as the New England Patriots get set to open the 2026 NFL season with a Super Bowl rematch against the Seattle Seahawks. Enough is said, so let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. What do you think is a reasonable contract for the Patriots and Gonzalez to come […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - JANUARY 18: Christian Gonzalez #0 of the New England Patriots lines up during an NFC Divisional Playoff game against the Houston Texans at Gillette Stadium on January 18, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Football is less than a week away as the New England Patriots get set to open the 2026 NFL season with a Super Bowl rematch against the Seattle Seahawks. Enough is said, so let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag. What do you think is a reasonable contract for the Patriots and Gonzalez to come to in terms of total salary, total guaranteed, guaranteed at signing, and signing bonus and any other parameters you want to throw in? – New England Guy I’ve heard some team reporters say Gonzo has essentially no leverage. Is that really true? Can he realistically hold out, and what happens if he refuses to practice? The only meaningful leverage I’ve heard is that if he doesn’t play by Week 10, his contract and fifth-year option could toll a year—bad for him if he wants to get paid sooner. – Maye The Force Be With You By his own words, Christian Gonzalez has not committed to playing in the Patriots’ season opener Wednesday night. Mike Vrabel, meanwhile, expects “every player that is healthy and under contract to practice and to play.” If the cornerback doesn’t suit up, this saga reaches a new level. As you stated, Gonzalez needs to play six games this year to accrue a year of service time. A holdout would prevent him from making progress toward free agency while then seemingly increasing the odds of a trade next offseason. I still do not believe it gets to that point. I’d continue to guess that Gonzalez plays Wednesday night, as the two sides will continue to try to get a deal done before then. As for the structure, I would continue to use Devon Witherspoon’s deal (below) as a framework, with a slight bump: Total value: $132 million AAV: $33 million Guaranteed money: $101 million Guaranteed at signing: $59 million My on-topic contribution: Do you see a world in which the O-line turns from a liability to a reasonable strength, making this a truly elite offense? (I do.) – ed.liebfried I do too, Ed. Will Campbell is healthy and had an overall solid training camp. He should take a step forward in Year 2, in addition to getting center Jared Wilson back at his natural position. The addition of veteran Alijah Vera-Tucker should make both of the second-year linemen’s lives easier as well. There are plenty of projections there, but they have the talent and potential to be an offensive line that at least ranks in the top half of the league. Especially with the Seahawks game in mind, have the Pats done enough (adding AVT, Gilliam and blocking TE’s) to protect Maye and give him the time to succeed? – Ricky Hot Pants As we discussed above, the offensive line group should take a step forward with the internal development of the young players and addition of Alijah Vera-Tucker. Additions like Reggie Gilliam should also allow the Patriots to play and take advantage of more heavy personnel groupings than they did in the Super Bowl, where they lived in 11 personnel. Those improvements should help the offense against Seattle’s four-man rush — which shined in the Super Bowl — and in the Patriots’ run game. From there, New England will need better answers against Mike Macdonald’s pressure looks this time around. In addition to the four-man rush, the biggest issue against Seattle in the Super Bowl was the Patriots’ lack of answers against the Seahawks’ pressure packages. New England failed to either have “hot” options available to Drake Maye or correctly adjust the protection pre-snap. The Patriots spent much of this offseason weaponizing Maye’s mind as he enters Year 2 in Josh McDaniels’ system, hoping to avoid similar issues moving forward. “I think just more comfort in what we are doing, more command, more understanding to be able to operate and get us into the best plays,” Vrabel said about Maye’s improvements from the end of last season. Do you think the Pats OLine could be better with Roten starting at Center to begin the year and start Wilson after a few games after he gets a little more familiar with the Center position in the NFL? – sjamesbossports I do not. I think Wilson is a good center prospect and Van Roten fits in better at guard whereas Ben Brown is likely the backup center. I’m sorry but adding 10 new players after cut down day, causes me to think the Patriots, scouting, drafting and player development is not good enough. 10 new players, suggest the had the wrong players in camp. Your thoughts? – Patriot in Chicago To me, it comes down to two main things: injuries and free agency. The Patriots are starting the year without OT Marcus Bryant, TE Julian Hill, RB Terrell Jennings, OLB Harold Landry III and ST Brenden Schooler. Each player was expected to assume a starting or backup role and deepen the roster. As for free agency, they did not hit on the middle class of free agents this year with guys like Mike Brown, Kindle Vildor and K.J. Britt compared to the likes of Khyiris Tonga, Jack Gibbens and K’Lavon Chaisson last season. What are your thoughts about Ponder being a starter week1 as DE coming from nowhere last year ? – 7i165 I am a fan of Elijah Ponder. He’s a great athlete off the edge and had some really strong moments against some of the best tackles in football last season. But, going from a rotational player who logged just 215 defensive snaps to a full-time, three-down starter is a major ask for a 24-year old that was an undrafted free agent. We will see if he is ready. I have heard next to nothing about Reggie Gilliam. What I have heard is more like the theoretical value of having a true fullback on the roster again. But did he look good in camp? Did he play in preseason? Is there any indication of how the offense has evolved with his addition? – NEsuper It was tough to evaluate Gilliam as the team really managed his workload this summer to help him deal with past injuries that have nagged him. There isn’t much concern that that will affect him during the season as he has been one of the league’s best fullbacks for multiple years. As we hinted on above, his arrival will allow the team to find more success in heavier, two-back personnel groupings. Last season, New England averaged just 3.1 yards and a negative EPA/rush in those looks. Buffalo, meanwhile, averaged 4.9 yards per rush and nearly 9.0 yards per pass with Gilliam on the field. He should make life easier for the whole offense. Who has been the biggest surprise (positive or negative) from Training Camp/Preseason that casual fans should pay more attention to as the season begins? – LandenPatz1 For the casual fans, it’s been pretty striking to see the turnover on special teams. Among the Patriots players who played over 100 snaps on the kick or punt team last season, they have lost: Brenden Schooler (NFI), Jack Gibbens, Marte Mapu, Jahlani Tavai, Jack Westover, Anfernee Jennings, Alex Austin and K’Lavon Chaisson. Elijah Ponder was also part of that group and could take a reduced role due to his standing on the defensive depth chart. That is massive turnover in the kicking game — which doesn’t even count Bryce Baringer’s injury — that has been replaced by rookies and some recent waiver claims. While special teams is often overlooked, it can make a big impact in a game. “The trust factor is what it comes down to in the kicking game because those kick returns, punt returns, a block punt, those usually lose you games. If you give up return touchdowns, and conversely if you hit them. those help you win and lose games,” VP of player personnel Ryan Cowden said. “So that’s why it’s such a vital piece of the game and you do sometimes want to rely on guys who’ve been there done that, but inevitably you have to lean into these young players.” Why do you think the Pats didn’t keep Saunders, even on the PS? Ball-hawking…

title: Carlson Gets the Call: Have the Saints found their solution at kicker?
summary: The New Orleans Saints appear to have found their answer at kicker with veteran Daniel Carlson, a two-time All-Pro who brings a proven track record and a powerful leg to New Orleans’ special teams unit. The former Las Vegas Raiders kicker signed with New Orleans on Aug. 24 and wasted little time making his case […]
full_text: Aug 28, 2026; Arlington, Texas, USA; New Orleans Saints placekicker Daniel Carlson (48) looks to attempt a field goal during the game between the Cowboys and the Saints at AT&T Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jerome Miron-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New Orleans Saints appear to have found their answer at kicker with veteran Daniel Carlson, a two-time All-Pro who brings a proven track record and a powerful leg to New Orleans’ special teams unit. The former Las Vegas Raiders kicker signed with New Orleans on Aug. 24 and wasted little time making his case for the Saints’ kicking job. Carlson took part in his first practice just two days later and then suited up for the Saints’ preseason matchup against Dallas two days after that. He converted both of his field-goal attempts, including a game-winning 53-yarder, in the Saints’ 27-24 victory over the Cowboys. Carlson’s quick transition helped him move ahead of Charlie Smyth and Tanner Brown, who had been competing for the job since Brown joined the Saints in June. Saints head coach Kellen Moore praised Carlson’s performance despite having just a brief window to evaluate him, while acknowledging the difficult decision the team faced at kicker. “We really only had two days with Daniel, and so obviously feel like he showed himself well,” Moore said. “Made a nice kick at Dallas. More time on task will be beneficial for him. Those are tough decisions — Tanner is a kicker in this league, Charlie is a kicker in this league, I think we had some really good guys there. Daniel is going to do a great job for us.” After spending his previous eight seasons with the Raiders, Carlson made 225 of 259 career field-goal attempts (86.9%) and earned first-team All-Pro honors in 2022. He will now take over the kicking duties in New Orleans, hoping to provide stability at a position that has been inconsistent for the Saints over the past few seasons.

title: New York Giants mailbag: Joe Schoen, Evan Neal, Jalin Hyatt, practice squad, more
summary: Brian Misdom asks: While this is older news, the season is quickly upon us and makes me wonder why the giants decided to extend Schoen before seeing any results on the field. It seemed premature – wouldn’t it have been prudent to see the fruits of the Harbaugh/Schoen pairing first? I just don’t see a […]
full_text: Brian Misdom asks: While this is older news, the season is quickly upon us and makes me wonder why the giants decided to extend Schoen before seeing any results on the field. It seemed premature – wouldn’t it have been prudent to see the fruits of the Harbaugh/Schoen pairing first? I just don’t see a lame duck GM as having the same distraction as a lame duck HC typically brings. Was there a real risk to our personnel operation if this wasn’t done over the summer? Ed says: Brian, Giants ownership has always liked the front office and scouting operation Schoen has put together. They have liked, as far as I can ascertain, how he communicates with ownership. Those things are important. The working relationship with Harbaugh is, of course, also incredibly important. By all accounts, the two have found common ground and an ability to work together. The fruits of that were shown in the Giants having what they felt was a fruitful offseason, both in the way they approached free agency and the draft. Harbaugh has talked about having the ability to “agree to agree” with the front office when he was in Baltimore. He has found that with Schoen. I think even the trades made in the week prior to the 53-man roster cut down show an ability for coach and GM to work together to build the roster the coach is looking for. The Giants liked what they saw in the relationship. Harbaugh was on board. Ownership saw no reason to make Schoen twist in the wind and keep answering questions about his job security. I am OK with that. Jimmy Siegel asks: Now that Evan Neal is in the rear view mirror, my question is what was it that Schoen and company didn’t see in the endless college film they no doubt dissected for months? I’ve always thought offensive lineman is one of the more easy transitions from college to pro. I believe that most first round OL tend to at least be quality starters in the NFL. But here’s a guy who let speed rushes fly by him like a turnstile. How was that missed by the Giants brain trust. Is the gap between speed rushers in college and the NFL that wide that it’s impossible to judge a college player? And yes, I know most teams had Neal as a top ten talent. So maybe my question should be what did the entire NFL miss with Neal? Ed says: Jimmy, I know that Joe Schoen has asked himself what, if anything, the Giants missed in their evaluation of Evan Neal. I know that he has gone back and studied the tape again. I also know that after re-watching that tape Schoen did not feel the Giants missed in their evaluation. He still believes he saw a player who, based on his college tape and what was known about him, deserved to be a top 10 pick. You are also right that most teams and talent evaluators agreed with Schoen, and that the pick was universally praised when the Giants made it. When I saw your question I went back and looked at a half-dozen or so pre-draft scouting reports on Neal. Almost everyone who evaluated him saw Neal as a future Pro Bowl or All-Pro caliber tackle. Evaluating players is not an exact science. I would disagree that the transition from college to NFL is easy for offensive linemen. College offensive linemen can be extremely difficult to evaluate. They often play little in a three-point stance. Many are hardly ever asked to run block. Many play in quick-passing offense that don’t ask them to do more than get in the way of a rusher for a second or so. Even at Alabama, Neal probably only squared up with real NFL talent two or three times each season. Evaluators knew there were a couple of issues with his pass protection, but felt those could/would be cleaned up with reps and NFL coaching. It didn’t happen. Why? Injuries? Coaching? The player himself? Being used at the wrong position? Nobody really knows. It is probably some combination of everything. It just didn’t work out. Daniel Frankel asks: For years I have felt that Harry Carson’s #53 deserved to be retired. I never enjoyed watching anyone else wear it. Now that Darius Muasau has been cut, do you think it would be a good time to retire The Captain’s number or at least to give that number to someone worthy of wearing the number, like Arvell Reese. Ed says: Daniel, the older I get the more I think numbers shouldn’t get retired in the first place. It gets a little silly after a while, and now we have numbers getting unretired so kids coming out of college who haven’t earned it yet can wear the number that goes with their brand. But, now that I’ve had my “get off my lawn” moment, if we are going to retire numbers then Harry Carson’s number should be among them. I don’t know why it has not been retired. The problem you run into in football, though, is that you run out of available jersey numbers. Still, Carson deserves that honor. Ed Helinski asks: Please describe the various amounts of money that practice squad players make? What kind of latitude do NFL teams have with deals for practice squad players? Might some be guaranteed deals? And how does the game check change when a player is elevated to the active roster? Ed says: Ed, the practice squad salaries are collectively bargained. The standard practice squad contract pays $13,750 per week. Teams can have up to six players who are “veterans”, designated as having two or more accrued seasons. Those players can earn a minimum of $18,350 per week and a maximum of $22,850. That’s it. There are no “guaranteed” practice squad deals. It is a week-to-week existence. Now, some undrafted free agents, like offensive tackle Ryan Schernecke, get guaranteed money when they sign. Schernecke received $247,500 guaranteed, which equates to a full season’s practice squad salary. Players elevated to a game day roster get the minimum pro-rated game day check for that week based on their experience level. Donald Leichter asks: Given the Giants’ obvious need for more run-stopping depth at defensive tackle, were you surprised they made no waiver claims despite having the No. 5 priority? Do you think they’re satisfied with the current group, or have you heard anything suggesting they’re pursuing a veteran run-stopper through a trade or free agency? Ed says: Donald, yes I was surprised they did not try to claim anyone. I do believe they would have made a claim or two if players they wanted had been there. Part of the process throughout the summer is identifying players you would like to claim if they are cut by other teams. I know that in the past the Giants have said there were players they wanted who ended up being kept by their teams rather than released. I would think that happened here, as well. As much as they know there are a few spots that need upgrading, they likely felt that what was available was not better than what they had. Matthew Sanzone asks: Questions from a practice squad dummy: 1. Do PS players travel with the team to away games? 2. Are they provided per diem money for expenses such as meals? 3. Do they have medical insurance as part of their compensation? Ed says: Matthew, let’s look at each of these. There is no set answer to that. Practice squad players who are going to play travel, of course. In some instances, they will travel as a reward. In many instances, they will not. Remember, that is 15 or so extra people to put on an airplace already filled with large people. Practice squad players get free access to meals provided at team facilities. If they are traveling with the team, they are treated like everyone else. Practice squad players get medical benefits. Here is a look from a few years ago at those benefits . Pat Lam asks: Adding Jalin Hyatt to the practice squad is a headscratcher. Do you have any insight as to why? Ed says: Pat, Hyatt was injured when the Giants were still in West Virginia and missed the rest of training camp and the entire preseason. He had been making some plays in practice, and the Giants were giving him an opportunity as a punt gunner. Perhaps the Giants feel like the injury, caused by an overzealous hit from a…

full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories as you start you Labor Day Weekend. Gauging John Harbaugh’s impact and what to expect in Week 1 | The Athletic Harbaugh has brought credibility to the organization. No one knows if this will ultimately work. Plenty of accomplished coaches have flamed out at later stops. But no other coach on the market this offseason could have generated this level of buy-in. A leader with a clear vision is leading the organization. Everyone believes in Harbaugh’s methods because he can point to his lengthy track record of success. The Giants feel like a professional organization for the first time in a long time. How that translates to wins and losses remains to be seen, but Harbaugh’s impact has already been profound. To Harbaugh’s credit: confidence. It used to drive me crazy at this time of year when general manager Joe Schoen and former coach Brian Daboll always ran from any expectation of winning games. That’s what made Harbaugh’s comments Wednesday about expecting to win so refreshing. Surely there has to be some anxiety about starting this new journey with a roster that clearly has flaws. But Harbaugh and the players seem genuinely eager to get started. Is Jihad Ward coming back to the Giants? View this post on Instagram 2026 NFL season X factors: Key players for all 32 teams | ESPN.com DT DJ Reader. Reader was once a premier run-stuffing nose tackle in this league, but his numbers are down over the past two seasons. His stop rate of 8.6% last season — the percentage of tackles that stopped the run for negative expected points, per NFL Next Gen Stats — was his lowest single-season mark since 2018. His stuff rate of 1.1% — the percentage of tackles that were for zero or fewer yards — was the lowest of his career. The splashy impact against the run is waning for the 32-year-old. How many snaps does Reader have in him at his age, and can he achieve more impact against the run in a new defensive system in New York? Without a renaissance Reader season, I’m worried that we’ll see another season in which the Giants’ defense is too easy to run on for its pass rush to really matter. Agent’s Take: Does Cam Skattebo need better advice after recent Giants antics? | CBSSports.com When situations like these arise, an agent should provide counsel to their client. It’s an agent’s job to tell a client what he needs to hear, not what he wants to hear. That isn’t always done. Some agents are reluctant to be candid for fear of being fired and instead become enablers. Skattebo plays in the United States’ biggest media market, so any missteps are more magnified in New York. The good news for Skattebo is that the regular-season opener against the Dallas Cowboys is less than two weeks away. The attention will primarily be on how he performs in his return from the injury. If Skattebo can pick up from where he left off last season, then anything relating to the offseason or preseason will just be a minor blip on the radar screen in the grander scheme of things. The Giants lineage and Ice Bowl pedigree Ben Mann brings as he tries to write his own Big Blue story | New York Post It is probably a bit of hyperbole to suggest Ben Mann was born to be a Giant. But there is Giants lineage coursing through his veins and NFL pedigree in his genes and there is a close family link that takes this otherwise nondescript 24-year-old — he’s a long snapper, for goodness’ sake — and vaults him into a space where few have entered. Method to the madness: Reason why Giants limited recording at practice | USAToday.com Entities are entitled to their “corporate secrets,” and the Giants are no different. Under new head coach John Harbaugh, there is much less media and fan access to practices, to the point where video, pictures, and the description of the action aren’t flowing freely on social media for the world to consume. Some teams haven’t clamped down as hard yet, though. In a recent press conference, Miami Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley admitted that he has fallen victim to fans posting videos of his practices and other teams using that footage against him. title: Survey results: Giants’ defensive line dominates… Fans’ list of concerns
summary: There’s an interesting dichotomy forming around the New York Giants. On one hand, there’s a pervasive sense of optimism surrounding the team. The Giants’ brass has believed that they have the core of a team capable of competing this year dating back to before free agency. Since that time, the additions to the roster have […]
full_text: Darius Alexander | Getty Images There’s an interesting dichotomy forming around the New York Giants. On one hand, there’s a pervasive sense of optimism surrounding the team. The Giants’ brass has believed that they have the core of a team capable of competing this year dating back to before free agency. Since that time, the additions to the roster have only strengthened that conviction. We’re still in hope season, but most fans have bought into the optimism as well. There are even some in the media who are whispering that the Giants could be a real sleeper despite Las Vegas giving the Giants’ the second-best odds to miss the playoffs in the NFC (per FanDuel). But there are also those who can’t shake the feeling of impending doom. It’s tough to blame them after a decade and a half of (mostly) being irrelevant. The overwhelming source of anxiety for fans lies on the defensive line — at least for now. The Giants themselves admitted that they weren’t happy with the defensive line group that they fielded through the preseason. They traded for mammoth nose tackle C.J. Okoye and Joe Schoen confirmed that the Giants will be adding a veteran in short order. Rookie nose tackle Bobby Jamison-Travis flashed in creating piles in the middle of the line, and also showed some upside as a hustle-based pass rusher. Second year defensive tackle Darius Alexander likewise showed off his impressive athleticism and However, neither young tackle was consistent enough throughout the preseason. They’re young, but the NFL isn’t going to wait until they’re fully developed. Which is why the Giants are bringing in another veteran — in addition to unwrapping D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris . It is worth remember that we still haven’t seen the Giants’ full defense on the field. Reader and Harris were spared the preseason, and we also don’t quite know just how Dennard Wilson will deploy and scheme his hyper-athletic linebackers and defensive backs. And therein lies the kernel of good news: The Giants don’t need their defensive line to be dominant, they just need them to be good enough to occupy blockers and occasionally penetrate. The secondary is a, well, secondary source of concern for fans. Deonte Banks and Greg Newsome II have performed well throughout camp and preseason, but there seems to be a persistent doubt that they can carry it over into the regular season. Dennard Wilson, Donald D’Alesio, and Addison Lynch have produced excellent secondaries at their previous stops, and the Giants’ group of DBs were all high-round picks for a reason. That the Giants’ coaches have a track record that suggests that they can get the group of Banks , Newsome II , Paulson Adebo , Colton Hood , Dru Phillips , Tyler Nubin , and Jevon Holland to play up to their respective draft pedigrees likely assuages fans’ anxiety there. It is interesting to me that fans are the least concerned with the special teams. The Giants are relying on a UDFA placekicker in Dominic Zvada and a UDFA rookie longsnapper in Ben Mann . There is definite risk in those unknowns, but fans seem to be confident after each had strong camps and preseasons. Likewise, Jordan Stout is a legitimate weapon at punter. I also have to note that I admire that the Giants are effectively carrying three return specialists in Braxton Berrios , Dalen Cambre , and Charlie Jones without having to use a single roster spot. The Giants can elevate each three times, giving them 9 games worth of return specialists before they have to roster one. That’s slick. We’ll see if it pans out, and if their decisions on the rest of the roster pan out as well.

title: 2 Giants make ESPN list of top players for 2026 season
summary: A pair of New York Giants players have been named to ESPN’s projected list of the top 100 NFL players for 2026. One prominent player was left off the list. ESPN ranked offensive tackle Andrew Thomas No. 81, and edge defender Brian Burns No. 81. Wide receiver Malik Nabers did not make the cut. ESPN […]
full_text: Andrew Thomas | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect A pair of New York Giants players have been named to ESPN’s projected list of the top 100 NFL players for 2026 . One prominent player was left off the list. ESPN ranked offensive tackle Andrew Thomas No. 81, and edge defender Brian Burns No. 81. Wide receiver Malik Nabers did not make the cut. ESPN said this about Thomas: Thomas is entering a season healthy for the first time in years. And when he’s healthy, he’s one of the league’s best left tackles. His 92.3% pass block win rate is the fifth best among all left tackles over the past three seasons. There is no reason to think that will dip with Thomas healthy and in his prime. – Signature stat: Last season, Thomas was one of three offensive tackles to rank in the top 15 of pass block win rate and run block win rate. The other two were the Rams’ Warren McClendon Jr. and the Vikings’ Brian O’Neill. Offensive tackles ranked ahead of Thomas were Jordan Mailata of the Philadelphia Eagles (No. 48), Lane Johnson of the Eagles (No. 40), Garrett Bolles of the Denver Broncos (No. 37), Trent Williams of the San Francisco 49ers (No. 28), Tristan Wirfs of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (No. 27), and Penei Sewell of the Detroit Lions (No. 12) ESPN said this about Burns: Burns is coming off a career-best 16.5 sacks and looks even better this summer. “He does so many things well, he’s going to excel,” said new coach John Harbaugh about Burns’ prospects in new coordinator Dennard Wilson’s defense. Burns also shouldn’t be getting a ton of double-teams with the continued development of Abdul Carter. He was doubled at a rate of just over 13% last season. Signature stat: Burns had the second-most sacks in the NFL last season, which marked the most by a Giants player in a single season since Jason Pierre-Paul’s 16.5 in 2011. This is probably a more realistic placement for Burns than the No. 14 he placed in the NFL Top 100 players from NFL.com. As for Nabers, his omission from the list should not be surprising. The list is based on expectations for the upcoming season, and no one is certain what Nabers will look like coming off his torn ACL.

title: NY Giants’ Cam Skattebo addresses rumors of rift with John Harbaugh
summary: Cam Skattebo on Thursday put to bed the social media-created idea that there is a rift between the running back and New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh. “There’s that video going around of me and Harbaugh on the sidelines of ”not liking” what I said or whatever,“ Skattebo acknowledged during an appearance on ‘Up […]
full_text: Cam Skattebo | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Cam Skattebo on Thursday put to bed the social media-created idea that there is a rift between the running back and New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh . “There’s that video going around of me and Harbaugh on the sidelines of ”not liking” what I said or whatever,“ Skattebo acknowledged during an appearance on ‘Up & Adams’ with Kay Adams. “I think the conversation was just less of a happy, joking conversation. It was just kind of a more serious conversation. It wasn’t nothing negative or nothing positive. There was just no emotion that needed to be shown.” Skattebo went on to explain that the conversation was about whether it was “more messed up” to knee the ball at the opponent’s 1-yard line or to go ahead and score. The Giants had quarterback Jake Haener take a knee to end their 23-6 preseason victory over the New York Jets. Skattebo said Harbaugh is “awesome.” “He’s just tough, man. He’s keeping the way you need to coach football in football,” Skattebo said. “A lot of the guys they get all this money and they get older and they don’t want to go out and practice hard and be in full pads every day. “He’s brought this culture where we’re gonna practice, we’re gonna practice for every minute that we’re allowed to … and we’re gonna do it in pads as much as we possibly can because that’s how football is played. “I really enjoy that.” Adams asked Skattebo about Harbaugh’s “infectious disease” comment after Skattebo got into a practice skirmish with defensive teammates. “Me and Harbs, we’re on the same page. We love each other. We’re awesome,” Skattebo said. “Me and him talk every single day. There’s no bad blood between us.” Skattebo said the remark was meant to illustrate that “what I did was infectious, an infectious disease, in that moment. Not that I’m an infectious disease person … I don’t think it was anything that was a big deal.” "Me and [John Harbaugh], we're on the same page, we love each other." 📝 🤔🙃😊☺️ pic.twitter.com/CcvRanquq3 — Kay Adams (@heykayadams) September 3, 2026

One fewer this season. This is the same captains list as last year … minus A.J. Brown, Reed Blankenship, and Jake Elliott … and plus DeVonta Smith and Jordan Davis. Can’t recall a time when an Eagles player was in Elliott’s position of previously being a multi-year captain in Philly … only to then lose that captaincy. That’s interesting. Experienced veterans who were notably not named captains: Elliott, Landon Dickerson, Cam Jurgens, Jonathan Greenard (previously a captain on the Vikings). title: Eagles News: “Don’t be surprised if Philadelphia has the NFL’s best defense”
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! I’m sure no one would disagree that the ceiling for Philadelphia’s defense is the league’s best. It was a top 10 unit last year and they arguably got better. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … 2026 NFL bold predictions: […]
full_text: Jul 30, 2026; Philadelphia, PA, USA; Philadelphia Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio speaks with the media during training camp at Jefferson Health Training Complex. Mandatory Credit: Bill Streicher-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to The Linc, the daily links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! I’m sure no one would disagree that the ceiling for Philadelphia’s defense is the league’s best. It was a top 10 unit last year and they arguably got better. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … 2026 NFL bold predictions: Potential surprises for 32 teams – ESPN PHILADELPHIA EAGLES — Don’t be surprised if … they have the best defense in the NFL this season. What I’m hearing: The questions on offense in Philadelphia are myriad and totally legitimate. The new coordinator, Sean Mannion, is a first-time playcaller and in just his third year as a coach at any level. Longtime offensive line coach Jeff Stoutland’s departure leaves a void, too. The Eagles also traded their best receiver to the Patriots in A.J. Brown. And on and on. Regardless, the Vic Fangio defense should be an absolute monster. Sure, the Jonathan Greenard pec strain is a blow to the pass rush, but he shouldn’t be out too long, and the Eagles expect guys such as Moro Ojomo to contribute there in the meantime. Jihaad Campbell should make an impact in his second season at linebacker, too. The secondary, fortified by the free agent addition of Riq Woolen, is ascending and already Super Bowl-tested. The interior defensive line duo of Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis is a strength. And the continuity under Fangio is a big reason to believe this unit will only be better. The Eagles look like the kind of defense that can carry a transitioning offense through early-season growing pains. NFL’s top 10 defenses in 2026? Texans, Seahawks, Rams headline ranking; don’t sleep on Jags, Bucs – NFL.com Defensive tackles Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis can wreck games with raw power right up the gut. Defensive backs Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean were just named first-team All-Pro in Year 2. And at linebacker, Philadelphia has a Pro Bowler with veteran savvy (Zack Baun) and a versatile sophomore with immense upside (Jihaad Campbell). What’s missing from Vic Fangio’s arsenal? An established edge rush. The Eagles have ranked in the bottom half of the league in pressure rate for three seasons running. Midseason trade acquisition Jaelan Phillips routinely heated up quarterbacks in the back half of last year, but then he signed a megadeal with Carolina in free agency. The Eagles attempted to mitigate that loss by trading for (and immediately extending) Jonathan Greenard, but the 29-year-old has been plagued this summer by a nagging pectoral injury. On the plus side, Greenard was taken off the PUP list and included in the initial 53-man roster, meaning he could be nearing a return to action. With an edge group that’s longer on promise than production (SEE: 25-year-olds Jalyx Hunt and Nolan Smith), Philly needs Greenard to provide the kind of steady disruption we saw in 2023 and ‘24. Who Will Have the NFL’s Best Defense in 2026? – The Ringer 4) EAGLES. Philadelphia actually improved its pressure rate last year, but holes emerged in the secondary and opposing quarterbacks picked at them. In particular, the outside corner spot opposite All-Pro Quinyon Mitchell was a revolving door of mediocrity, and the Eagles are hoping that enigmatic Riq Woolen—whom they acquired in free agency—can plug that leak this season. It’s never a great sign when a defensive coach as highly regarded as Macdonald is in Seattle finds no need for a player in his defense, but Woolen is clearly more talented than the Eagles’ options last year. Philadelphia also added linebacker Jonathan Greenard to give them a stronger outside pass rush. Camp hype is peaking for a potential breakout season from Jalyx Hunt as a difference-making edge rusher. The Eagles also have a ton of excellent space defenders over the middle and an All-Pro nickel in Cooper DeJean, and they’re optimistic about Jalen Carter, who flashed dominant interior line play in 2025 but was inconsistent and battled injury. Philadelphia Eagles live chat: Ask me anything – BGN Enjoyed answering your questions. I’ll try to get to any you still have for me if you leave them in the linked article. Leave your questions in the comment section (sign up for a free account if you haven’t already) and I’ll do my best to answer whatever you throw at me. Whether it’s about Darius Cooper (The GOAT), Jalen Hurts, Sean Mannion, training camp takeaways, recent roster cuts, the upcoming season, the best places for food if you’re visiting Philly for a game this year, the new SB Nation app (which you should download!) , the return of The NFC East Mixtape podcast , my new role working with the PHLY Eagles crew for Eagles gameday coverage , the Phillies’ postseason outlook, or anything else, let’s get into it! Please subscribe on YouTube and hit that like button. There is officially less than a week to go until the 2026 NFL season starts and when it does we will have two games between all four NFC East teams. What are some important things about each squad as we get ready to dive in? More specifically, what are some sneaky important things? RJ Ochoa and Brandon Gowton discuss on the latest edition of the NFC East Mixtape. You can see that we have a BRAND NEW NFC East Mixtape YouTube Channel so make sure to subscribe as the show will live here exclusively in video format. BUT you can also listen to the show! On Blogging The Boys and/or Bleeding Green Nation podcast feeds as well as the SB Nation NFL Show feed! Handing out 10 awards from Eagles 2026 training camp – PhillyVoice 1) The ‘I Dunno’ Award 🤷‍♂️: The Eagles’ offense. The Eagles’ offensive line is heading into this season healthier than it was last season. Lane Johnson is good to go, Cam Jurgens’ back seems fine, and a bunch of depth guys showed during training camp that they’re ready to contribute, if needed. I feel good about the line heading into this season. They could be a top three type of line again. I also feel good about DeVonta Smith. He is built mentally to be an alpha receiver, and he has the physical skills to pull it off. The rest? Ehhhhhh, we’ll see. Can the rest of the Eagles receivers at least keep opposing defenses from giving Smith excessive extra attention? Are the tight ends good enough? Will the run game flourish in an entirely new scheme? Will the timing of the passing offense and intricacies of the play action game gel quickly? Or will that be a season-long struggle? And finally, will Jalen Hurts bounce back from a shaky season in 2025? I don’t know. All of the above can go either way. We’ll see! Excited to See – Iggles Blitz Jalen Hurts will be in the new offense. He was up and down this summer, as I expected. While there will be ups and downs in the regular season as well, I expect him to be better. He’ll have a true gameplan to work with instead of installing plays or running them for the second or third time. He’ll have a full complement of starters around him. Throwing to DeVonta Smith with Lane Johnson blocking for you is better than throwing to Hollywood Brown with Fred Johnson at RT. Hurts feels like a man on a mission. I’m excited to see how he does. Saquon Barkley had a great summer. He was disappointing last year, for a variety of reasons. Like Hurts, Barkley seems really locked in. I think we could see a monster season from him. DeVonta Smith gets a chance to be WR1 after the departure of AJ Brown. Smitty isn’t physically dominant, but he is a top talent. Don’t forget that he was a Top 10 pick and won the Heisman Trophy in college. He’s not exactly chopped liver. Smitty could have a big year. Eagles mailbag: Optimism and pessimism for 2026,…

title: Three Rivers Report: Do the Steelers regret moving on from George Pickens?
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers and former head coach Mike Tomlin made a tough decision to trade star receiver George Pickens to the Dallas Cowboys amidst alleged turmoil between Pickens and the locker room. Dallas is very happy with the trade, as Pickens turned in a huge season in 2025, and the Steelers pivoted to trading for […]
full_text: The Pittsburgh Steelers and former head coach Mike Tomlin made a tough decision to trade star receiver George Pickens to the Dallas Cowboys amidst alleged turmoil between Pickens and the locker room. Dallas is very happy with the trade, as Pickens turned in a huge season in 2025, and the Steelers pivoted to trading for talented receiver DK Metcalf from Seattle and rewarded him with a huge extension. Hindsight is 20/20, but Pickens has flourished and clearly matured by playing on the franchise tag with no pushback, while Metcalf has been on social media arguing with fans and even taking pictures of people and making fun of their appearance. Now, if Metcalf performs very well, nobody will care about the off-the-field antics, but if he doesn’t, the talk will only grow surrounding his demeanor and immaturity. The 2026 season will be huge for Metcalf. For now, here is Friday’s Three Rivers Report.
