title: Steelers 2026 record prediction
summary: We are nine days away from the Pittsburgh Steelers’ 2026 season officially beginning when they host the Atlanta Falcons in Week 1. With the season (finally) here, I’ll be going game by game and predicting every contest on the Steelers’ schedule. Ryland Bickley did his own game-by-game picks back in May on the day of […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - SEPTEMBER 21: Aaron Rodgers #8 of the Pittsburgh Steelers looks to pass prior to an NFL football game against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on September 21, 2025 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images We are nine days away from the Pittsburgh Steelers’ 2026 season officially beginning when they host the Atlanta Falcons in Week 1. With the season (finally) here, I’ll be going game by game and predicting every contest on the Steelers’ schedule. Ryland Bickley did his own game-by-game picks back in May on the day of the schedule release, and you can go and read that to compare our predictions. But, before then, let’s dive in. Week 1: vs. Atlanta Falcons The Falcons’ quarterback situation is a disaster. Tua Tagovailoa looked like a baby chasing bubbles in the preseason, and Michael Penix’s knees are being held together by scotch tape and hope. If there was any opponent I would have picked for a Week 1 game, Atlanta would have been it. Plus, they’ve never won a game in Pittsburgh. Steelers start the season off with a win. Final prediction: Steelers 24, Falcons 10 (1-0) Week 2: at New England Patriots The Steelers narrowly escaped Foxborough in 2025 with a win, despite forcing five turnovers. They won’t be as lucky this time, as New England will be coming off a mini-bye week after kicking off the season on Wednesday, September 9. Final prediction: Patriots 23, Steelers 17 (1-1) Week 3: vs. Cincinnati Bengals In what I expect to be a high-scoring tilt, the Steelers are able to steal the first of two matchups with the Bengals to get to 2-1 on the season. Final prediction: Steelers 31, Bengals 28 (2-1) Week 4: at Browns (Thursday night) If this were still Mike Tomlin’s team, I’d write down a loss in Sharpie. However, hopefully the Steelers’ Thursday night struggles come to an end under Mike McCarthy and they are able to handedly defeat a bad Browns team. Final prediction: Steelers 23, Browns 6 (3-1) Week 5: vs. Indianapolis Colts The Colts’ loss to the Steelers last season kick-started a downward spiral in the second half of the season. Their defense got much weaker over the offseason, and their offense lacks a true No. 1 receiver while leaning too heavily on Jonathan Taylor. It’s a game Pittsburgh should win. Final prediction: Steelers 27, Colts 19 (4-1) Week 6: at Tampa Bay Buccaneers I’m not huge on Tampa in 2026, but their draft was one that impressed me. Rueben Bain looks like he’ll be an instant impact player, and Ted Hurts could emerge as the No. 2 receiver in the offense. In a close one, Pittsburgh drops its second game of the year. Final prediction: Buccaneers 24, Steelers 23 (4-2) Week 7: vs. New Orleans Saints (Paris) I picked the Saints to win the NFC South, but Pittsburgh should bounce back against a younger team that still has a somewhat low ceiling. Final prediction: Steelers 20, Saints 16 (5-2) Week 8: vs. Cleveland Browns The Steelers haven’t lost a regular season game to the Browns at home since 2003. That won’t be changing this season. Shedeur Sanders will probably be under center by the time this game is played, or maybe he will already be pulled in favor of Dillon Gabriel. Whomever is the quarterback, the Steelers will win. Final prediction: Steelers 30, Browns 12 (6-2) Week 9: Bye I think everyone would sign up for the Steelers being 6-2 at the bye. Week 10: at Cincinnati Bengals (Sunday night) The Bengals get their win back and even the season series. Final prediction: Bengals 27, Steelers 20 (6-3) Week 11: at Philadelphia Eagles The Steelers always have a hard time in Philly. I don’t expect that to change until proven otherwise. Final prediction: Eagles 26, Steelers 16 (6-4) Week 12: vs. Denver Broncos (Black Friday) Although Denver has a high-caliber defense, the Steelers are able to hold their offense in check and avoid a third straight loss. Final prediction: Steelers 17, Broncos 13 (7-4) Week 13: vs. Houston Texans (Sunday night) In what will be Mike Tomlin’s return to Pittsburgh, the Steelers face a similar fate that they did on wild card weekend to close out their 2025 season. While the game is closer, Houston’s defense proves to be too much. Final prediction: Texans 20, Steelers 13 (7-5) Week 14: at Jacksonville Jaguars (Monday night) After losing three of their previous four games, the Steelers and their offense get back on track and defeat Jacksonville. Final prediction: Steelers 27, Jaguars 23 (8-5) Week 15: vs. Baltimore Ravens Pittsburgh has won five of the last six home games against the Ravens, and their roster is simply much better. They win in Week 15. Final prediction: Steelers 23, Ravens 17 (9-5) Week 16: vs. Carolina Panthers There is a greater than zero chance that Kenny Pickett starts this game. The Panthers will be awful. Pittsburgh wins in its easiest game of the year. Final prediction: Steelers 34, Panthers 10 (10-5) Week 17: at Tennessee Titans I’ve said all offseason that the Titans will surprise people. Cam Ward and Carnell Tate have big days as they keep their own playoff hopes alive against Pittsburgh. Final prediction: Titans 27, Steelers 21 (10-6) Week 18: at Baltimore Ravens While this game won’t be for the division, it very well could be a win-and-in situation for Baltimore. Pittsburgh prevents that from happening, sweeping the Ravens once again. Final prediction: Steelers 28, Ravens 23 (11-6) Let us know what you think in the comments . summary: Pittsburgh Steelers wideout DK Metcalf is coming off a down year, by his standards. The Steelers traded for the two-time Pro Bowler last March and then immediately signed him to a four-year extension before he put up just 59 catches, 850 yards, and six touchdowns. Considering that he currently is the seventh-highest paid wide receiver […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 16: DK Metcalf #4 of the Pittsburgh Steelers runs with the ball during an NFL football game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Acrisure Stadium on November 16, 2025 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Pittsburgh Steelers wideout DK Metcalf is coming off a down year, by his standards. The Steelers traded for the two-time Pro Bowler last March and then immediately signed him to a four-year extension before he put up just 59 catches, 850 yards, and six touchdowns. Considering that he currently is the seventh-highest paid wide receiver in the NFL, that’s not the return on investment Pittsburgh was hoping for in Year One. In Year Two, Metcalf needs to have a big year and be a bigger part of the Steelers’ offense – something Aaron Rodgers says needs to be a priority, “We gotta get the ball to DK,” Rodgers said via Mark Kaboly . “He’s our No. 1 for a reason.” Metcalf’s best season came in 2020, when he put up 1.303 yards and 10 touchdowns. Wide receivers tend to do well in head coach Mike McCarthy’s system. Dallas Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb posted three consecutive 1,100 yard seasons from 2022-24, including a 135 catch, 1,749 yard season in 2023. When taking into account all of the talent the Steelers added this offseason, that should open up more opportunities for Metcalf in the passing game, as defenses won’t be able to simply hone in on No. 4. full_text: BIRMINGHAM, ALABAMA - DECEMBER 29: Marcus Sanders Jr. #5 of the Georgia Southern Eagles looks to his sideline during the fourth quarter of the JLab Birmingham Bowl against the Appalachian State Mountaineers at Protective Stadium on December 29, 2025 in Birmingham, Alabama. (Photo by Jason Clark/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks are still on the lookout for talent, always “Chasing Edges.” Here is their latest tryout list from the VMAC as of Friday’s NFL transaction wire. We’ve already covered wide receiver Luke Floriea and undrafted rookie tackle Tristan Leigh , but as you can see, the Seahawks are hitting the small school guys pretty hard. Chandler Brayboy has a killer name, and was also a pretty accomplished WR at Elon with over 2,600 career yards and 19 TDs. The speedy 2025 UDFA ran a 4.47 40-yard dash at his pro-day and spent time on the Jacksonville Jaguars practice squad. Marcus Sanders Jr had over half of his career receptions at Georgia Southern in 2025, hauling in 50 catches for 797 yards with 5 TDs. Sanders has a career YPC average of 14.3 yards, showing his explosive capability. Layne Pryor is an intriguing TE, who was previously on the Houston Texans practice squad after an impressive pro day in 2025 for the University of Northern Iowa . He could be a fullback candidate with his testing numbers. Tight end Layne Pryor recorded the most reps on the bench press at UNI’s 2025 pro day with 31. The 6-2, 260-pound All-MVFC Honorable Mention selection recorded a 36.5-inch vertical and a nine-foot-three-inch broad jump before heading outside. On the field, Pryor ran the second-fasted 40 with a 4.60 before a 7.13 three-cone and a 4.5 shuttle. At the very least, it sure seems like the Seahawks are looking for special teams depth. Seattle returns to practice on Saturday so we might have some news on a signing coming imminently. Keep checking Field Gulls to see if any of these players make their way to the practice squad or active roster.

title: Christian Gonzalez availability for Seahawks-Patriots in question amid contract talks
summary: The New England Patriots did not have many bright moments during their Super Bowl loss to the Seattle Seahawks. However, one bright spot that helped prevent the Seahawks victory from being an even worse blowout was cornerback, Christian Gonzalez. For example, Gonzalez single-handedly prevented likely long touchdowns to both Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Rashid Shaheed. Over […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 08: Christian Gonzalez #0 of the New England Patriots breaks up a pass intended for Jaxon Smith-Njigba #11 of the Seattle Seahawks during the second quarter in Super Bowl LX at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots did not have many bright moments during their Super Bowl loss to the Seattle Seahawks. However, one bright spot that helped prevent the Seahawks victory from being an even worse blowout was cornerback, Christian Gonzalez. For example, Gonzalez single-handedly prevented likely long touchdowns to both Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Rashid Shaheed . Over his first few years in the league, Gonzalez has clearly proven himself to be one of the best cornerbacks in the NFL. This is why he has been at the center of contract extension talks, much like Devon Witherspoon was earlier this summer. Witherspoon (who has the same agent as Gonzalez) was able to sign a long-term extension, making himself the highest paid cornerback in NFL history . By virtue of timing ( and Robert Kraft’s own statement ), Gonzalez is widely expected to surpass that number. However, negotiations between Gonzalez and the Patriots do not seem to be going so great. It has gotten to the point where Gonzalez has been coy about his availability to play in week one against the Seahawks. When asked if he will play on Wednesday night against Seattle, Gonzalez responded, “I’m focused on today.” #Patriots CB Christian Gonzalez on if he’ll play Wednesday night vs. the Seahawks: “I’m focused on today.” When asked specifically about Seattle, Gonzalez made sure to praise the organization and how well they’ve kept players. 👀 (🎥 @lauwalsh10 ) pic.twitter.com/BXdNGyMpMk https://t.co/gA5flm3JJs — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) September 3, 2026 Gonzalez could very well end up playing for the Patriots in Week 1. However, this response to a fairly simple question is not the best message New England fans want to hear entering their 2026 season. In the event that Gonzalez does not suit up against Seattle, that will be a huge blow to the Mike Vrabel led defense. Gonzalez’s status will definitely be one for Seahawks fans to keep on eye on.

full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 10: Khalid Kareem #92 of the Atlanta Falcons reacts after the game against the New Orleans Saints at Caesars Superdome on November 10, 2024 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Ella Hall/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers are signing edge rusher Khalid Kareem from the Atlanta Falcons’ practice squad, according to Greg Auman of Fox Sports . Kareem spent the previous two seasons with 49ers defensive coordinator Raheem Morris in Atlanta. According to Auman, Kareem is en route to Melbourne, suggesting he’ll play in Week 1. This move is a necessity, as Sam Okuayinonu was recently ruled out with a foot injury . It’s as close to a 1-for-1 swap as it gets. Kareem is 6’4″, 268 pounds. Okuayinonu is 6’1″, 269 pounds. Kareem came into the NFL with his arm length in the 83rd percentile and his hands in the 95th percentile. Morris will likely rely on Kareem to be disruptive against the run, much like Okuayinonu is when he’s on the field. As close as a 1-for-1 swap with Sam Okuayinonu as it gets. Kareem played against the Rams in Week 17 last year with the Falcons, so there's no guesswork for Raheem Morris. Kareem made this play on 4th & 1 in the first quarter. I'd sign him for the celly alone. https://t.co/Mjl7T89qtN pic.twitter.com/mvNURKFN5R — Kyle Posey (@KP_Show) September 4, 2026 Kareem doesn’t have a ton of experience, despite being drafted in the 5th round of the 2020 NFL Draft. Since 2022, he’s played fewer than 200 snaps. Kareem appeared in four games last season, but never surpassed 26 snaps in a game. Kareem had four stops in 31 snaps on the edge last season, along with five quarterback pressures. One of those stops and pressures came against the Rams in Week 17. So there’s no real guesswork as to how Kareem can hold up against Sean McVay’s offense. That’s a benefit. Depending on Romello Height’s ankle injury , this may not be the final move the 49ers make ahead of Week 1. What these injuries are doing is putting more on Nick Bosa and Keion White’s plates. Remember, the 49ers added Kevin Givens to the practice squad. He could be a game-day activation and play on the edge to give the defense a bigger body against the Rams’ heavy personnel sets. Robert Saleh did that with Givens occasionally last season when the team was shorthanded on the edge. The team has not announced a corresponding move yet. If Okuayinonu’s injury is serious, we could see the 49ers place him on the Injured Reserve. Kyle’s update, 6:46 p.m. PT : The team officially placed Sam Okuayinonu on the Injured Reserve List.

title: Sean McVay says Aaron Donald will be traveling with Rams to Australia
summary: Last we heard about Aaron Donald going to Australia, all we knew was the Los Angeles Rams were trying to “figure out” the recently retired defensive lineman’s status for Week 1. Friday, Rams head coach Sean McVay told reporters that Donald will be making the trip to Australia, though there was no confirmation on if Donald would […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - JANUARY 14: Aaron Donald #99 of the Los Angeles Rams stands on the sidelines during the national anthem prior to an NFL wild-card playoff football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on January 14, 2024 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last we heard about Aaron Donald going to Australia, all we knew was the Los Angeles Rams were trying to “figure out” the recently retired defensive lineman’s status for Week 1. Friday, Rams head coach Sean McVay told reporters that Donald will be making the trip to Australia , though there was no confirmation on if Donald would play. This can go one of two ways. If Donald is making that trip to Australia, then there’s a good chance he’s going to play. It’s hard to fathom a player making a trip like that just to sit on the sidelines. Then again, Donald could want to just be with his teammates, and the coaches don’t want him to be rushed back. It could also be some gamesmanship from the Rams, getting the 49ers to prepare for Donald rather than assuming he won’t play Sunday. The takeaway is that this doesn’t confirm whether Donald is playing. Obviously, if Donald wasn’t on the flight, it’s that’s another story—which would work to the 49ers’ advantage. That hasn’t happened. The 49ers already took off for Australia this week. The Rams will be flying out a bit later. The two different travel plans for this odd situation will be a talking point leading up to Thursday and possibly after the game. While it would be fortunate for the 49ers to not be playing against someone who has wrecked things for them more than once in a matter of seconds in a game, Donald hasn’t played a snap in two seasons. So even if he does play, we don’t know what version of Aaron Donald the world will be getting. That said, fans would probably rather not even have that question answered in Week 1 and have Donald come back after the 49ers and Rams have played.

title: Will the 49ers need to manage Mike Evans’ snaps this season?
summary: Last season was the first season Mike Evans didn’t have 100 targets since he entered the NFL in 2014. To give you an idea of the type of wide receiver the San Francisco 49ers are getting, ’25 was also the first time Evans fell below 50 percent in contested situations since 2017. Last season was […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CA - JUNE 03: Mike Evans #5 of the San Francisco 49ers looks on during a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on June 3, 2026 in Santa Clara, CA. (Photo by Matthew Huang/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Last season was the first season Mike Evans didn’t have 100 targets since he entered the NFL in 2014. To give you an idea of the type of wide receiver the San Francisco 49ers are getting, ’25 was also the first time Evans fell below 50 percent in contested situations since 2017. Last season was the first time Evans played single-digit games. After just turning 33 in August and dealing with a couple of different injuries in training camp and the preseason, Kyle Shanahan said Evans is unlikely to practice every day of the week during the regular season. Will they manage his usage during the games? ESPN’s Ben Solak named Evans the X-Factor this season, and believes that might be the case: I loved the Evans signing. Getting Kyle Shanahan the type of receiver he had lacked since becoming the head coach of the 49ers — a big, long, downfield ball-winner, short-yardage specialist and red zone mismatch — opened new and exciting possibilities in the offense. Evans is also much better on the classic 49ers routes than he’s given credit for. Among all receivers over the past two seasons, Evans is third in yards per route run (6.1) on deep, in-breaking routes. His 6-foot-5, 230-pound frame is hard to miss in the middle of the field. But Evans is 33 years old, so managing his snaps is important. Once Ricky Pearsall was ruled out for the season because of a right UCL tear, I was worried Evans would take too many snaps this season, especially coming off a hamstring injury in 2025. And then Evans started to miss time in camp: a quad strain in late July, then some talk about groin issues. Worrisome drumbeats for an older receiver in August. I still really like the blend of skills in a 49ers receivers room featuring Evans, rookie De’Zhaun Stribling , and veterans Deebo Samuel Sr . and Demarcus Robinson . But if Evans cannot stay on the field or is absent of twitch when he’s on it, there’s not enough downfield playmaking in the group (unless Stribling is the Offensive Rookie of the Year). The floor for any Shanahan-led offense is very high, but the ceiling this year is set by Evans. The stat about Evans on in-breaking routes is incredible. Shanahan’s bread and butter has been high-low concepts that put second-level defenders in conflict, which helps part the middle of the defense like the Red Sea. We’ll likely find out the hard way whether Evans needs to be managed throughout the season. If he’s continually listed on the injury report, gets nicked up during games, or needs to miss a series or two, that could very well be the case. But there’s also a lot of history suggesting Evans can play through injuries. The 49ers are treating him with kid gloves, and for good reason. Evans is good enough to propel the offense into a tier that makes them Super Bowl contenders. The prudent move is to ensure you have him available for all 17 games.

title: 2 different travel plans add to the Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay rivalry
summary: The San Francisco 49ers landed in Australia yesterday, or today, depending on the time zone used. The Los Angeles Rams plan to fly in the day before the game and leave right after. Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay are on differing sides of travel plans, which only adds to the rivalry between the two coaches. […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - OCTOBER 2: Head Coach of the Los Angeles Rams with Head Coach Kyle Shanahan of the San Francisco 49ers on the field after the game at SoFi Stadium on October 2, 2025 in Inglewood, California. The 49ers defeated the Rams 26-23. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers landed in Australia yesterday, or today, depending on the time zone used. The Los Angeles Rams plan to fly in the day before the game and leave right after. Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay are on differing sides of travel plans, which only adds to the rivalry between the two coaches. The thought process of landing early is so the 49ers can acclimate to the time zone and won’t hop off the plane and head straight to the stadium. Given the age and injury status of the 49ers roster, this isn’t a bad idea and will allow the players time to work through any swelling or anything else caused by the long flight. The Rams are on the opposite side. After their travel plans of get in and get out worked last season in London against the Jaguars, McVay is sticking with the “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” motto. Throttling the Jaguars is a good reference point for the travel discussion. So, which coach is right? Truthfully, if the 49ers win on Thursday, it won’t be because of their travel plans, and if they lose, it isn’t because the Rams are “smarter.” Still, that’s how it will be framed based on the outcome of the game. Executing an effective game plan against the Rams’ defense has little to do with travel plans. The worry is that if the Rams come out flat and the 49ers take advantage, the blame will shift to flying in so close to kickoff. As an NFL head coach, you have to give your team every advantage possible, and both coaches are doing what they think is best in this odd situation of playing down under. The funniest part will be the result of this game adding to the Shanahan/McVay debate on who is the better and smarter coach. That argument should be determined by the results on the field, not the differing traveling ideologies.

title: The 49ers’ cap space allows them to be aggressive ahead of the trade deadline
summary: Heading into the regular season, no team has more cap space in 2026 than the San Francisco 49ers. In fact, according to Over the Cap, the 49ers’ $45.8 million is more than $12 million more than Robert Saleh’s Titans. Of course, teams are mindful of spending, as they need to keep future contracts and extensions in […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 13: San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch enters the field prior to a preseason NFL football game against the Tennessee Titans at Levi's Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Heading into the regular season, no team has more cap space in 2026 than the San Francisco 49ers. In fact, according to Over the Cap, the 49ers’ $45.8 million is more than $12 million more than Robert Saleh’s Titans. Of course, teams are mindful of spending, as they need to keep future contracts and extensions in mind. On the surface, the Niners are over the cap in 2028 with just 42 players. But that is still accounting for Brandon Aiyuk’s $42.35 million cap hit in ’28. I’m going to go out on a limb and say Aiyuk won’t be on the roster in 2028 — just a hunch. The 49ers have the financial flexibility to add an impact player on ahead of the trade deadline. According to general manager John Lynch, the team can make it easy on the front office if they’re going to consider making any deals: Win. Lynch told The San Francisco Standard, That’s not like a charge to a team, ‘Hey, you want us to keep adding? Go earn it. But that’s just the reality of this league. Put yourself in position, then if it fits and the deal’s right, then yeah. I think our history shows we’re not averse to that, but I do believe you have to put yourself in position to even have those conversations.” The Niners have been linked to pass rushers all offseason. That won’t change after Sam Okauyinonu was ruled out for Week 1 with a foot injury. If Sam O is out for multiple weeks, and Mykel Williams misses the first four games on the PUP , the need for another capable body becomes dire. Maxx Crosby remains on the radar. The Raiders are starting Kirk Cousins in 2026. If they have a winning record by the trade deadline in that division, Cousins will have worked miracles. There were some names thrown out as potential trade targets in a feed post earlier this week: The one worth pushing the chips into the middle of the table is Jared Verse. He’s 26 with two years left on his rookie contract. In theory, you could exercise Verse’s fifth-year option. Realistically, you’re signing him to an extension after this season. He won’t be cheap, but it’d be worth it. You’d also have an easier time convincing Verse to sign an extension as opposed to the Browns. Plus, there’s a little added incentive, as he’d have the opportunity to stick it to the Rams twice a year, and potentially again in the playoffs. These are the kinds of discussions the 49ers will have over the next couple of months. That is, if they win.

full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JANUARY 11: Sam Okuayinonu #91 of the San Francisco 49ers lines up before the snap during an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on January 11, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images In news that came as no surprise, the 49ers will be without defensive end Sam Okuayinonu for their season opener. The Niners initially listed Okuayinonu as questionable with a foot injury and he did not make the long journey to Melbourne, Australia with the rest of the team on Thursday as they prepare to face the Los Angeles Rams next week. That was a clear sign Okuayinonu would likely not be hopping on a later plane to join the team and make his season debut, and the 49ers have now downgraded him to out. It is a significant setback at a position where the 49ers have scant depth. Okuayinonu would have been expected to start at defensive end across from Nick Bosa. In his absence, Keion White will be the favorite to take that spot, with rookie Romello Height — who has been dealing with an ankle injury — seemingly set for a decent workload if deemed healthy to play. San Francisco has Ogbo Okoronkwo and Vincent Anthony Jr. on the practice squad. With Okuayinonu out, it appears inevitable Okoronkwo will be elevated to the gameday roster. The 49ers are already trying to piece things together at defensive end before a ball has even been snapped in the regular season. Bosa is their only outside pass rusher whom the Rams will fear and he has been dealing with knee tendinitis following his ACL reconstruction. It is a desperate situation for the Niners to be in up front, and Okuayinonu’s absence makes it worse.

title: Titans GM Mike Borgonzi expertly navigated 53-man roster cuts
summary: The Tennessee Titans had to waive or release a minimum of 37 players when cutting down from 90 to 53 by Sunday’s deadline. General manager Mike Borgonzi did not stop there. After successfully making three waiver claims, and signing two veterans via free agency, Borgonzi had to waive/release an additional five players. After finalizing the […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - JANUARY 22: New General Manager Mike Borgonzi of the Tennessee Titans reacts during an introductory press conference at Ascension Saint Thomas Sports Park on January 22, 2025 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Tennessee Titans had to waive or release a minimum of 37 players when cutting down from 90 to 53 by Sunday’s deadline . General manager Mike Borgonzi did not stop there. After successfully making three waiver claims , and signing two veterans via free agency, Borgonzi had to waive/release an additional five players. After finalizing the initial 53-man roster, the Titans were awarded LB Owen Pappoe, CB Melvin Smith , and DT Nazir Stackhouse off waivers. They signed S Terrell Burgess and OT James Hudson in free agency. To make room, they waived CB Erick Hallett II, WR Xavier Restrepo, LB Mo Diabate, S Jerrick Reed II, and released OT Austin Deculus. These moves were swiftly met with mixed reviews. Fans were especially disappointed to see Restrepo get waived , after the fan-favorite sophomore wideout initially made the 53-man roster. Hallett was also a worthwhile inclusion on the initial 53 after playing well during training camp and the preseason. What came next proved Borgonzi navigated 53-man roster cuts with proven expertise. All four waiver-eligible Titans cleared waivers and re-signed back to the practice squad. Restrepo, Diabate, Hallett, and Reed all landed back with the Titans’ practice squad. In fact, the only post-53-roster-cut who didn’t re-sign back to Tennessee’s practice squad was Deculus. Deculus, a vested veteran, did not have to clear waivers and was immediately free to sign with any team of his choosing. After a terrible preseason period, it’s likely Tennessee didn’t want him back anyway. Appropriately navigating roster cuts means upgrading the talent on your 53-man squad while understanding who you can successfully pass through waivers. Borgonzi did that well, getting back all of his desired assets via the practice squad. Malik Herring was the only Titans cut who joined a rival 53-man roster. Borgonzi knows how to structure a 53-man roster and practice squad.

summary: The Daily Slop – 5 September 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 26: Jayden Daniels #5 of the Washington Commanders attempts to break a tackle against Cooper DeJean #33 of the Philadelphia Eagles during the first quarter in the NFC Championship Game at Lincoln Financial Field on January 26, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 5 September 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Sports Illustrated How an Injury-Plagued 2025 Can Help Jayden Daniels in the Long Run The Commanders’ starting QB and breakout star in 2024 is anxious to show the football world what he’s been working on for the past five months They will give Daniels more responsibility, and command at the line, which the quarterback himself thinks leans into one of his strengths. Learning a new system, with longer, more verbose calls and more variables before the snap, is one thing. But applying it is another, and the call-it periods, where Daniels couldn’t see what was coming on a script, were built to accelerate his ability to do that. Quinn also hired a Brian Flores disciple, Daronte Jones, to run a system that might be the NFL’s most complex, which only adds to how difficult the summer was going to be for Daniels. The response from Daniels? As the coaches saw it, he looked like a quarterback who couldn’t get enough of it, and wanted to be pushed the way he was. “I like the vibe that they create together”, [said Dan Quinn], “because they push one another in a way of, O.K., I don’t know if we can get all this , and, of course, Jayden is like, Put the play in, the protection in, everything . I like that they are hungry in that way together.” And the results, in the quarterback’s eyes, are already showing up. In a nutshell, he has more room to talk in the huddle. The reward? He has the autonomy to put his own twist on whatever the call is. Jayden Daniels on Commanders OC David Blough’s scheme: “The balance of play-action passes, the bootlegging, stuff that we’re able to run to marry up with our run game, get those guys moving laterally, it’s going to help out to be able to get some shots in to showcase what I can… pic.twitter.com/zVOlH1Ffvz — SleeperNFL (@SleeperNFL) September 4, 2026 The flexibility there, Daniels learned, extends to actually being able to change things on the fly—which, philosophically, should allow the Commanders to go to unscripted things right up until the snap, based on what the defense is showing the QB. The offense has a lot of answers baked in, and gives Daniels the latitude to come up with his own. Great nugget from the @AlbertBreer piece on Jayden Daniels via SI today. Apparently DQ shortened the play clock in practices. pic.twitter.com/q18peqWpH0 — Grant Paulsen (@GrantPaulsen) September 4, 2026 “I’m getting more comfortable, where I might call a play and I know the final formation, but I might put a little shift or a motion on it beforehand, and [Blough] doesn’t know that I’m doing that,” he said. “So we break the huddle, and honestly, he’s thinking that we f—ed up; I might have called a play wrong. And he’s screaming, and I’m just giving him one of those— I got it . And he’s like, O.K., he’s got it. He’s doing his own little thing . “Honestly, how we look as an offense, I’m super excited to see how Blough can call a game,” Daniels said. “You get 60 plays in the game, so how he schemes up a lot of different things, because there are times where [Sean] McVay or the guys like Ben Johnson, KOC, they scheme people open based on what they’re watching and tendencies. So I’m excited for that.” Commanders QB Jayden Daniels is anxious to show the football world what he’s been working on for the past five months after an injury-plagued 2025, writes @AlbertBreer pic.twitter.com/wXcXF48WPw — Sports Illustrated (@SInow) September 4, 2026 To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated Fast, Physical and Joyful: Inside Daronte Jones’ Vision for Commanders Defense Fast and physical can be considered buzzwords because they come up so often in conversations about pretty much any NFL defense, but Reaves included joy, which is a bit different and shows another layer of Jones’ vision for Washington. “He’s a very intelligent dude, very passionate guy. He loves ball, and he loves to teach football. The guys that are out there will love ball and will love to learn, and love to, you know, celebrate each other, not just themselves. That’s the genetic makeup of him.” Clearly, the desired identity Jones wants goes far beyond how the team plays physically; it focuses on how each player communicates and responds to the others. Another major offseason emphasis for Washington has been creating more takeaways. Rather than waiting for those opportunities, Reaves explained that the Commanders are trying to make attacking the football automatic. “We’ve programmed the subconscious to always think about the ball,” Reaves said. “We work drills every day, and we work things every day to where even if the whistle’s blown, right, we’re still punching at the ball. You never know when the ball is going to come out.” That repetition is designed to make defenders recognize the vulnerable moments an offensive player presents without having to stop and think about it. “Just always training your mind to go after it because there are vulnerable positions when the offense does have the ball, and we have to maximize those opportunities to take it off of them.” The approach fits directly into the fast and physical part of Jones’ identity. Playing aggressively is one thing, but doing it with purpose gives Washington a chance to turn tackles into game-changing possessions. So, the Commanders are doing everything they can to overcome that obstacle by getting comfortable with silent counts. “There’s a couple different ones that we use,” head coach Dan Quinn said. “So, just getting the reps at that. We’ve done some in the evenings and the walkthroughs and just more volume of it, honestly. Most teams like us have more than one that they use and so you can kinda lean into one. Now I need more work at the second one, but Nick’s experience really shows through on that.” The Commanders spent much of the offseason hyping up Allegretti’s intelligence and experience as the main reasons they’re giving him a chance at center. He’s spent most of his career at guard — 2,553 snaps, to be exact — but he feels like center is his natural position. The Commanders feel like his ability to make protection calls at the line of scrimmage will be a boon for the offensive line and raise the performance of the entire group. Allegretti believes he is ready for the challenge, even if it is against one of the best teams in the conference. “I feel really comfortable with Jayden,” Allegretti said. “I always communicated with him like I was a center, just because that’s who I am at my core … Happy to be back there. full_text: The Washington Commanders’ NFL draft class has been working within the organization for months now. The selections have immersed themselves in the organizational culture, strength and conditioning programs and offensive/defensive systems they’ll be asked to execute starting Sept. 13 against the Philadelphia Eagles . We’ve learned a ton about how they’re fitting in, with far less leaning on draft profiles and college tape for reference. That has provided a clearer picture of these prospects – that term applies until we see them play significant regular-season snaps – and what they’ll realistically contribute during the 2026 campaign. Those thoughts will evolve over time, as we see how they adjust and develop to the NFL game. Let’s go over where they are right now and how much of an instant impact general manager Adam Peters’ draft class can make: LB Sonny Styles Don’t get the consternation over Sonny Styles these past few weeks. Never did. Never will. On-site reporters typically lauded Styles’ performance during training camp, while also mentioning some missteps. Everyone else poured over 29 preseason snaps, with most focusing on some faults. What a freaking shock the rookie in his third-ever season at linebacker looked hesitant at times in that sample size. He didn’t play everything perfectly? He didn’t look like the second coming of Chris Hanburger or London Fletcher ? You don’t say. Overall, he did just fine. Not sure who expected that off the jump or to even start the regular season. Styles will be just fine. There’s no harm in Frankie Luvu taking some pre-snap responsibilities. He’ll be a defensive mainstay and coordinator Daronte Jones will add things to his plate when appropriate. Confidence in Styles shouldn’t wane. He’s a rookie. He has a great work ethic, elite athleticism and want to. He’s learning and developing. He’s going to be a playmaker as a rookie. Book it. WR Antonio Williams The third-round pick out of Clemson really turned it on during training camp’s later stages, with observers highlighting moments that showed advanced technique and separation ability for a rookie. Despite quality depth in his position group, it’s fair to expect Antonio Williams will be the No. 3 option, either in the slot or outside at or near the regular season opener. Those are lofty expectations for a Day 2 pick playing a position with a difficult NFL transition, but Williams has shown himself well and is earning trust with the Commanders staff. Will he make an impact similar to fellow third-rounder Terry McLaurin (58-919-7)? Never say never, but that seems tough with the receiver quality in the room. A profound impact is in the cards. Don’t panic if he starts slow and his playing time dips. The Commanders have the talent to step and let him develop and prepare for a future time in the spotlight. EDGE Joshua Josephs The fifth-rounder from Tennessee has shown flashes during training camp and the preseason. I mean, anyone see that all-effort fumble recovery versus Detroit?!? Joshua Josephs also got plenty of first-team work with Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson out, which will help in the long term. Josephs is far from a finished product (obviously) and, as our Jamual Forrest points out , the edge rusher must learn to stay disciplined – anyone see that long read-option touchdown allowed versus Detroit?!? — to stay on the field. He’ll be part of the edge rusher rotation behind Oweh, Chaisson and Dorance Armstrong once he returns from a one-game suspension. That’s a solid group that will allow Josephs to contribute without the requirements or heavy snap count of a feature player. That’s what you want for a promising Day 3 pick. RB Kaytron Allen The post-draft excitement about Allen was sky high. Maybe it was the Penn State rushing record or the desire to be called Fatman, but fans loved Kaytron Allen from the outset. He’s an individual worth rooting for, but he might be a short-yardage option at the start. Bill Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White will see most all of the carries, as they should considering their track records. Also, Jeremy McNichols will play an offensive role when he returns off IR . The point in saying all that: expectations should be kept realistic. There are examples of late-round running backs turning it on as rookies. Washington might not need that unless there’s an injury. To submit your NFL 2026 season predictions, just CLICK THIS LINK . OL Matt Gulbin As it stands on this Friday afternoon (Sept. 4), the Michigan state product is Nick Allegretti’s primary backup at center. Given the veteran’s calf issues this summer, that’s a vital role right now. Is Gulbin ready for full-time duty? That seems like a scary prospect considering all that’s required of a Commanders center. Unless there’s a roster addition soon, that’s how Washington will open the season. Gulbin has been complimented by many within the Commanders organization, which has had options to add a veteran backup and declined. Center seems like Gulbin’s spot over guard right now, so continued development is more important than anything. In an ideal world, Allegretti plays well, stays healthy and takes every regular-season snap. QB Athan Kaliakmanis The seventh-round pick from Rutgers played his way onto the 53-man roster with a strong camp and preseason. He wasn’t perfect by any stretch but showed arm talent and willingness to push the ball down the field. This is a long-term play, with Kaliakmanis auditioning all year for the chance to be Jayden Daniels’ backup after Marcus Mariota leaves Washington.

title: Washington’s front seven could be backbone of the 2026 Commanders
summary: Washington’s defense has been the Commanders’ demise in Dan Quinn’s tenure two years in, but the 2026 unit should bring fans a different level of optimism. The front seven especially has a chance to be the backbone of the team, and according to Commanders staff and reporters at practice, injured players are beginning to return […]
full_text: Washington’s defense has been the Commanders’ demise in Dan Quinn’s tenure two years in, but the 2026 unit should bring fans a different level of optimism. The front seven especially has a chance to be the backbone of the team, and according to Commanders staff and reporters at practice, injured players are beginning to return at the right time. Edge K’Lavon Chaisson, who suffered a knee injury during Washington’s joint practice with the Miami Dolphins, has returned to practice after being limited to side work and ultimately missing the preseason. Chaisson is an important piece of Washington’s revamped front seven and one of the team’s primary pass-rush specialists. The other, Odafe Oweh, has yet to return from his calf injury , but Dan Quinn expects him to be back at practice next week. It’s no secret that quarterback Jayden Daniels is the lifeline of this football team. Washington will ultimately go as far as he takes them. But that puts more pressure than ever on the rest of the roster to support him, and it starts with the unit where general manager Adam Peters invested heavily this offseason. During training camp, albeit in limited time, we got a glimpse of what Washington envisioned with Oweh and Chaisson. Speed and power off the edge created problems for the offensive line, and this explosive duo has easily given Washington the type of athleticism it lacked at times over the last two seasons. Beyond the star free-agent additions, however, one player who will be asked to step up sooner than initially expected is rookie edge Joshua Josephs. With Dorance Armstrong now suspended for the first game of the season, Josephs is stepping into a role where he can be an impactful presence immediately. It won’t just be about generating pressure for Josephs; staying disciplined within his assignments will be a major factor as a rookie. Rookies tend to be schemed against when quarterbacks and coaches identify who’s being rotated onto the field. It’s a big test to go up against one of the NFC’s best immediately — Washington plays at Philadelphia in Week 1 — but Joseph’s physical traits can stress any offensive lineman in the passing game. Josephs isn’t the only rookie who can make an immediate impact for this front seven. Washington’s off-ball linebackers are versatile, and No. 7 overall selection Sonny Styles is the most explosive and athletic out of the group. Defensive coordinator Daronte Jones has been conservative in the preseason, which has indirectly contributed to the national skepticism surrounding Styles. People are misrepresenting what Styles is capable of for any defensive coordinator. The one true question that does exist for Styles at this point is just how quickly the Ohio State product will adjust to the speed of the NFL. That will impact his ability to think freely and play downhill decisively. What certainly helps Styles, though, is the development of Frankie Luvu in Jones’s system. He won’t be asked to figure everything out on his own. Quinn stated this week that Luvu will share pre-snap duties with Styles, calling plays and having green dot responsibilities. Luvu’s in-scheme development could be particularly important, as Styles has a veteran resource while allowing Washington to ease him into one of the defense’s most important communication roles. Dan Quinn said linebacker is a position that requires leadership and rookie Sonny Styles has shown that. He'll work with Frankie Luvu and both players will be making calls on the field/having green dot responsibilities. pic.twitter.com/4DPGE0du2X — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) September 2, 2026 Luvu had a down year last season, like plenty of Commanders, but new coaches have ways of reigniting the flame in players simply by demonstrating their belief in them. That’s where Luvu’s added responsibilities and leadership come in, especially with the departure of Bobby Wagner, who was the defensive general for Washington the last two seasons. While optimism about the front seven’s potential is warranted, it will continue to cause problems for the team if Washington cannot stop the run,. The interior line will go as far as Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw will take them, but Tim Settle and Shy Tuttle are essential pieces in the interior line. They’ll be relied on to be difference-makers in the run game and absorb blocks while maintaining gaps. It’s a selfless role, but it allows the rest of the defense to operate effectively. The front seven will be protecting its secondary and giving that unit plenty of opportunities to make plays on the football, but if the idea is to create havoc for the opposing quarterback and get them uncomfortable, this year’s unit is the best it’s been during Quinn’s tenure. It’s Daniels first when it comes to determining how far the 2026 Commanders can go. But for me, Washington’s front seven is the clear No. 2. On the latest Trap or Dive Podcast , we do a deep dive on Washington’s defense and where exactly our confidence lies for each position group on the defense. Podcast YouTube : Comment and let us know your confidence level for each position group for Washington’s defense. Don’t forget to also subscribe to the Trap or Dive Podcast.

title: How Commanders could operate with seven receivers on 53-man roster
summary: The Commanders chose to keep seven receivers on their initial 53-man roster. That’s a bit higher than the normal five or six.   Washington was among five teams to keep seven receivers on its initial 53-man roster, with every organization having slightly different reasons for retaining that number.   Sometimes its a placeholder until other […]
full_text: The Commanders chose to keep seven receivers on their initial 53-man roster. That’s a bit higher than the normal five or six. Washington was among five teams to keep seven receivers on its initial 53-man roster, with every organization having slightly different reasons for retaining that number. Sometimes its a placeholder until other moves can be made to even things out. The Commanders have held at seven to this point for a few reasons. They’ve got punt returner Jaylin Lane in the position group. Kick returner Luke McCaffrey’s there, too. They also have deserving veterans in Treylon Burks and Dyami Brown who probably won’t take a practice squad spot (and could find work elsewhere). Terry McLaurin, Stefon Diggs and rookie third-round pick Antonio Williams are immovable objects on the roster and will be on-field mainstays during this season. That’s how you get to seven. McCaffrey was someone thought to be on the bubble, but I think there’s a decent chance he doesn’t make it through waivers. As a returner, capable slot receiver and fairly recent Day 2 draft pick , it’s highly possible someone puts in a claim. If that’s not worth the risk, then you’re sitting at seven. The Commanders are thin at other spots – cornerback comes to mind, as does running back – but there are good players at those positions who are worthy of a game-day elevation. New practice squad signing Terell Smith could help in the cornerbacks room and on special teams. Even if Robert Henry Jr. needs more development, Craig Reynolds has experience to step up and help the running backs. That allows the Commanders to continue with relative bloat at one spot. On game day, you’ll probably have an inactive receiver, likely Brown or Burks considering the special teams value with McCaffrey and Lane. The primary receiver rotations won’t change. As previously mentioned, it’s fair for McLaurin, Diggs and Williams to see the most action. Brown could be a stretch-the-field option if he’s active while Burks could be a big-bodied target, depending on the best possible matchups. Those guys can provide injury protection should something go wrong in-game. They can provide Diggs some relief should his snap counts be relatively down, as they were last season in New England . Lane has improved as a receiver and has serious speed. McCaffrey can help as a taller slot, as he has previously proven. The Commanders have options, especially with tight-end usage expected to be high. Chig Okonkwo will also play off the line, so the Commanders have tons of receiving options. Will they keep seven all season? That seems unlikely, especially if another position group gets beset by short-term injuries. The player they move in the situation could be based on performance and need as they continue to mold the roster to best serve all position groups.
author: Scott Bair

title: McBride, Wingard bury college grudge as safety joins Cardinals
summary: With college feud behind them, the Cardinals' No. 1 tight end and veteran safety are becoming fast friends.
full_text:
TEMPE, Ariz. -- For seven years, four months and 18 days, Andrew Wingard held a grudge against  Trey McBride .

 It all started with a play that has faded into a distant memory. Few can recall the moment on that Oct. 26, 2018, night, when Colorado State and Wyoming played the 110th edition of their Border War rivalry. The way Wingard, a senior on that Cowboys team, tells it, he was on the ground after making a tackle when McBride, a Rams freshman tight end at the time, speared him in the back and kneed him in the ribs.

 Wingard took offense -- and then some.

 McBride, on the other hand, contests Wingard's account of the play.

 "I don't know about the spear in the back, things like that," said McBride, currently a star tight end for the  Arizona Cardinals . "It was just playing through the whistle, whatever it is.

 "Me and him got a little tangled up. It was unfortunate, but yes, he's held a grudge for a while."

 But McBride didn't realize how long Wingard held a grudge.

 "I knew he was frustrated at the play," McBride said. "The whole fanbase was mad at me, Wyoming. But like I said, it was such a long time ago. I honestly, it kind of spaced my mind.

 "And then as you see him throughout your years and you keep playing against him, you just kind of always go back to like, man, hopefully he forgot about it, and he never did."

 Wingard had chances to let it go, but he wouldn't. He carried it from the mountains of Fort Collins, Colorado, site of Saturday's 118th Border War, to the plains of Laramie, Wyoming, to the shores of Jacksonville, Florida, to cities around the NFL. After the two faced each other in November when Wingard was still playing for the Jaguars, McBride came over to Wingard to tell him he respected him. All Wingard could say in response was "F--- you." Looking back on it now, Wingard regrets that he didn't leave his feelings inside the white lines during the 60 minutes they played.

 But in March, Wingard finally released his grudge against McBride in the Arizona desert.

 It was time, Wingard felt. The two were no longer bitter college rivals. Wingard was signing with the Cardinals as a free agent, and they were going to be teammates. As fate would have it, the first person Wingard saw when he arrived at the Cardinals' practice facility in Arizona to sign his contract on March 16 was McBride.

 "It was kind of like the 'Step Brothers' moment where it was like, OK, I'm over it sort of thing," Wingard said of the 2008 Will Ferrell comedy. "And it was funny because he was the first guy I saw when I came in and signed my contract and it was just like, all right man. Yeah, I'm over it. I'm over it.

 "So, we're cool now."

 McBride thought the moment was funny.

 "We made eye contact and the first thing he said was, 'All right man, we can be friends now because we're teammates,'" McBride said. "So, it was just cool."

 Now, Wingard said, McBride is "one of my guys on the team."

 The two have come so far, and it only took a decade.

 However, those who knew McBride and Wingard in college weren't surprised by how either acted on the play and after.

 "I can tell both players had a similar personality trait of being ultracompetitive and somewhat edgy," former Wyoming coach Craig Bohl said. Bohl convinced McBride to take a recruiting trip to Wyoming as a high schooler but knew the chances of landing McBride were "slim and none" because McBride's older brother was already at Colorado State.

 "I can tell you, if the roles were reversed, I would say Trey would probably hold a grudge that long also."

 Former Colorado State tight end Cam Butler played alongside McBride for two seasons before missing the 2020 season with a foot injury, and said McBride was "great to play with."

 "He would be an awful person to play against because he just doesn't care," Butler said.

 Former Colorado State offensive coordinator Dave Johnson couldn't think of which scuffle it was that McBride got into it with Wingard. And for good reason. It wasn't that McBride had a short fuse, but if an opponent was "putting a little mustard on a player after a tackle," then McBride wouldn't put up with that, Johnson explained.

 "Trey was known to get into scuffles," Johnson said, "so it's a little difficult to pinpoint which one you're talking about, because he was apt to be involved in a couple things during the course of games."

 And the Border War just meant emotions ran even higher.

 The two schools are separated by just 62 miles, an exact distance Bohl quickly rattled off. Bohl said he always got along with the Colorado State head coaches but knew "a lot" of the opposing players "had some spark" between them because some had known each other, grew up with each other or played each other before they got to college.

 "The Border War, it was everything for those two schools," Butler said. "We didn't like them. They didn't like us. It was that kind of thing."

 The game is played for the Bronze Boot, a trophy the winning team has kept since its introduction in 1968. The pomp and circumstance for the long, heated rivalry goes beyond the game. On Friday, the day before the game, the Wyoming ROTC will hand the game ball off to the Colorado State ROTC, which will then carry the ball back to Fort Collins.

 "It goes back years and years and years across families," Bohl said. "You've got some families where one person went to CSU, the other person went to Wyoming, and so there's respect, but there's no love lost between the two."

 Butler remembered on the Monday of one of his Wyoming game weeks, former Rams running backs coach Bryan Applewhite stood in front of the offense and instead of going over stats, like he'd typically do in that weekly meeting, Applewhite pulled up a photo of Wingard with one specific instruction: Don't let him affect the game.

 "I know Trey some, I mean, he and [Wingard], if you put those two in a box, that's why they [were so] competitive,'" Bohl said. "They ain't going to be warm, fuzzy guys.

 "Now, they're probably going to be best of friends."

title: 2026 NFL rookies guide: Stat leaders, fantasy picks, top QBs
summary: Here's what to know about this group of rookies, including Rookie of the Year front-runners, fantasy favorites and QB updates.
full_text:
Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season will feature plenty of rookie debuts. Although No. 1 draft pick Fernando Mendoza won't make an appearance for at least a few weeks, the rest of the top-five selections should have an early impact (Jets edge rusher  David Bailey , Cardinals running back  Jeremiyah Love , Titans receiver  Carnell Tate and Giants linebacker  Arvell Reese ). And there are plenty of non-first-rounders who have created preseason hype, including 49ers receiver De'Zhaun Stribling , Broncos running back Jonah Coleman  and Colts safety A.J. Haulcy .

 Which 2026 draft picks could have huge seasons? Who might contribute on your fantasy football roster? Here's our guide to everything you need to know about the rookie class.

 NFL draft analyst Jordan Reid and betting analyst Pamela Maldonado start by naming early Offensive and Defensive Rookie of the Year contenders (including their DraftKings odds to win). Then NFL analyst Matt Bowen picks five under-the-radar players to watch, national NFL reporter Dan Graziano gives notes on the rookie QBs, and fantasy analyst Eric Moody projects the top 10 rookie performers in fantasy. To cap it all off, we included Mike Clay's  projected rookie stat leaders .

 

 
 Jump to: 
 OROY candidates  | DROY candidates   
 Under-the-radar  | Fantasy picks 
 Quarterback notes  |  Projections 

 
 

 Reid's top Offensive Rookie of the Year candidates 
 

 1. Jeremiyah Love , RB, Arizona Cardinals  (+550) 
 Love became the first running back drafted in the top five since Saquon Barkley in 2018 (No. 2 overall). That obviously gives him high expectations, but he could meet them as the focal point of new coach Mike LaFleur's offense in Arizona.

 Love will not only contribute as a rusher but also as a pass catcher, where he can routinely take advantage of mismatches. In his lone preseason game against the Raiders, he showcased what he's capable of with 73 yards (58 rushing, 15 receiving) on 14 touches.

 
 

 2. Jadarian Price , RB, Seattle Seahawks  (+650) 
 Replacing reigning Super Bowl MVP   Kenneth Walker III won't be easy, but Price should bring a similar skill set to Seattle's offense. Where Price could bring more value, though, is in the passing game. Despite never surpassing double-digit receptions at Notre Dame, he showed plenty of comfort when asked to be an option out of the backfield.

 Price should also shine because of a  Brian Fleury offense featuring plays with two RBs and a mixture of downhill running concepts. His 3.96 yards after contact per rush ranked 25th among FBS rushers last season.

 
 

 3. Carnell Tate , WR, Tennessee Titans  (+600) 
 The No. 4 pick is expected to transform into a go-to target for second-year quarterback  Cam Ward . Tate is a diverse route runner who can execute routes at all levels of the field, but I expect him to stand out in the vertical passing game where he can accelerate past defenders. He averaged 17.2 yards per catch during his final season at Ohio State, which ranked seventh in the FBS among players with at least 50 receptions.

 
 

 

 4. De'Zhaun Stribling , WR, San Francisco 49ers  (+1100) 
 Stribling was a controversial pick at the top of the second round, but he had a strong preseason that included seven receptions in his first preseason game. And with  Ricky Pearsall  missing the entire season after knee surgery , Stribling should have an easier path to targets in coach Kyle Shanahan's system.

 A physical presence at 6-foot-2, 207 pounds, Stribling is also a detailed route runner who had 409 yards after the catch last season (33rd most in the FBS among all WRs). Shanahan is among the best coaches at glorifying the well-rounded skill sets of wideouts, and his work with Stribling should be no different.

 
 

 5. KC Concepcion , WR, Cleveland Browns  (+1800) 
 Concepcion is a sleeper candidate to win OROY because of the multiple ways he could shine as a rookie. He not only has inside-out versatility in new coach Todd Monken's offense, but he's also a dynamic returner who can create positive plays on special teams. In Year 1 with Monken, playmakers outside of TE Harold Fannin Jr . are still unknown. Concepcion could quickly climb the ranks of reliable options and prove to be one of the more explosive young players in the NFL.

 

 

 Maldonado's top Defensive Rookie of the Year candidates 
 

 1. Sonny Styles , LB, Washington Commanders (+750) 
 It's how Washington plans to use Styles that makes his case intriguing. The Commanders will want to take advantage of his ability on blitzes after Styles generated pressure on 20% of his blitz opportunities at Ohio State. He also had the lowest missed-tackle rate among linebackers in this draft class. That gives the No. 7 pick multiple ways to build a DROY résumé: tackles, sacks and impact plays.

 
 

 2. Arvell Reese , LB, New York Giants (+850) 
 As the No. 5 pick, Reese immediately steps into a starting role that will give him the snap volume needed to contend. The concern is what position those snaps will come from. With Abdul Carter and Brian Burns on the edges, Reese might be limited in the linebacker role. He can still contribute as a blitzer, but the Giants might barely blitz -- Dennard Wilson's defense in Tennessee last season ranked 28th in blitz rate. Reese's versatility would need to translate into enough splash plays to win this award.

 
 

 3. Dillon Thieneman , S, Chicago Bears (+2500) 
 As a calculated long shot, the first-round pick is already Chicago's starting strong safety. He should be around the ball plenty after playing 40% of his snaps in the box last season. Thieneman recorded 94 tackles in his final college season, while missing just 7.8% of his attempts.

 Safeties rarely win DROY, but the last one to do it was Mark Carrier with the Bears in 1990. Thieneman is worthy of bringing the award back home given his immediate role.

 
 

 4. Caleb Banks , DT, Minnesota Vikings (+7000) 
 Banks enters the season with a starting opportunity on Minnesota's defensive line, and he has the size to become an immediate interior disruptor. Although his college production was inconsistent, his pass-rush upside was considered among the best of the interior defensive linemen in his class.

 Coordinator Brian Flores can also move the No. 18 pick around his multiple-front defense to create favorable matchups. Banks' first-round pedigree and disruptive ability give him a reasonable path to win this award.

 
 

 5. Mansoor Delane , CB, Kansas City Chiefs (+1100) 
 The Chiefs traded up for the first-round cornerback to address a major need following the departures of Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson . Delane can also make impact plays as a blitzer for coordinator Steve Spagnuolo, generating pressure on 38% of his blitz opportunities in 2025 with LSU.

 Though only three cornerbacks have won DROY this century, he has the draft capital, starting role and versatility to be a strong candidate.

 

 

 Bowen's under-the-radar rookies 
 

 1. Malachi Fields , WR, New York Giants 
 Fields has the physical profile at 6-foot-4, 218 pounds to win one-on-one targets as the boundary X receiver. Plus, the third-rounder can get the ball on deep in-breakers and underneath throws. Fields is pushing for the No. 2 role in New York, and his skill set should complement that of WR1 Malik Nabers .

 

 
 

 2. Treydan Stukes , S, Las Vegas Raiders 
 The Raiders' second pick after drafting Mendoza, Stukes has seen reps with the first-team defense in camp. He has the range and instincts to play from depth in split-field or post alignments, and he brings a coverage element to new coordinator Rob Leonard's system. Look for Stukes to even align at the nickelback position.

 
 

 3. Jonah Coleman , RB, Denver Broncos

title: 2026 NFL season X factors: Key players for all 32 teams
summary: What do Marvin Harrison Jr., Jared Verse and Travis Hunter have in common? The success of their teams could depend on them.
full_text:
The NFL season is but five days away -- we've almost made it! And as such, we've almost talked about these NFL teams and previewed this NFL season in as many ways as we can. Almost.

 Today, I have for you my yearly look at 32 X factors -- one for each team. X factor players, as I understand them, are players who can dramatically swing the season with their individual play. A helpful way of defining an X factor is "if this team has a surprisingly great year, I'm certain that this one player had a great season." X factors are the straw in the wind -- the way they bend is the way everything will go.

 Last year's X factors featured Seahawks RB  Kenneth Walker III  (Super Bowl MVP, I dunno if you heard), Cowboys WR George Pickens and Patriots WR Stefon Diggs . It's not just the good ones who are winners, unfortunately. Bills WR Keon Coleman , Steelers OT Broderick Jones and Buccaneers LB SirVocea Dennis were also key X factors ... whose season went the wrong way.

 Finding an X factor for each team is as much about what they aren't as what they are. Here are my self-imposed X factor restrictions, which force us to talk about players who we wouldn't otherwise touch on in such detail.

 No quarterbacks. Obviously , an elite season at quarterback will have a bigger impact on the team than any other position. Same with a disastrous one. Some quarterback X factors are certainly bigger than others (What if Kyler Murray is lights-out in Minnesota? What if Bryce Young falls apart in Carolina?). But all quarterbacks are huge factors. Which means none of them made this list.

 No coaches . See above quarterback explanation. All coaches are X factors, so we're not going to talk about them here.

 No rookies . Every team will experience a huge and surprising leap if it drafts  Puka Nacua in the fifth round. I think Bryce Lance is a huge X factor for the Saints, but there isn't much to say about it besides "drafting a starting wide receiver on Day 3 is really helpful." Safely assume I think every rookie your team drafted (and even a few of the UDFAs) are X factors, and read on.

 Now that we've defined what an X factor is (and isn't), we can get into the nitty-gritty. There were a few good candidates for each team, but I had to land on one per franchise (or cheat and do two -- which I did). Here they are, starting with a desperately needed breakout in Arizona.

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 NFC WEST 
 

 Arizona Cardinals : WR Marvin Harrison Jr . 
 There are only a few players on the Cardinals' roster who I'm confident are above-average starters. On defense, there is safety Budda Baker and edge rusher Josh Sweat , and tight end Trey McBride and wide receiver Michael Wilson on offense. With rookie and third pick Jeremiyah Love , a prospect I loved coming out of Notre Dame, we are close to a third offensive player -- all skill position guys.

 So imagine if Harrison can take a leap under a new offensive coaching staff. New head coach Mike LaFleur, a branch off the old Sean McVay tree, comes from an offense that doesn't typically enjoy a traditional X-receiver -- 6-foot-4, big frame, running all sorts of sideline routes. As such, it's fair to expect the Cardinals to move Harrison around the formation more than he has been to this point in his career. Over the past two seasons, 78.6% of Harrison's targets have come from out wide (24th among 106 wide receivers), and he has averaged 13.1 air yards per target (17th). Some easier targets from the slot and in motion would be welcome for a player whose superpower in college was route running.

 The Cardinals' quarterback play figures to be rough this season, but hits on Love and Harrison could give Arizona such a deluge of playmakers that its offense remains dangerous even with below-average quarterback play. And if they end up investing by drafting a quarterback high in 2027, a Harrison breakout would make the bedrock for that quarterback's development all the richer.

 
 
 

 

 Los Angeles Rams : LB Nate Landman 
 The Rams' defense will be elite with Myles Garrett , Aaron Donald , Kobie Turner and Byron Young up front and Trent McDuffie , Jaylen Watson , Kam Curl and Quentin Lake in the secondary. These are good players at key positions with a few elite players to boot. I believe in this group immensely.

 But if something goes wrong, the linebacker spot feels like the culprit. I expect the Rams to play a ton of dime personnel and other one-linebacker packages as they strive to get their best 11 on the field. They feel great about Landman, whom they signed to a one-year deal in March 2025 and gave a three-year extension eight months later after he quickly developed into a starting linebacker. Sometimes, those breakouts work great ( Zack Baun ). Sometimes, they can be total fool's gold.

 In an effort to hide from the Rams' pass rush and avoid their new cornerbacks room, I expect offenses to get the ball out quickly to backs and tight ends -- a passing attack that will challenge Landman in coverage and force him to tackle in space. Another avenue to attack this loaded Rams' defense: get in heavy personnel and run the air out of the ball. Again, Landman will be the first line of defense for finding run stops and TFLs to give his pass rush opportunities to shine.

 I'm a Landman believer. But if 2025 was a magical season whose heights cannot be recaptured, opposing offenses will quickly put him under the microscope as the one Achilles' heel on the Rams' defense.

 

 
 

 San Francisco 49ers : WR Mike Evans 
 I loved the Evans signing. Getting Kyle Shanahan the type of receiver he had lacked since becoming the head coach of the 49ers -- a big, long, downfield ball-winner, short-yardage specialist and red zone mismatch -- opened new and exciting possibilities in the offense. Evans is also much better on the classic 49ers routes than he's given credit for. Among all receivers over the past two seasons, Evans is third in yards per route run (6.1) on deep, in-breaking routes. His 6-foot-5, 230-pound frame is hard to miss in the middle of the field.

 But Evans is 33 years old, so managing his snaps is important. Once Ricky Pearsall was ruled out for the season because of a right UCL tear, I was worried Evans would take too many snaps this season, especially coming off a hamstring injury in 2025. And then Evans started to miss time in camp: a quad strain in late July, then some talk about groin issues. Worrisome drumbeats for an older receiver in August.

 I still really like the blend of skills in a 49ers receivers room featuring Evans, rookie De'Zhaun Stribling , and veterans Deebo Samuel Sr . and Demarcus Robinson . But if Evans cannot stay on the field or is absent of twitch when he's on it, there's not enough downfield playmaking in the group (unless Stribling is the Offensive Rookie of the Year). The floor for any Shanahan-led offense is very high, but the ceiling this year is set by Evans.

 

 
 

 Seattle Seahawks : S  Ty Okada 
 The Seahawks' stars in the defensive backfield -- cornerback Devon Witherspoon and safeties Nick Emmanwori and Julian Love -- are well-known. The key departures of cornerback Riq Woolen (Eagles) and safety Coby Bryant (Bears) challenge their depth, especially when lighter personnel such as dime is needed. The plan was for their second-round pick, safety Bud Clark , to replace Bryant in the starting lineup, but Clark suffered a broken right ankle in the second preseason game and is out for the season.

 One of the young players who must rise to fill the accumulating voids is Okada, the fourth-year safety out of Montana State. An undrafted free agent who worked his way up the depth chart, Okada had to start multiple stretches last season when Love and Bryant went down because of injury. He proved effective at…
