title: An Eagles Q&A: Is Hurts acclimating? Will Lemon contribute?
summary: There is no shortage of storylines surrounding the Eagles as they ready for an intrigue-filled 2026 season.
full_text:
There is no shortage of storylines surrounding the Philadelphia Eagles as they ready for an intrigue-filled 2026 season.

 From Jalen Hurts and a new-look offense to expectations for rookie wide receiver Makai Lemon , there are plenty of questions for a team that finished 11-6, atop the NFC East before losing in the wild-card round to the 49ers.

 Let's examine a few key subplots with the opener versus the Washington Commanders on Sept. 13 ( 4:25 p.m. ET, Fox ) rapidly approaching.

 

 

 How is Jalen Hurts acclimating to the new offense? 

 The feedback internally has been positive. For all the discussion about the number of coordinators Hurts has worked with, the scheme has largely remained the same in the Hurts/Nick Sirianni era. The West Coast-style system being implemented by Sean Mannion , though, is a significant departure from how they've operated in the past. It's a heavy under-center operation. Hurts will often have his back to the defense when executing play-action instead of the more panoramic view from shotgun.

 Passing game coordinator Josh Grizzard described a timing-based aerial attack which requires Hurts to have consistent footwork and trust in his pass catchers to be at the right place at the right time.

 "I think it's the commitment from the whole group," Grizzard said on what has impressed him most about the passing offense so far.

 "I think what you saw from the spring and where we're at right now, with everybody's understanding of the spacing of the field and the attention to fundamentals and details has really come a long way."

 There's going to be growing pains, no doubt. We witnessed some of that during the summer. Hurts threw double-digit interceptions during training camp -- much more than we're accustomed to seeing from him. Some of those fell on the receivers, some can be chalked up to a lack of synchronization in a new scheme, and some were on the QB. It's worth noting Hurts is making more over-the-middle throws in this offense and he got burned a handful of times while doing so.

 The real test for Hurts' commitment to this style of play will come during the regular season when the inevitable bumps in the road hit. The consensus to this point is he is bought in and fighting hard through the learning curve.  

 

 Is Makai Lemon ready to contribute? 

 Expectations should be tempered early.

 First-round picks always garner attention, and the interest was even higher around Lemon given A.J. Brown 's departure this offseason. But thoughts of him making a major impact out of the gate cooled as he missed minicamp and a good chunk of training camp with a hamstring injury.

 

 Lemon acknowledged it was the same hamstring giving him issues in the spring and summer. He raised some curiosity when he said he needed to be "more professional off the field" when speaking on the injury. Receivers coach Aaron Moorehead interpreted that as Lemon believing he needed to be "proactive with his pre-hab and his rehab and his stretching and all the things he needs to before practice, and come early."

 "I basically told him, 'Whatever Smitty [ DeVonta Smith ] does, you do.' And he's taken to that a little bit," Moorehead said.

 The coaches say Lemon attacked the mental part of the game with high intensity as he waited to get healthy. There's no substitution for on-field experience, however, and it will likely take a while for Lemon to fully get the timing of this offense down. He was able to play in only one preseason game and it didn't go particularly well, as he finished with three catches for 3 yards and had a pass glance off his hands that led to an interception.

 Lemon is expected to get playing time right off the bat but it's more likely that Smith and Dontayvion Wicks receive the bulk of targets while the rookie gets his footing.

 

 What has been the biggest under-the-radar development? 

 The emergence of offensive line depth.

 "If any of you would've given me a truth serum and said, 'What are you looking for in training camp?' it would be how our interior offensive line depth panned out," general manager Howie Roseman said recently.

 It was a natural place to have your eye trained. Left guard Landon Dickerson and center Cam Jurgens spent the bulk of last season battling through injuries that clearly impacted their play. And there wasn't much proven talent behind them entering the offseason.

 Second-year guard/centers Willie Lampkin and Drew Kendall shined during training camp, however, and rookie guard Micah Morris , selected in the sixth round out of Georgia, impressed as well.

 The team's third-round pick, tackle Markel Bell , appears to have earned the role of swing tackle and could be the eventual replacement for Lane Johnson at right tackle.

 It's no secret the success of the Eagles has largely been predicated on their line play, and there's a sense of relief that the well appears full. It also reflects kindly on new offensive line coach Chris Kuper, who has had the daunting task of replacing one of the greats in Jeff Stoutland.

 

 Is the defense prepared to carry this team early if need be? 

 No question. This group has top-3 potential.

 There are All-Pro caliber players at every level, from defensive tackle Jalen Carter up front to linebacker Zack Baun in the middle to corners Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean in the back end. The addition of CB Riq Woolen , who has flashed his playmaking abilities a bunch this offseason since coming over from Seattle, could help make this one of the best secondaries in football.

 Not everything has gone right for the defense. Edge Jonathan Greenard , the Eagles' big offseason acquisition/ Jaelan Phillips replacement, injured his pec and missed all of training camp. They'll need Jalyx Hunt to keep the momentum from his red-hot summer going to help fuel the pass rush as Greenard heals and gets back up to speed.

 He'll have help from Nolan Smith Jr. and an interior line trio of Carter, Jordan Davis and Moro Ojomo that's as good as any in the NFL.

 Philly is loaded on the defensive side of the ball -- a luxury that, at a minimum, should keep the Eagles in every game.

title: What the new Seahawks owners can learn from the Allens' legacy
summary: The Khoslas are now officially the new owners of the Seahawks. And the previous team owners -- Paul and Jody Allen -- can be a blueprint for success.
full_text:
SEATTLE -- It's one of Matt Hasselbeck's favorite memories from his 10-year run as the  Seattle Seahawks ' quarterback, and it still gives him the feels more than two decades later.

 "I'm getting goosebumps now," he said while recalling the moment in a phone interview with ESPN last month.

 It was January of 2006, as the Seahawks were about to take the field for the NFC Championship Game against the Carolina Panthers at what was then called Qwest Field. No one knew ahead of time who had been selected to raise the 12 Flag, which happens right before kickoff of every Seattle home game.

 After Carrie Underwood performed the national anthem, Hasselbeck heard the familiar orchestral music that signals the start of the ceremony. He looked high above the south end zone to see who was doing the honors.

 It was the team's owner and literal savior, Paul Allen.

 "When they played that song and then he comes on and he was fired up, that was like ... let's go!" Hasselbeck said. "And then the crowd reaction to it, raising the flag and his reaction, it was really awesome. It was an incredible thing."

 The scene hit as hard as it did for Hasselbeck and the packed stadium largely because of what Allen meant to Seattle, having rescued the Seahawks from a near-relocation to Southern California when he bought the team in 1997 from former owner Ken Behring. But also because it was a rare case of Allen stepping into a spotlight that he mostly avoided. His sister, Jody Allen, shunned attention even more when she took control of the team in the wake of his death in 2018.

 The Allen family's tenure as the Seahawks owners ended Thursday with the closing of the franchise's $9.612 billion  sale to a group led by Sun Microsoft co-founder and venture capitalist Vinod Khosla. The proceeds are being donated to charity in accordance with Paul Allen's wishes, a colossal act of philanthropy that will be part of the family's legacy as Seahawks owners, along with saving professional football in Seattle -- and winning.

 

 Over the past 29 years under the Allens, the Seahawks reached the Super Bowl four times, won it twice and made the playoffs 17 times. Their 268 regular-season wins in that span are fifth most in the NFL.

 Khosla will bring to his new role the expertise that made him a titan of the tech and venture capital worlds. But the Khosla family -- with Vinod serving as chair, wife Neeru as controlling owner and their son Neil as vice chair -- would do well to follow the script that was laid out during one of the NFL's most successful ownership tenures: trust your decision-makers and supply them with the resources they need to win.

 "We are honored to be entrusted as the next stewards of the Seattle Seahawks," Vinod Khosla said in July when the deal was reached. "We look forward to building on the winning legacy Paul Allen created and to earning the trust of the Seahawks organization and fans everywhere."

 What can the Khoslas learn from their predecessors?

 "I think just how to walk that really, really difficult line that sometimes owners have of ... really empowering your people to win, of really making sure that you're in the role you're in of engaging them and growing them and developing them, but not making it about yourself," said Brock Huard, who played quarterback (1999-2001, 2004) for the Seahawks under Paul Allen and began co-hosting a radio show on Seattle Sports 710-AM in 2009.

 "That's what Paul and Jody and their teams did. They never made it about Paul and Jody. They made it about the players and the coaches and the championships, while all the while pushing and demanding to never stand pat."

 
 PAUL ALLEN RARELY attended league meetings with his fellow owners -- Jody Allen sometimes skipped them as well -- but when the Microsoft co-founder would show up, his presence was felt.

 "There's always somebody that's a little richer, a little more powerful, had a little more going for him than you do ... Paul Allen was that guy," said Steve Raible, an original Seahawks receiver and the team's long-time radio voice.

 The Seahawks became a first-class organization during Paul Allen's ownership tenure and remained one under his sister in part because of their willingness to spend their immense wealth and arm the organization with resources.

 In 1999, Paul Allen cut the check for an eight-year, $32 million contract that pried Mike Holmgren from the  Green Bay Packers , which made him the league's highest-paid head coach with an annual average that doubled what he was making. Allen went big-name hunting again in 2010, luring Pete Carroll away from USC with another huge-for-the-time deal -- a reported $35 million over seven years.

 Hasselbeck recalls one year under Holmgren in which the team traveled in "two of the most ridiculous airplanes of all time."

 "They were so nice," he said. "The bathroom near my seat was nicer than the powder room in my house -- and bigger."

 

 Allen's purse strings were never an issue when it came to enticing free agents to come to Seattle. But the city's remoteness at one point was a factor. That started to change in 2007, when he began building a new 200,000-square-foot training facility on the shores of Lake Washington. The Virginia Mason Athletic Center, with its state-of-the-art amenities and picturesque setting, helped turn the Seahawks from an NFL outpost to a destination. Allen spent $60 million to build it in 2007, not counting the prior costs to buy and decontaminate the land.

 This year, the Seahawks ranked fourth on the NFLPA report cards , with high marks for everything but Lumen Field's artificial turf. They received their second straight A-minus in the team travel category after C grades in 2023 and 2024.

 What changed? Jody Allen splurging for a new team charter -- a Boeing 747 equipped with enough lie-flat seats for every player on the 53-man roster.

 It was in keeping with the Allens' willingness to spend money and a question they would often ask in pursuit of winning: "What do you need?" The Seahawks have paid off the investment by going an NFL-best 15-2 on the road over coach Mike Macdonald's two seasons.

 The organization received an A-minus this year for the VMAC's training room, which underwent a significant renovation in 2025 after players voiced concerns via the survey. The Seahawks have made plans to further expand their headquarters in the coming years, something that will now be overseen by the Khoslas.

 "[They're] committed at that facility to chase edges, to give them every edge imaginable," Huard said of the franchise under the Allens, "whether that's mentally, whether that's physically, whether that's emotionally, whether that's the commitment to science technology and development ... to constantly push the edge, constantly push the evolution off 'How can we do this better?' That takes resources many times, and I don't think that there was ever hardly a 'no.'"

 The Khoslas will face significant investment decisions in the coming years. Super Bowl-winning quarterback Sam Darnold will be eligible next offseason for an extension that could be worth well over $50 million per year in new money. The NFLPA has been lobbying for grass playing surfaces in every NFL stadium, and the union made another push this summer when several World Cup venues -- including Lumen Field -- temporarily installed it per FIFA requirements.

 When asked on X in early August about possibly switching to grass for good, Vinod Khosla  responded : "I'd defer to people at the @seahawks who know better than me. The team that got us the Super Bowl."

 
 THE ALLENS WERE rarely heard from publicly, but they were more involved than many assumed based on the low profiles they both kept.

 In 2017, as the Seahawks were coming off a 10-5-1 season in which they finished first in the NFC West, they made a curious addition to the organization. Former Cleveland Browns head coach Mike Pettine wasn't hired to be part of Carroll's…

title: Why Bucs' Mayfield has 'extra motivation' heading into season
summary: The self-imposed deadline has passed for Tampa Bay's quarterback as he now turns his attention to the season.
full_text:
TAMPA, Fla. -- When it comes to playing with a chip on his shoulder and betting on himself, Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield isn't kidding when he says, "That's something I'm pretty familiar with."

 Throughout his career, Mayfield has shown both a willingness to fight and prove doubters wrong, but also that his tolerance for what he perceives as disrespect does have its limits. Are the Bucs testing them by having him play out the final year of his deal ? Or will they get the most out of a player who "wants his lick back" in 2026?

 He didn't get the contract extension he wanted by his self-imposed training camp deadline this summer, and sources say there haven't been any talks since the Bucs' last offer on July 30.

 Mayfield said once his deadline expired that he didn't want to have further discussions until the offseason, and he told his agent, Tom Mills, not to bother him unless he's "actually recognized" for his value.

 

 The Bucs have been vocal about not wanting Mayfield to leave , with general manager Jason Licht saying last week during a preseason game broadcast, "I'm very optimistic about it."

 "He wants to play," Licht said. "He wants to prove to us that he is the franchise quarterback that we said that he was.

 "So, we'll just have to see how it plays out. I'll never close the door on anything in the short term, but right now, he's focused on football."

 And then perhaps revealing the volatile nature of these situations, Licht gave a more measured response four days later.

 "Well, we certainly respect him wanting to focus on the season," Licht said. "We're focused on the season. I've been here long enough [over 12 years] to know that in this league, I don't want to make predictions on what could happen, what will happen, what won't happen."

 Despite the distractions that might come with all of this, Mayfield's teammates have had his back.

 "I expect Baker to be Baker, and I expect him to lead us like he always does and I expect him to bring the best out of us," left tackle Tristan Wirfs said. "I think he's gonna play with his hair on fire."

 

 

 STRAIGHT FROM LUBBOCK, Texas -- following Texas Tech's 41-16 season finale loss to Texas in 2013 -- Mayfield drove his Chevy Tahoe to Austin, right up to the back door of his Lake Travis High School football coach Hank Carter's home for a surprise visit.

 Moments before, Carter had been on the phone with a coaching pal at Texas Tech -- where Mayfield had become the first true freshman walk-on quarterback to start a season opener for a BCS school -- and told him, "Hey man, y'all are screwing this up. Why hasn't he been put on scholarship yet?"

 Speaking to ESPN, Carter recounted the moment when Mayfield took a seat in his office at his home that day. Not only had Mayfield started seven games for the Red Raiders and accounted for 15 touchdowns and not been put on scholarship, but he was informed that they did not have one available for him that spring and couldn't give him one until something opened up.

 And he was informed that coach Kliff Kingsbury was opening up the quarterback job for competition, which didn't sit well.

 

 Carter asked, "Well, what do you think you're going to do?"

 Carter said Mayfield responded, "'What am I going to do?' He goes, "I've got all my s--- packed in my car right now. I'm out. I already left."

 Carter's response? "Oh my god."

 Mayfield delivered the news to Kingsbury on Dec. 10. The following day, when it was announced that he'd won the Big 12 Freshman Offensive Player of the Year award, he made his departure public.

 Mayfield and Carter picked up the conversation a few days later. Carter offered to help him find another school. But Mayfield had already made up his mind.

 "I think I'm going to go to [Oklahoma]," Mayfield said.

 He publicly declared his intentions to enroll there on Dec. 19, and on Jan. 3, the Sooners defeated Alabama 45-31 in the Sugar Bowl, with freshman Trevor Knight at quarterback.

 "I go, 'Bake, this quarterback just hung 40 points on Nick Saban,"' Carter said. "I was like, 'Are you sure?'"

 Mayfield told him, "Coach, I know that guy. He's a great guy," Carter said. "But then he said, 'I'll beat him out. I'll beat him out. I've wanted to go there my whole life. That's always been the school we rooted for.'

 "He was just like, 'Screw it, I'm going,'" Carter said. "And I did not think that was the best decision, but I was wrong. He obviously knew exactly what he was doing. ... And yeah, the rest is history."

 A Heisman Trophy, first-overall selection in the 2018 draft and three playoff appearances later, Mayfield finds himself in a situation to prove himself once again with the Bucs, who did not meet his July 28 deadline for a new contract. Instead, he'll play out the remainder of his contract, which ends after the season, and let the chips fall where they may in the offseason.

 According to Mayfield, "Sometimes you have to put yourself backed into a corner and fight your way out."

 And that's where he stands heading into the season with the Bucs, hoping to lead Tampa back into the playoffs after falling short last year.

 "His mentality is that underdog mentality he's had since I'm sure he was 8 years old starting to play football," Tampa Bay offensive coordinator Zac Robinson said. "That'll never leave that guy, and it's a good thing.

 "He believes in himself. Whether other people believe in him too, he really doesn't care."

 

 

 MAYFIELD ASSEMBLED THE team before the Bucs' first camp practice and briefed them on his contract situation, emphasizing that it would not be a distraction and his focus was strictly on them and football. His teammates said the message was heartfelt and well-received.

 "I'd say just how committed he is," right guard Cody Mauch said. "I mean, he set a deadline. He said his deadline's the beginning of training camp and he's sticking to it. And now he's like, 'I promise I'm all about ball.'

 "It sucks to see him go through this and whatnot, but it's not going to change his mentality, the way he plays. I mean, he's going to go ball out and it's going to get made right."

 Wide receiver Tez Johnson said Mayfield has been "true to his word" and "we trust him and we love him."

 "When he said it's all ball for us, it was strictly all ball," Johnson said. "He's so eager to just go out there and just prove to the world that he belongs, and he deserves to be in that talk with the quarterbacks."

 Nose tackle Vita Vea who had his own contract dispute that was ultimately resolved with a new deal on Aug. 19, empathized with Mayfield's frustration. While Vea was holding in -- attending practices but not participating -- Mayfield used his media availability to not only express frustrations about his own deal but to advocate for Vea's re-signing.

 "Baker is the heart and soul of this team," Vea said. "You see the energy he brings on game day. We feed off of that too, not only the offense.

 "I hope things get figured out with him. I know we'd all love to have him. Everybody loves Baker. That's somebody that you wish to have on your side on game day."

 Mayfield spent the summer working to master Robinson's offense -- his fourth in four seasons in Tampa, although it has strong similarities to the one he operated under Liam Coen in 2024. He's also worked on some of the issues he felt he fell short in last year, like his rhythm and needing to tighten up his footwork.

 "If you're out of rhythm in this system -- whether it's timing of the routes and the concepts -- bad things are going to happen," Mayfield said. "It starts with my feet and going through that and trusting the timing of that and going through the progressions, checking the ball down."

 Quarterbacks coach Chandler Whitmer, who spent last season tutoring Heisman Trophy winner Fernando Mendoza en route to a national championship at Indiana, has been a stickler for footwork, to the point that Mayfield has joked that he wants…

title: Inside Commanders DC Daronte Jones' unusual coaching journey
summary: From living in his car to various college offices, Washington defensive coordinator Daronte Jones has paid his dues.
full_text:
ASHBURN, Va. -- The gale-force Chicago wind shook Daronte Jones' car and rattled his nerves. It did not blow the future  Washington Commanders  defensive coordinator off his path, but it made him question his life choices.

 It was March 2002, nearly three weeks after Jones landed a job at Division III North Park University on the city's northwest side, and he was sleeping in a red 1988 Honda Prelude.

 He endured a night that ended up steeling his resolve as winds reached 50 mph. At around 11 p.m., he called his aunt Lisa Simmons in Maryland.

 "She picked up thinking it was an emergency, which it really wasn't, but it could have been, mentally," Jones said. "The car was rocking side to side.

 "I remember calling home and naturally the family was like, 'Just come home. What are we doing?' That was a moment where you really had to think about how much you're willing to sacrifice, and is it worth it?"

 Jones didn't go home.

 That was the first decision in a long list of sacrifices the first-time NFL defensive coordinator had to make early in his coaching career. He lived out of his car for two months in Chicago. Then, in 2010, while a grad assistant at UCLA, he slept in the cornerbacks' meeting room for most of his year with the Bruins. Two years after that, as a University of Hawaii assistant, he slept in his office for a year before moving into an alumnus' pool house.

 Along his journey -- often with his pet python, Goldie Gambino, living in his book bag -- he also coached high school for two years and nearly left the profession twice -- attending law school at one point, and applying to the U.S. Capitol Police at another in hopes of becoming a Federal Air Marshal. However, like on that frigid night in the Windy City, he always resolved to stick it out.

 "It was like, 'Is it ever going to end?'" Jones told ESPN. "I was like, 'Maybe it's not for me.'"

 The big breaks finally came, which have led Jones, who is a native of Anne Arundel County in Maryland, to Washington, where he has been entrusted with improving a defense that was arguably the worst in the NFL last season. His background could be a good match for the task ahead.

 A turbulent start to his career helped him develop a deep appreciation for future opportunities -- and for finally reaching this point in his career. It taught him patience; it taught him humility.

 "It's very easy to see when someone has been through it to get to where they're at," safety Jeremy Reaves said. "He went the route not a lot of people go for. How he is on the field is what you'd expect: the sense of urgency. He understands what an opportunity means. He understands opportunities are few and far between, so when you get one, you have to take advantage."

 

 

 BEFORE ARRIVING IN  Washington, Jones had held 14 different jobs during his coaching career, from Division II to Division I-AA, high school, the Canadian Football League to multiple Division I stops and stints with three NFL teams.

 But one of the most formative roles isn't included on his résumé: North Park University.

 Jones spent six months at the tiny school in 2002, but left before coaching a game.

 When he arrived at North Park as a defensive assistant, Jones, fresh off a graduate assistant role at Lenoir-Rhyne University in Hickory, North Carolina, was told he could sleep on a couch in an apartment with other coaches. Jones didn't trust the couch, which, he said, had looked like it had been pulled off the street -- so he slept in his Prelude.

 He spent his first two months at the school sleeping in the car. He kept a suitcase in his locker but other clothes in the Honda -- along with his nearly 3-foot pet Albino Burmese python. Jones said he would park his car near the facility in a different spot each night. On cold nights, he said he'd crack the windows for airflow, turn on the heat and try to stay warm.

 Simmons often lent him money when she could. But she said Jones told her, "'I'll just work it out; I'll stay in the car.' He said, 'All I need you to do is call me and wake me up.' So I would get up early and call him, 'Daronte, it's time to get up.' We really wanted things to work out for him, and he was willing to make the sacrifice. We would support him the best we could."

 Simmons never wavered. Every morning at 4 a.m., Jones would receive a call from his aunt, then head to the facility to shower before others arrived.

 Throughout this time, Jones said he had been telling the other coaches on staff he was living in a hotel. When some found out he wasn't, they offered him the pantry in their apartment, which was on the porch and attached to the kitchen with screens that needed fixing. Jones said the room was full of boxes and was so narrow, his double mattress couldn't lie flat -- it was curled on the outside because it wouldn't fit.

 His grandfather told him how to fix and seal the screens, and Jones bought a space heater to keep him and Goldie Gambino comfortable. "I'd sleep in jeans, sweats, a hoodie, leather jacket to stay warm," Jones said. "But it was better than the car."

 Four months later, he accepted a restricted earnings job at Nicholls State. Though the opportunity at North Park might have seemed to be a waste, having never coached a game for the Vikings, the sacrifices Jones made in Chicago became a key theme throughout the rest of his journey.

 

 

 JONES NEARLY DROPPED out of coaching -- twice.

 The first time occurred in 2004 when he was 25 and coaching defense at Jeanerette High School in New Iberia, Louisiana. It was his first year at Jeanerette but second year coaching high school in Louisiana. Jones had given himself a deadline: become a college Division 1 position coach by age 26 or quit.

 He took the LSAT with plans to attend Southern University's law school with an Omega Psi Phi fraternity brother. Then, Mike Lynn, who was Jones' former position coach at Morgan State, where he played offensive line, became the head coach at Bowie State. Their connection led to a job offer. But Jones said he wasn't sure that he wanted to accept. He could continue teaching in high school, then attend law school classes at night.

 Zeb Simon, Jones' boss at Jeanerette, told him it was a no-brainer and issued him an ultimatum.

 "I'm going to give you a choice," Simon said. "Either you go or I'm going to fire you.'"

 Jones went.

 "It took me about a couple weeks to make that decision," he said.

 

 Five seasons into his stint with the Bulldogs as assistant head coach and defensive coordinator -- the last of which saw his defense ranked No. 1 in Division II -- Jones reached another crossroads. The move to Division I wasn't happening. So, after the 2009 season, he applied for a job with the U.S. Capitol Police, hoping to become a Federal Air Marshal. He had received an offer, and they were in the process of doing a background check when UCLA called.

 "Maybe it's time for me to look at something else because now I'm in my 30s, and I was like: 'I've got to do something,'" Jones said he was thinking at the time.

 The Bruins offered him a graduate assistant's job. It meant going from a salary of $64,000 a year to $1,000 per month while living in the Los Angeles area. He first consulted Damon Wilson, his boss in 2009 at Bowie State, about the UCLA opportunity. But it was longtime advisor Lional Vital, who spent part of four seasons in the NFL and also served as a scout and executive for 30 years, who convinced him.

 "You've already been homeless," Vital told him.

 Unable to afford the cost of living in Southern California, Jones made his "home" in the UCLA cornerbacks' meeting room, where he spent most of the year sleeping on an air mattress alongside another graduate assistant, Chris Polizzi -- now Iowa's special teams coordinator -- who slept on a futon. The arrangement disappointed Wilson.
